title: Helfgott meet-in-the-middle: an explicit 'all p > X' theorem for any ES sub-route with X ≤ 10¹⁸
connection: Ternary Goldbach became 'every n' only when the analytic threshold dropped below the numerical verification horizon (8.875·10³⁰). ES is verified to 10¹⁸; any effective all-large-p statement for (★), b=1, ES₅ or Type II with p₀ ≤ 10¹⁸ closes ES.
why: Turns the goal from 'prove for all p' into 'make some asymptotic statement effective with a concrete constant', which is how Vinogradov→Helfgott actually moved.
first_step: Make a table: every asymptotic/conditional ES statement in FRONTIER §2.4/§5 (H⁻_BM, Thm 2.2, ES₅ Thm 3.5) with the explicit p₀ it would need and the explicit constants it currently lacks.

title: Explicit Burgess constants (Treviño-type) for the Legendre-sum T(p) in M_BM
connection: Helfgott needed fully explicit major arcs; the ES analogue is an explicit version of Thm 2.2 (M_BM(p) ≥ (3/16π² − o(1)) log²p), whose o(1) comes from Burgess on Σ(−m/p)w(m).
why: An explicit M_BM ≥ c·log²p for all p ≥ p₁ is a prerequisite of every H⁻_BM-type route and is purely a bookkeeping task with existing explicit Burgess inequalities.
first_step: Treviño, 'The Burgess inequality and the least kth power non-residue', IJNT 11 (2015) 1653–1678, arXiv:1412.3062 gives explicit Burgess estimates (verified, data/z52b/upgrades_leads_check.md); check that its ranges cover the weighted hyperbolic sum T(p) and compute the resulting explicit p₁.

title: Smoothing as a decisive ingredient: smooth weights on (u,B,C) for a weighted R_w(p)
connection: Helfgott's minor arcs only closed after choosing smoothing functions optimally. ES: replace R(p) by R_w(p) = Σ w(u,B,C)1[4uBC−u−B=p] with smooth nonnegative w; R_w(p) > 0 ⇒ ES(p).
why: Error terms in Poisson/Voronoi-based treatments of R(p) depend heavily on sharp cut-offs of the hyperbolic region; smoothing is free for a positivity statement.
first_step: Numerically compare Var_p(R_w(p)/M_w(p)) over primes near 10⁷ for sharp vs. Gaussian/Beurling–Selberg weights; pick the weight minimising the left tail.

title: Vinogradov bilinear decomposition of the (★) count
connection: Vinogradov's Type I/II bilinear sums made ternary Goldbach unconditional. R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 (4C)} is a sum over factorizations ab = 4Cp+1; split by the sizes of a, b, C into 'Type I' (one factor short: congruence sums in C) and 'Type II' (both medium: bilinear forms in (a,b)).
why: Gives a structured place where cancellation must be found; the Type I part may be treatable pointwise in p by elementary counting.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_{a,b} α_a β_b 1[ab ≡ 1 mod 4C, ab = 4Cp+1] with dyadic ranges; compute numerically which range carries the solutions for p ~ 10⁸–10¹⁰.

title: Sparsity index: why binary Goldbach is stuck and ES is worse
connection: Binary Goldbach has a main term n/log²n among ~n terms and never got pointwise; ES has main term ≍ log²p among ≍ p log p 'trial events' (PARITY_AUDIT trial form).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from any problem ever upgraded; directs search to reformulations with denser events (fewer trials, larger main term).
first_step: Define sparsity = log(main term)/log(#trials) for each ES reformulation (★, b=1, ES₅, e-slice, I3 words) and tabulate; look for the least sparse one.

title: Montgomery–Vaughan power-saving exceptional set for ES or (★)
connection: MV proved E_Goldbach(N) ≪ N^{1−δ} by large sieve + zero density + Siegel-zero analysis; ES has only E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) and 3/4 is sharp for CRT sieves (EXCEPTIONAL_KARY3).
why: A power-saving exceptional set would need exactly the non-CRT input the campaign identified (residue-dense large sieve); MV is a model of how that input looked for Goldbach.
first_step: Read MV §§3–6 and identify the step that becomes 'large sieve over moduli 4uB with p in the variable'; check whether the ES analogue of their Siegel-zero case analysis is available.

title: Goldbach exceptions are tied to one exceptional character — are ES/(★) failures tied to a character?
connection: In MV the only way to have many Goldbach exceptions is a Siegel zero. Analogue: (★)-failures (14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) and b=1 failures (193, 2521, 66529) might share an extreme value of a single character statistic (e.g. least non-residue ℓ(p), or L(1, (·/p))).
why: If failures of sub-routes are 'explained' by one character, a Deuring–Heilbronn-type dichotomy becomes plausible.
first_step: For the 17 known sub-route failures and random controls compute ℓ(p), Σ_{m≤100}(m/p)/m, L(1,(·/p)) and the class number of Q(√p); compare ranks.

title: Chen switching for ES: Type I ↔ Type II role switch to upper-bound 'near misses'
connection: Chen bounded the bad P₃ contribution by sieving the switched set. ES: a 'near miss' at level C is a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a wrong class; switching d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d and C ↔ another parametrisation (Type I ↔ Type II) may convert hard lower bounds into upper bounds of a switched count.
why: Lower bound = (computable total) − (upper-bounded bad part) is the only robust way sieves get existence.
first_step: List all involutions/bijections between ES certificate sets (Type I/II, (★)↔b=1, level switching) and check whether any maps near-misses of one family to near-misses with a computable total in another.

title: Almost-prime levels: choose C with 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂ (two primes) and study the class of q₁ mod 4C
connection: Chen-type results produce almost-primes in linear sequences. If 4Cp+1 = q₁q₂, the certificate condition at level C is q₁ ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a single-prime class condition.
why: Reduces a divisor-class problem to an equidistribution question for prime factors of almost-primes in a progression, a better-studied object.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ measure: fraction of C with 4Cp+1 = P₂, and the rate at which a factor hits −1 mod 4C versus the model 2/φ(4C).

title: Schnirelmann/Mann in the space of fractions: ES as U + (U+U) ∋ 4/n
connection: Schnirelmann turned a positive density for P+P into 'every n'. ES asks 4/n ∈ U+U+U (U = unit fractions). Translate to: 4/n − U meets U+U, and look for Mann-type sumset theorems for sets of rationals with structured denominators.
why: 4-term ES is trivial (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)) and 3/m always splits into ≤ 3 terms), so the problem is exactly the 'order 3 vs order 4' gap of a basis — a classical additive-combinatorics shape.
first_step: Formalize U+U as {a/b : b has a divisor pair (d,e) with d+e ≡ 0 mod a}; study the measure/density of 4/n − U ∩ (U+U) for n in a dyadic range.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706
upgrade: Schnirelmann constant (Goldbach-type every n with bounded number of primes)

title: Diophantine approximation spectrum of 4/p by three unit fractions
connection: Schnirelmann-type arguments start from approximate representations. Define δ(p) = min_{x,y,z} |4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z| over x,y,z ≤ p^A; ES(p) ⟺ δ(p) = 0. Study the gap structure of the set of values near 4/p.
why: If near-solutions are abundant at scale p^{−k} and the set of 3-term sums has a 'no isolated gap' property near 4/p, existence might follow by a continuity/pigeonhole step.
first_step: Compute the k smallest nonzero |4/p − Σ| for p ≤ 10⁵ and look for universal patterns in the residual numerators.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706
upgrade: Schnirelmann constant (Goldbach-type every n with bounded number of primes)

title: Powers-of-two slice: ES solutions with x = 2^k
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used the lacunary set of powers of 2. ES slice: 4/p = 1/2^k + 1/y + 1/z needs (2^{k+2} − p)/(p·2^k) to split into two unit fractions; e.g. via the divisor p it needs (2^{k+2} − p) | (2^i + 1) for some i ≤ k+2.
why: A lacunary, explicit family of candidate first denominators with rich multiplicative structure (2^i+1 factors via cyclotomy) — the ES analogue of Linnik's 2^v.
first_step: Compute, for p ≡ 1 (mod 24) up to 10⁷, the fraction of p having an ES solution with a power-of-2 denominator and the distribution of the least k.

title: Measure of joint failure along a lacunary level sequence C ∈ {2^j}
connection: Linnik's key estimate is the small measure of α where Σ e(2^v α) is large. Analogue: the set of p failing (★) at every level C = 2^j, j ≤ J, should have density ≈ Π_j(1 − P_j); measure its correlation structure.
why: Lacunary levels give nearly independent constraints (moduli 2^{j+2} are nested though!) — quantifies how much independence nested moduli really give.
first_step: Compute failure indicators at C = 2^j for p ≤ 10⁸ and estimate joint failure probabilities versus the independent model.

title: Universal-form reduction: a map from representations by a universal quadratic form to ES certificates
connection: Linnik/Watson reduced 7 cubes to ternary forms; Hilbert used identities + Lagrange. Seek a quadratic form Q_p (or a fixed universal Q) and an explicit rational map Φ such that every representation Q(v) = g(p) yields an ES solution for p; universality/three-squares then proves ES.
why: Not a polynomial identity in p (so Mordell–Schinzel does not apply directly); the map may depend on the representation. Must be compatible with T1 (Type I/II fail at odd squares).
first_step: Search small Φ: take ES (★) triples (u,B,C) for many p and test whether u, B, C, or 4uC−1 are systematically sums of two/three squares with coordinates linked to p.

title: Smooth-number restriction (Vaughan–Wooley) with smooth moduli in APs (Drappeau/Harper)
connection: Smooth numbers drove progress on G(k). ES: restrict certificates to smooth (u,B) or smooth 4C, where distribution in progressions to large moduli is better (friable Bombieri–Vinogradov beyond 1/2).
why: Smooth moduli are where the strongest level-of-distribution results live; ES certificates are numerically often smooth.
first_step: Drappeau, 'Théorèmes de type Fouvry–Iwaniec pour les entiers friables', Compositio 151 (2015), arXiv:1307.7554 (verified) gives beyond-√ distribution for friable integers; check whether it applies to sums Σ_{C smooth} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)}; measure numerically the fraction of (★) solutions with y-smooth C for y = p^{0.1}.

title: g(4)=19 descent: analytic threshold + greedy reduction to the verified range
connection: BDD reduced every n below 10³⁶⁷ to the verified range by subtracting biquadrates. ES has no subtraction structure, but the e-slice form reduces ES(p) to a property of N = (p+e)/4 < p; formalize a 'descent' that moves a hard instance to a smaller one.
why: If certificate existence at p could be read off from data at N ≈ p/4 that is itself verifiable recursively, verification scales.
first_step: Measure: for the hardest primes (DISPROOF_AVENUES list) how many e ≤ 1000 give N = (p+e)/4 with ≥ k divisors; is there always an e with N highly composite?

title: Ternary-form reduction with Duke–Schulze-Pillot as the closing theorem
connection: Linnik's 7 cubes: identity reduces the problem to n − (cubes) being represented by a ternary quadratic form in an AP, closed by ternary-form theory. ES: find an ES-certificate family equivalent to 'some N(p) is primitively represented by a positive ternary form in a fixed genus'.
why: DSP gives every sufficiently large n in the spinor genus (ineffectively) — an 'all large p' ES theorem even if ineffective would be new.
first_step: Search the (★)/b=1/ES₅ certificate shapes for a sum-of-three-squares interpretation (e.g. 4Cp+1 = d d' with d = x²+y²+z²-type constraint); test on data.
refs: Watson, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951) 153-156 (A simple proof that all large integers are sums of at most seven cubes)
upgrade: Linnik: every large n is a sum of 7 cubes

title: Divisor counts in a class as coset theta series of the split form xy
connection: Watson's trick works with sums of squares in arithmetic progressions (coset theta series). D_t^−(N) = #{xy = N, x ≡ −1 (t)} is a representation number of the indefinite binary form xy on a lattice coset.
why: Puts ES level counts into the language of (indefinite) lattice cosets where theta-lifts and Siegel–Weil apply; METAPLECTIC_ES already gives the generating function.
first_step: Write Σ_N D_t^−(N)q^N as a coset theta series of xy and compare with METAPLECTIC_ES Thm K; then try a theta lift to a ternary/quaternary positive form.
refs: Watson, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951) 153-156 (A simple proof that all large integers are sums of at most seven cubes)
upgrade: Linnik: every large n is a sum of 7 cubes

title: Decoupling/energy for the hyperbolic ES surface {4uBC − u − B}
connection: BDG decoupling bounds moments of exponential sums over curves. Additive energy of the ES-word set (#{w₁ = w₂} with w = 4uBC−u−B ≤ N) controls the second moment Σ_n R(n)².
why: Second-moment control is the ingredient of every almost-all → pointwise attempt via variance; decoupling-type bounds for this specific surface could be sharp.
first_step: Compute the energy E(N) = Σ_{n≤N} R(n)² for N up to 10⁷ and fit N·(log N)^a; compare with what a decoupling inequality for (u, B, uB) would predict.

title: Efficient congruencing in the level variable
connection: Wooley's method lifts solutions p-adically and compares congruence classes at several scales. ES solutions as solutions of p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) for growing 4uB: congruencing across scales of the modulus.
why: Odd but not empty: ES is literally a family of congruences whose modulus is a variable; congruencing-type iteration handles such 'modulus as variable' counts in VMVT.
first_step: Write the count of (u,B) with 4uB ≤ Q and p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB as a mean value of a Weyl-like sum and see if the efficient-congruencing recursion has an analogue.

title: Linnik dispersion for the fixed-p level sum Σ_C D(4Cp+1; −1 mod 4C)
connection: Linnik proved an asymptotic for every n of #{n = p + x² + y²} = Σ_p r₂(n − p): a pointwise result for a sum of divisor-type functions. R(p) is a sum over C of restricted divisor counts of 4Cp+1.
why: The dispersion method is one of the few techniques giving pointwise-in-n asymptotics for sums of arithmetic functions over a sparse family — exactly ES's shape, though the main term is only polylog.
first_step: Compute Disp(p) = Σ_C (D_C(p) − 2/φ(4C)·τ*(4Cp+1))² for test p and compare with M(p)²; if Disp ≪ M², a dispersion-type proof is not excluded numerically.
refs: Linnik, The dispersion method in binary additive problems (AMS 1963)

title: Divisor function in APs to a single modulus 4p as the base asymptotic
connection: Σ_{C≤X} τ(4Cp+1) is a divisor sum in the progression 1 mod 4p; asymptotics are known for X ≥ (4p)^{2/3+ε} (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown/Fouvry–Iwaniec-type). The ES count refines τ to the class d ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: Starts from a pointwise-in-p theorem that is already true, and asks for a twist by the 'self-referential' modulus 4C — a precise, new-looking question.
first_step: Write D(4Cp+1; −1 mod 4C) via additive characters mod 4C and apply Voronoi summation in C to the twisted divisor sum; identify which terms are new.
refs: Linnik, The dispersion method in binary additive problems (AMS 1963)

title: Lagrange descent on near-certificates via a composition law
connection: Lagrange got every p by producing m·p = sum of 4 squares with m < p and descending m using Euler's identity. ES needs a composition law on 'defective' certificates (defect m) that lowers |m|.
why: Descent is the oldest almost→every mechanism; ES lacks an obvious composition, but the SL₂ form (matrices [[a,p],[c,d]]) has matrix multiplication.
first_step: Define defect for SL₂-form near-certificates (e.g. congruence a ≡ −1 only mod c/m); test whether products/quotients of two near-certificates with the same defect yield smaller defect.

title: Chord–tangent operations on the ES cubic surface family
connection: Euler's identity is a composition law on norm forms. The ES surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a cubic surface; secant/tangent constructions (Manin) generate rational points from rational points.
why: Rational points are plentiful; the question is whether some composition preserves integrality or near-integrality across fibres n.
first_step: Implement the secant operation on U_n(ℚ) and measure denominators of the third point when the two inputs are integral points of nearby fibres (n, n') with n' | n·k.

title: Pigeonhole over complementary divisor sets: |Div(N₁)| + |Div(N₂)| > φ(e) forces a certificate
connection: Lagrange's lemma: the sets {x²} and {−1−y²} each have (p+1)/2 elements so they meet. ES e-slice: for a coprime split N = N₁N₂ (N = (p+e)/4), if |Div(N₁) mod e| + |Div(N₂) mod e| > φ(e), some a | N₁ and b | N₂ satisfy a ≡ −b, so −1 ∈ Rat_e(N).
why: A clean sufficient condition reducing ES to finding e with N highly composite relative to φ(e).
first_step: For p in the hard list, search e ≤ 10⁴ maximising (|Div(N₁)|+|Div(N₂)|)/φ(e) over coprime splits; report how close to 1 the best ratio gets.

title: Zagier-type involution with a unique fixed point on an ES-related finite set
connection: Zagier: a finite set with two involutions; one has exactly one fixed point ⇒ odd cardinality ⇒ the other has a fixed point = representation. ES: find a finite set S_p (defined by ES-like equations) with an involution whose fixed points are ES certificates and another with a unique fixed point.
why: Parity replaces analysis entirely; it is the only known 'proof from the Book' mechanism for an every-p existence theorem of this flavour.
first_step: Enumerate small finite sets S_p = {(a,b,c,d) ∈ ℕ⁴ : quadratic/cubic ES-like relation = p} with natural windmill-type involutions; compute |S_p| mod 2 for p ≤ 10⁴ and look for sets with provably odd size.

title: Naive parity of a level count is trivial — record the lemma and the needed asymmetry
connection: D_t^−(tp+1) is even unless tp+1 = s² with s ≡ −1 (mod t), i.e. unless p = t − 2; so parity of single-level counts carries no information (pairing d ↔ N/d). Zagier needed an asymmetric second involution.
why: Clears a trap: any parity proof needs a set where the obvious involution is broken (e.g. by a non-symmetric constraint like d < N/d with an extra condition).
first_step: Write the lemma; then search for natural subsets (e.g. d in a half-interval, or d with an extra character condition) where the count is not forced even and test its parity distribution.

title: Dedekind's Gaussian-integer proof analogue: an order where ES(p) ⟺ p is a norm
connection: Fermat two squares follows from ℤ[i] being Euclidean. Find a (possibly noncommutative) ring/order R and norm-like map such that ES certificates ↔ elements of 'norm' p with congruence side conditions; then a class-number-one/Euclidean property gives existence.
why: Quaternion orders and theta quotients already appear in the repo; the missing piece is a ring whose class number is 1 and whose norm condition matches the ES congruences.
first_step: Read the quaternion-order memos (git grep -il quaternion); compute class/type numbers of the orders arising there.

title: Thue's lemma / short vectors in lattices L_{p,λ} producing (★) triples
connection: Thue's pigeonhole gives |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ λy (mod p). Choose λ from ES structure (e.g. λ ≡ −4⁻¹ or ratios from Rat_e) and test whether short vectors produce positive (★) data.
why: Pigeonhole-in-a-box is the cheapest every-p mechanism; ES's linear congruence p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) has a modulus depending on the unknowns, so a 2-D lattice must be found for each candidate level.
first_step: For fixed C (or u), (★) says 4uC − 1 | p + u: build the lattice {(x,y) : x ≡ y·λ_C mod (something)} and check numerically whether LLL-short vectors give solutions.
upgrade: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x^2 + y^2

title: Small vector + congruence ⇒ equality, for the cubic ES polynomial (Ankeny-style)
connection: Thue/Ankeny: if F(v) ≡ 0 mod M and |F(v)| < M then F(v) = 0. For F = 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with |v| ≈ X: |F| ≈ pX² and Minkowski gives |v| ≈ M^{1/3}; the scales match when M ≳ p³, X ≈ p.
why: The scale bookkeeping does not immediately fail; the open question is whether an affine sublattice of index ~M on which F ≡ 0 (mod M) exists.
first_step: Classify affine sublattices of ℤ³ on which F vanishes mod q for primes q (e.g. the Type II slices y,z ≡ 0 mod p); see if CRT combinations of such slices reach M ≳ p³.
upgrade: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x^2 + y^2

title: Class number one in the genus: search for an ES-encoding lattice with a one-class genus
connection: Gauss's three squares: local solvability + one class in the genus of x²+y²+z² ⇒ global. ES is locally solvable everywhere (Bright–Loughran); if ES(p) ⟺ a lattice L represents an invariant of p, and gen(L) has one class (or one spinor genus), ES follows.
why: The most classical local→global mechanism; repo has quaternion/lattice reformulations whose class numbers may never have been computed.
first_step: For each lattice reformulation in the repo, compute the class number of its genus (Sage/Magma genus enumeration) for small parameters.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Auxiliary-prime skeleton of the three-squares proof applied to ES windows
connection: Gauss/Dirichlet: choose an auxiliary prime q with (−n/q) = 1, build a form of determinant 1 representing n, then use one class. ES windows: auxiliary prime q ≡ 3 (4), (q/p) = −1, K = (p+q)/4 (FORCED_WINDOW). Mirror each step: is there an object 'of determinant 1' built from (p,q) whose uniqueness forces −1 ∈ Rat_q(K)?
why: The auxiliary-prime step is already in the campaign; the missing 'uniqueness of the class' step is the one Gauss had and ES lacks.
first_step: Write the window certificate as a statement about a binary/ternary form built from (p, q, K) and compute its genus/class structure for small cases.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Cauchy-lemma analogue: simultaneous control of (u+B, uB)
connection: Cauchy's lemma represents a number and its 'trace' simultaneously. (★) in pair form: s = u+B, q = uB with s ≡ −p (mod 4q) and s² − 4q a square. Seek an inequality region in (s,q) where existence is forced, as Cauchy's b² < 4a, 3a < b²+2b+4 does.
why: Simultaneous norm/trace representation is the mechanism behind every-n polygonal theorems; ES's (s,q) formulation is of the same shape (sum and product of two unknowns).
first_step: Plot, for many p, the set of (s,q) satisfying the congruence and check where the 'square discriminant' condition is hit; look for a region of guaranteed hits.
refs: Nathanson, Proc. AMS 99 (1987) 22-24 (A short proof of Cauchy's polygonal number theorem)

title: Power-size main term requirement: lift ES to a variety with power-many points fibred over certificates
connection: Tartakowsky/Kloosterman work because the Eisenstein term ≍ n^{k/2−1} beats cusp-form bounds; ES's main term is log²p. Seek V_p → {ES certificates of p} with fibres of size p^δ (nontrivial geometry), so V_p's point count has a power-size main term that vanishes iff ES(p) fails.
why: Changes the competition 'polylog main term vs. error' into 'power main term vs. error' — the only regime where every-n theorems for forms were ever proved.
first_step: Construct candidates V_p (e.g. adjoin variables parametrising the Type II h-family or the factorizations of 4Cp+1 into 3 factors) and compute their point counts and singular series.
upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: Kloosterman refinement in the level variable t for Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1)
connection: Kloosterman's refinement made 4-variable forms work by averaging Kloosterman sums over the Farey denominators. The all-level ES count Σ_t D_t^−(tp+1) is a divisor problem whose Fourier expansion in t produces Kloosterman sums (cf. the Type I Heegner/Kuznetsov note).
why: Kuznetsov is already used for the Type I sum; applying it to the level sum at fixed p is the pointwise version.
first_step: Write Σ_{t≤T} D_t^−(tp+1) via additive characters, identify the Kloosterman sums S(m,n;c), and estimate their contribution using Weil + Kuznetsov for fixed p.
upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: Spinor-exceptional square classes as the exact model of T1
connection: For ternary forms the integers t·m² in spinor-exceptional classes are represented by only half the spinor genera (Schulze-Pillot); everything else large is represented. T1 says Type I/II solutions vanish exactly at odd squares — a 'square-class' exception of the same shape.
why: If an ES certificate family is a ternary representation problem whose spinor exceptions are exactly the odd squares, DSP would give all large non-square p (ineffectively).
first_step: Compute spinor-exceptional classes for ternary forms of small discriminant; look for one whose exceptions are {m²} and whose representations of p biject with Type II data.

title: Correlate f_I(p), R(p) with class numbers h(−4p), h(−kp)
connection: Duke/Iwaniec: representation numbers of ternary forms ≈ class numbers. If some ES count correlates with h(−kp) for small k, a class-number-sized main term may be hidden in a weighted ES count.
why: Cheap test of whether ES counts carry class-number information beyond the BM/genus layer.
first_step: For primes p ≤ 10⁷, regress R(p)/log²p and f_I(p)/log²p on h(−4p)/√p, h(p)·reg/√p and L(1,(·/p)); report partial correlations.

title: An ineffective 'all large p' theorem is acceptable progress
connection: DSP (via Siegel) is ineffective yet counted as a full upgrade. For ES, an ineffective theorem 'ES(p) for p > p₀ (ineffective)' would already be a first-ever all-large result.
why: Opens Siegel-type inputs (L(1,χ) ≫ q^{−ε}) that the campaign may have discarded because they are ineffective.
first_step: Re-read BM_CORRECTED_COUNT §3 and check where a Siegel lower bound for L(1,(·/p)) or L(1,χ_{−4uB}) could replace Burgess and what it yields.

title: Linnik with a varying auxiliary split prime: ℓ = least prime with prescribed (p/ℓ)
connection: Linnik's ergodic method needed (−n/ℓ) = 1 for a fixed ℓ; varying ℓ with n is how one covers every n if the method is uniform in ℓ. ES: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 shows the BM layer is pointwise free using the least ℓ with (n/ℓ) = −1; find an ℓ-adic dynamical argument for certificates using that ℓ.
why: Bounded ℓ ≤ 4ℓ(n) is already known to suffice for BM positivity; a dynamical/Hecke argument at that ℓ could control the next layer.
first_step: Look for an ℓ-Hecke correspondence on ES certificates (e.g. on the quaternion/SL₂ form: matrices of determinant ℓ acting on [[a,p],[c,d]]) and test whether it maps certificates of p to certificates of p.
refs: Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss-Michel-Venkatesh, Ann. Math. 173 (2011) (Distribution of periodic torus orbits and Duke's theorem for cubic fields) / Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems (Duke's theorem and Linnik's ergodic method)
upgrade: Linnik's ergodic method (equidistribution on spheres) -> ELMV

title: Always-existing objects (CM points / closed geodesics of discriminant tied to p) landing in a target region
connection: Duke's theorem works because Heegner points of discriminant −d always exist (h(−d) ≥ 1) and equidistribute. ES needs existence; find objects attached to every p (e.g. CM points of disc −4p, geodesics of disc p) such that landing in an explicit cusp/congruence region ⟺ an ES certificate.
why: Equidistribution then forces existence for all large p (possibly ineffectively) — the general almost→every template of Duke/Linnik.
first_step: Try: reduced forms [a,b,c] of disc −16p or −4(4Cp+1); check whether 'a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), a small' type conditions encode (★); measure how deep in the cusp the region lies (it may be too deep — the B2 issue).
refs: Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss-Michel-Venkatesh, Ann. Math. 173 (2011) (Distribution of periodic torus orbits and Duke's theorem for cubic fields) / Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems (Duke's theorem and Linnik's ergodic method)
upgrade: Linnik's ergodic method (equidistribution on spheres) -> ELMV

title: Escalation of certificate menus: the ES 'truant' tree
connection: Bhargava's escalation: adjoin the smallest truant each time; finitely many escalators. ES: start with a certificate menu (Mordell identities, (★), b=1, ES₅, windows), find the least prime not covered, adjoin the cheapest family covering it, iterate; study the growth of the escalation tree.
why: Gives an empirical picture of how many families are needed up to X (B1 says bounded menus fail under Hypothesis H — the escalation rate measures how fast menus must grow).
first_step: Implement escalation over the repo's family menu up to 10⁸ and plot menu size vs. X.

title: Per-level explicit thresholds: R_t(n) is exactly a divisor count — make each level's failure set explicit
connection: 290 theorem: explicit per-form cusp bounds + finite checks. ES levels have no cusp part (METAPLECTIC Thm K: R_t = D_t^− − β_t), so each level's failure set is an explicit multiplicative condition on tn+1. Compose them escalator-style.
why: Explicit per-level failure sets turn the menu escalation into a computation on multiplicative sets (thin sets S_t).
first_step: For t ≤ 64 describe {n : D_t^−(tn+1) = 0} as 'tn+1 has all prime factors in a subgroup avoiding −1 mod t' and compute the densities of intersections.

title: Waldspurger-type formula: is some ES deviation a central L-value?
connection: Ono–Soundararajan proved Ramanujan's form under GRH because coefficient² ∝ L(1/2, f⊗χ_n) (Waldspurger), which GRH bounds. ES: look for an ES generating function with a cuspidal component whose p-th coefficient² is a twisted central value.
why: If such a formula existed, GRH (or subconvexity) would bound the deviation pointwise; METAPLECTIC says level series are Eisenstein + theta quotients, so a cusp form would have to come from a different construction (e.g. products/derivatives).
first_step: Decompose products of two level series (or the all-level series) into Eisenstein + cuspidal parts at small level numerically (Sage modular symbols) and look for nonzero cuspidal components.
upgrade: Ramanujan's ternary form x^2+y^2+10z^2 (stuck at conditional)

title: Sporadic exceptions U(n) = {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} vs. Ramanujan's 2719
connection: Ramanujan's form had sporadic exceptions explained by a finite computation + GRH. The finite U(n) exception list might be sporadic in the same sense, or the start of a structured family (a reciprocity family as in Apollonian packings).
why: Deciding 'sporadic vs structured' tells whether U(n) is a good proxy target for ES.
first_step: Factor the U(n) exceptions, compute their residues mod 840 and character values (n/ℓ) for ℓ ≤ 50, and extend the U(n) search to 10⁸ if not already done.
upgrade: Ramanujan's ternary form x^2+y^2+10z^2 (stuck at conditional)

title: Many-variable relaxations: ES with an extra term tied to the others
connection: Hasse principle holds for forms in many variables (Davenport, Heath-Brown, Hooley). 4-term ES is trivial; find intermediate 'k-term ES with constraints' (e.g. 1/x+1/y+1/z+1/w with w forced to equal xyz·k, or two terms merging 1/a+1/b = 1/c) that are circle-method accessible and imply 3-term ES.
why: Interpolates between trivial (4 free terms) and hard (3 terms); the implication step is the interesting part.
first_step: List 4-term constrained families and for each check (i) does a solution give a 3-term solution, (ii) number of variables after eliminating constraints.
refs: Davenport, Phil. Trans. A 251 (1959)/ Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963)
upgrade: Hasse principle for forms in many variables

title: A certificate scheme whose only hard condition is primality of linear forms (Green–Tao–Ziegler unconditional)
connection: Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg made Hypothesis-H-conditional fibration arguments unconditional when only linear polynomials must be prime, via Green–Tao–Ziegler. ES: search for a certificate parametrisation where, for fixed p, it suffices that a finite system of linear forms in free auxiliary variables be simultaneously prime.
why: GTZ would then give infinitely many such auxiliary tuples for each p — an unconditional every-p mechanism. Thm C (bounded witnesses fail under H) does not obviously forbid unbounded prime-based witnesses.
first_step: Enumerate ES certificate shapes where a denominator or factor is a free prime (e.g. Type I f prime, window prime q) and check whether remaining conditions can be made linear in auxiliary variables.
upgrade: Hypothesis H conditional -> unconditional for linear polynomials (fibration method)

title: Integral-point fibration on U_n by the curves x = const (two-term problems)
connection: Fibration method for rational points; integral versions exist for some schemes fibred into affine conics (Harpaz, JEMS 2019, conditional on stated hypotheses). Fixing x makes ES a two-term problem 1/y + 1/z = 4/n − 1/x, a divisor problem.
why: U_n is a log K3-type affine cubic surface (check); an integral fibration method with a BM-type local condition would be a structural every-n mechanism.
first_step: Harpaz, 'Integral points on conic log K3 surfaces', JEMS 21 (2019), arXiv:1511.04876 (verified: sufficient conditions under stated arithmetic/geometric hypotheses, not unconditional); check whether U_n fits the framework and which hypotheses fail.
upgrade: Hypothesis H conditional -> unconditional for linear polynomials (fibration method)

title: Linnik's three principles for the least ES certificate
connection: Linnik made Dirichlet effective-for-every-q with: log-free zero density, zero-free region, Deuring–Heilbronn repulsion. ES analogue: bound the least level C(p) (or least e) carrying a certificate by p^L, organising the proof as (a) 'density' of bad character configurations, (b) a 'zero-free' range for small moduli, (c) an exceptional character making other families easier.
why: Every bound C(p) < ∞ already is ES, so the content is the three-part architecture: separating 'few bad characters' from 'one exceptional character'.
first_step: Write the BM-level positivity proof (least ℓ with (p/ℓ) = −1) as principle (b), and formulate precisely what principle (a) would have to say about order-≥3 characters mod 4C.

title: Exceptional character helps: Deuring–Heilbronn for ES families
connection: In Linnik's theorem a Siegel zero repels other zeros and makes primes more regular in other progressions. For ES, if (·/p) is 'exceptional' (QR at all small primes), the BM main term at small levels vanishes — but maybe other certificate families (b=1 line, windows with q where (q/p) = −1 is forced large) become abundant.
why: A dichotomy 'either the characters are regular (use H⁻_BM-type counting) or one is exceptional (use the repelled families)' is how Linnik/Heilbronn escaped worst cases.
first_step: Among primes with large least non-residue ℓ(p) (p ≡ 1 mod 840·k), compare counts of (★), b=1, ES₅ and window certificates to controls.

title: Dirichlet's product trick: a product of all level series with nonnegative coefficients
connection: Dirichlet: Π_χ L(s,χ) = ζ_K(s) has nonnegative coefficients, so no L(1,χ) vanishes. ES: look for a product/combination of the twisted level series Σ_χ σ_χ(tn+1) whose coefficients are nonnegative and whose value 'at s = 1' (or at the p-th coefficient) is forced positive.
why: Positivity of a combination is how non-vanishing statements are proved for every modulus; METAPLECTIC Thm K gives exactly these character-twisted series.
first_step: From Thm K, form Σ_{χ mod t} σ_χ(N) products over a few levels t and test numerically which combinations have nonnegative coefficients that vanish at p only when R(p) = 0.

title: Class-number formula positivity for the BM correction T(p)
connection: Dirichlet's real-character case: L(1,χ) = (const)·h > 0 because h is a positive integer. M_BM = M₀ − T(p) with T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB); express T(p) through L(1, (·/p)·ψ) for small auxiliary ψ, i.e. through class numbers of Q(√±p m).
why: If T(p) ≈ c·L(1,(·/p))·(log p) + …, then integrality/positivity of class numbers and known upper bounds of L(1,χ) give an exact grip on the main term, beyond Burgess.
first_step: Write T(p) as a Dirichlet series in (·/p) with multiplicative weights; extract the main term as a combination of L(1,(·/p)χ) and check numerically against computed T(p).

title: Erdős–Bertrand size contradiction: ES failure forces 4Cp+1 into thin multiplicative sets for every C
connection: Erdős proved Bertrand by showing C(2n,n) would be too small if no prime lay in (n,2n]. ES failure at p means: for every C, 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) (e.g. C=1: 4p+1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4; C=2: 8p+1's prime factors lie in {1,3} or {1,5} mod 8). Compare Π_C(4Cp+1) — whose prime-factor multiset is fixed by CRT — with these restrictions.
why: Converts ES into a sieve problem with explicitly known 'prime factor census' (each prime q divides 4Cp+1 exactly for C in one class mod q).
first_step: Formalise the constraint set S_C = {N : no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} for C ≤ 32 and compute, for the hard primes, how many C ≤ X have 4Cp+1 ∉ S_C (each such C is a certificate).

title: Prime-factor census by CRT: q | 4Cp+1 iff C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ (mod q)
connection: In Bertrand/Chebyshev the prime factorisation of a binomial coefficient is explicit. Here every prime q ∤ 2p divides 4Cp+1 exactly on one class C ≡ c_q (mod q); a single-prime certificate exists iff 4c_q | q+1 for some q ≡ 3 (mod 4) (C = c_q < q). Higher certificates combine several q's at a common C.
why: Makes the certificate problem an explicit combinatorial problem on the residues c_q(p); single-prime certificates have probability ≈ τ((q+1)/4)/q, summing to ≍ log²p — the main term in a transparent form.
first_step: Compute the single-prime-certificate count S₁(p) = #{q ≡ 3 (4) prime : 4c_q(p) | q+1} for p ≤ 10⁸ and its share of R(p); check whether S₁(p) alone ever vanishes for p in the hard list.

title: Harman-style comparison sieve: R(p) versus the average of R(n) over a short interval around p
connection: Harman's sieve gets primes in every short interval by comparing a decomposition with a model where asymptotics are known, discarding only small nonnegative terms. ES: compare R(p) with ⟨R(n)⟩ over n ∈ [p−H, p+H] in the same residue class mod 840, using Type I/II information on the multiplicative structure of 4Cn+1.
why: Averages of R over short intervals are accessible (E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4})); the comparison step is the pointwise-transfer mechanism.
first_step: Numerically measure |R(p) − ⟨R⟩_H|/⟨R⟩_H for H = p^θ, θ = 0.1..0.5, and see which H makes the comparison tight.
upgrade: Primes in short intervals for every x

title: Large-values / 'zero-density' estimate for levels at fixed p
connection: Hoheisel's every-interval theorem needed that few zeros are far right (zero density). ES analogue: at fixed p, show that only few levels C have a large deviation of the level count D_C(p) from its expected 2/φ(4C)·(…), so the many 'good' levels carry R(p) > 0.
why: Large-values estimates are statements about one object (here one p) and many 'frequencies' (levels) — the right quantifier order.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of level deviations for fixed p ~ 10⁹ and test a large-values inequality of the shape #{C ≤ X : |dev_C| > V} ≪ X·(stuff)/V².
upgrade: Primes in short intervals for every x

title: Intermediate milestone: (★)-primes in every short interval
connection: Every interval [x, x + x^{0.525}] contains primes (BHP) and the ES exceptional set in short intervals satisfies E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4}) ((D)30), so every such interval contains primes satisfying the sub-route — check that this holds for (★) itself and for Mordell-hard classes.
why: A cheap, honest 'every interval' theorem; it calibrates which short-interval statements are already free and which are not (e.g. intervals of length (log x)^A).
first_step: Verify that the short-interval exceptional-set bound applies to (★) restricted to p ≡ 1 (mod 840) and combine with BHP for primes in progressions to get the statement; then ask for the shortest H where it holds.
upgrade: Primes in short intervals for every x

title: Burgess shift trick on the level variable
connection: Burgess amplifies a short character sum by shifting n → n + ab and using multiplicativity. ES events at level C involve the residue of 4Cp+1 modulo divisors; shifting C → C + kd preserves 'd | 4Cp+1'. Use shifts to relate the certificate count on a short C-range to a complete sum handled by Weil.
why: A Burgess-type argument for divisor events in a short level range would give certificates with small C (C ≤ p^{1/4+ε}), a pointwise statement.
first_step: Write #{C ≤ X : ∃ d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} with d in a fixed range as a character sum over C mod d and try the (n + ab) shift with Hölder.

title: Least non-residue lens: ES failure ⇒ p is a QR modulo every small prime (via the BM layer)
connection: Linnik's large sieve shows n(p) ≪ p^ε for almost all p; Burgess gives n(p) ≪ p^{0.152} for all p. If 'no certificate at levels ≤ L' forced (p/ℓ) = 1 for all ℓ ≤ L^c, then Burgess would contradict failure once L^c > p^{0.152}.
why: SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 already shows BM-level positivity via ℓ(n); the question is how far the forcing extends when certificates (not just main terms) are required.
first_step: Test empirically: among primes with no (★) certificate at levels C ≤ K, what is the distribution of ℓ(p)? (If ℓ(p) is not forced large, the lens fails for (★).)

title: Heilbronn case split: ES under GRH-type regularity, and ES under its failure
connection: Heilbronn proved h(−d) → ∞ by: if GRH holds, Hecke; if it fails, the false zero itself forces the result. ES: prove (a) ES for all large p assuming a regularity hypothesis R on the characters (·/p), (·/ℓ) and (b) ES for all large p assuming ¬R (some exceptional character), with (b) using the exceptional bias.
why: Each half is conditional, the union unconditional — a proven almost→every template that tolerates ignorance about which case holds.
first_step: Formulate R as the minimal statement H⁻_BM needs (BM_CORRECTED §3.3 says no standard conjecture implies it — find the weakest one that does), then analyse what ¬R gives for the window/b=1 families.
upgrade: Heilbronn: class number h(-d) -> infinity (Gauss conjecture)

title: ES (or (★)) assuming infinitely many Siegel zeros
connection: Heath-Brown: Siegel zeros ⇒ twin primes; Friedlander–Iwaniec (IMRN 2003): under a strong Siegel-zero hypothesis, asymptotics for primes in APs in ranges beyond GRH-type reach. If exceptional characters exist, primes behave like integers with χ(p) = −1, which might make ES certificates (whose density depends on χ_{−4uB}(p)) more abundant at all large p.
why: One half of a Heilbronn-type split; also a test of whether ES's difficulty is 'parity-like'.
first_step: Friedlander–Iwaniec, 'Exceptional characters and prime numbers in arithmetic progressions', IMRN 2003 no. 37 (verified: conditional on an exceptionally strong Siegel-zero hypothesis); then model ES counts when (·/p) agrees with a fixed χ_D at all small primes.
refs: Heath-Brown, Proc. London Math. Soc. 47 (1983) 193-224 (Prime twins and Siegel zeros)

title: Heath-Brown's 'one of three' for ES windows
connection: Heath-Brown: among any three multiplicatively independent integers, one is a primitive root for infinitely many p. ES windows: failure at window e requires the divisor classes of N_e = (p+e)/4 to avoid −1 in their ratio set (often: lie in an index-2 subgroup without −1). Show three suitably independent windows cannot all fail.
why: Pigeonhole over several candidate families is an every-type argument that needs no single family to work.
first_step: For (★)-failing primes, record for small windows e the subgroup generated by the prime factors of N_e mod e; look for algebraic relations among three windows that make simultaneous avoidance impossible.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)
upgrade: Artin primitive root conjecture: all but two exceptions

title: Index argument: subgroup generated by prime factors of N in (ℤ/4C)*
connection: Artin-type proofs control the index of ⟨a⟩ in F_p*. ES level C fails iff no subproduct of prime factors of N = 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (4C). If the factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1, failure is automatic; if −1 ∈ H, failure needs few factors. Study the index of H as p varies.
why: Separates the 'algebraic' failure (−1 ∉ H) from the 'combinatorial' one (too few factors), which need different tools (characters vs. zero-sum theory).
first_step: For the hard primes and C ≤ 100, compute H = ⟨prime factors of 4Cp+1⟩ mod 4C and classify each failing level as algebraic or combinatorial.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)
upgrade: Artin primitive root conjecture: all but two exceptions

title: Audit EH/BV-conditional ES statements for smooth-moduli (MPZ) versions
connection: Zhang got bounded gaps by replacing EH with an equidistribution statement for smooth moduli only. Check each conditional ES result in CONDITIONAL_ES.md: which moduli does it need, and would Polymath8's MPZ(ϖ,δ) (smooth moduli, fixed residues) suffice?
why: Turns a list of conditional results into unconditional ones whenever the moduli can be taken smooth — exactly the Zhang move.
first_step: Read CONDITIONAL_ES.md and tabulate: hypothesis, moduli used, residues fixed or varying, whether smooth restriction loses only a constant.
upgrade: GPY -> Zhang/Maynard (conditional EH -> unconditional bounded gaps)

title: Maynard multidimensional weights over an auxiliary parameter
connection: Maynard: with k linear forms, sieve weights force at least m of them prime. For fixed p, take k candidate certificate families indexed by an auxiliary integer t (e.g. windows q(t) in progressions) and use multidimensional weights to force at least one success.
why: Converts 'one family must succeed' into a sieve-weight positivity problem over t, where averaging is legitimate (t is free, p fixed).
first_step: Identify a free auxiliary variable t such that each family's success at t is a 'primality-like' event of a polynomial in t; write the GPY/Maynard ratio for the toy model.
upgrade: GPY -> Zhang/Maynard (conditional EH -> unconditional bounded gaps)

title: GCD-graph overlap analysis of the level events E_C
connection: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard proved Duffin–Schaeffer by controlling overlaps of approximation events via GCD graphs. ES: events E_C(p) = {level C has a certificate}; a Chung–Erdős lower bound needs Σ P(E_C ∩ E_C′) small, and overlaps depend on gcd(4C, 4C′) and on shared prime factors of 4Cp+1, 4C′p+1.
why: Quasi-independence on average is what upgrades 'expected number → positive probability'; the GCD-graph method is the strongest known tool for that step.
first_step: Over primes p ≤ 10⁸ estimate P(E_C ∩ E_C′)/(P(E_C)P(E_C′)) as a function of gcd(C,C′) and C/C′; fit a Duffin–Schaeffer-type overlap model.

title: Profinite zero–one law for ES certificate sets
connection: Gallagher's zero–one law makes metric Diophantine sets have measure 0 or 1. In the profinite completion of ℤ, the set of p̂ admitting a certificate at a finite level is open; its complement is closed of Haar measure 0 (almost-all theorem). Characterise the complement (contains square-mimicking points, B1).
why: The integers are a countable dense subset; ES says no integer lies in the closed null set. Knowing its exact shape (squares only? more?) is the profinite form of the problem.
first_step: Compute, for M = 840·k with k ≤ 30, the residues mod M not covered by certificates with all parameters dividing powers of M; compare with the squares mod M.

title: Use p = a² + b² to create bilinear structure (Friedlander–Iwaniec style)
connection: FI broke parity using Gaussian-integer arithmetic for x² + y⁴. Primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) are norms ππ̄; rewrite certificate conditions (e.g. 4Cp+1 = dd′) in terms of (a,b) and Gaussian integers to obtain Type II bilinear sums with structure.
why: Mordell-hard primes are all ≡ 1 (mod 4), so this extra structure is always available and unused in divisor formulations.
first_step: Express 4Cp + 1 = 4C(a²+b²) + 1 and look for factorisations over ℤ[i] or ℤ[√−C] (4Ca² + 4Cb² + 1) that align with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C).

title: Is ES parity-sensitive? A Selberg-parity test for certificate counts
connection: FI/Heath-Brown matter because sieves cannot distinguish parity of Ω. Test whether the ES certificate indicator correlates with λ(4Cp+1) or λ of the divisor: if certificate detection is 'parity-blind', sieve-theoretic approaches are not blocked by parity.
why: Clarifies whether parity-breaking technology is needed at all.
first_step: Compute Σ_C λ(d)·1[d certificate at level C] over all certificates for many p; compare with the total count.

title: Switching d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d: only d ≤ √(4Cp+1) needed, then the trial form
connection: Titchmarsh/Linnik handle large divisors of p−1 by switching to the complementary divisor. For ES both d and N/d are ≡ −1 (mod 4C), so R(p) = 2·#{small d}, and for small d, C is forced: C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ (mod d) with 4C | d+1 (trial form).
why: Shows that R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d(p) | d+1} with c_d(p) = −(4p)⁻¹ mod d — a single explicit arithmetic condition per d, ready for Type I equidistribution in d.
first_step: Implement the d-indexed formulation and test whether the events {4c_d(p) | d+1} for d in dyadic ranges behave like independent events with probability τ((d+1)/4)/d.

title: Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec well-factorable weights for the 'self-referential modulus'
connection: BFI pushed level of distribution beyond 1/2 for well-factorable weights. ES events have modulus 4C that is itself a factor of the divisor equation (d ≡ −1 mod 4C with d | 4Cp+1); exploit factorability of the weights in C.
why: The self-referential modulus is ES's distinctive structure; BFI-type dispersion is designed for moduli with flexible factorizations.
first_step: Rewrite R(p) with C = C₁C₂ factorable weights and check whether the resulting sums fit the BFI dispersion template (sum over moduli of a fixed residue).

title: Linear correlations of restricted divisor functions (Matthiesen-type) with p as a coefficient
connection: Matthiesen proved asymptotics for Σ_t Π_i f(L_i(t)) for divisor-type f via the Green–Tao machinery. R(p) is Σ_C of a restricted divisor function of the linear form 4pC + 1; with more structure (several levels) it becomes a correlation.
why: Gives asymptotics with uniformity questions in the coefficient p — the precise point to check.
first_step: Matthiesen, 'Linear correlations of multiplicative functions', Proc. LMS 121 (2020), arXiv:1606.04482 — verified: fixed linear forms only, coefficients may NOT grow with the range; so the needed input is a uniform-in-coefficients version — state it precisely and look for partial results (e.g. for τ-type functions via Kloosterman methods).
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)

title: Transference principle: dense subsets of ES certificates relative to a pseudorandom majorant
connection: Green–Tao: a dense subset of a pseudorandom set inherits linear patterns. ES certificate sets for varying p sit inside the majorant {all factorizations of 4Cp+1}; transference could show a positive-density subset of p's certificate data forces patterns that are certificates for other p's.
why: Odd: it moves information between different p, which is not ES; but a pattern-based closure (certificate for p₁,p₂ ⇒ certificate for p₃) would be an every-type mechanism.
first_step: Search the (★) data for linear patterns: triples (p₁,p₂,p₃) in AP whose certificates are linearly related.
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)

title: ES along almost all polynomial families n = f(m)
connection: Skorobogatov–Sofos prove Schinzel on average over polynomial families. Ask: for 100% of quadratic families f (ordered by height), does Type II hold for all large m (or all m)? The square family m² is the T1 exception; maybe 'square-like' families are the only exceptions.
why: A different 'almost all' axis (over families, every member) that interacts directly with T1 and with the repo's exponential families.
first_step: For random quadratics f(m) = am² + bm + c with small height, compute the Type II failure set among m ≤ 10⁵ and see if failures concentrate on families that are squares up to linear change.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)
upgrade: Schinzel Hypothesis H for 100% of polynomials (stuck mirror)

title: Siegel's two-character trick for ES: a positive-coefficient product over two primes
connection: Siegel bounds L(1,χ₂) below by using ζ L(χ₁) L(χ₂) L(χ₁χ₂) ≥ 0 together with an exceptional χ₁. ES: combine the certificate counts at p and at an auxiliary prime p′ (or the characters (·/p), (·/p′), (·/pp′)) in a positivity identity, so that failure at p would force excess at a related object which is bounded.
why: Positivity products across two objects are how individual lower bounds were first obtained from average information.
first_step: Look for an identity: Σ over certificates of pp′ (composite!) = (certificates of p)·(…) + (certificates of p′)·(…) + mixed; check numerically whether the mixed term is small/positive.
upgrade: Siegel's theorem (average class numbers -> individual lower bound)

title: Ineffective lower bound for M_BM via Siegel instead of Burgess
connection: Thm 2.2 gets M_BM ≥ (3/16π²) log²p via Burgess. Siegel's L(1,χ) ≫ q^{−ε} might give the full M_BM ∼ M₀ for the dominant small-modulus part, ineffectively.
why: Would sharpen the unconditional main term (constant) at the cost of effectivity; useful for any ineffective all-large-p route.
first_step: Isolate the contribution of moduli 4uB ≤ (log p)^A in T(p), express it via L(1,·) values of characters of conductor ≤ (log p)^A twisted by (·/p), and apply Siegel–Walfisz-type input.
upgrade: Siegel's theorem (average class numbers -> individual lower bound)

title: Inverse Frey: encode the failure of ES at p as an object with impossible properties
connection: Frey/Ribet/Wiles: a hypothetical solution yields an elliptic curve whose mod-ℓ representation would come from a nonexistent level-2 form. ES failure gives no point, but it gives a huge family of constraints (no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, for all C). Package these constraints as a Galois/automorphic object (e.g. a 'character' on level structures) and seek a rigidity contradiction.
why: The FLT pattern 'counterexample ⇒ object ⇒ contradiction' is the archetypal every-n proof; ES's failure data are rich enough to define objects.
first_step: Formalise the failure data as a function F_p(C, a) = 1[class a mod 4C contains a divisor of 4Cp+1]; check whether ES failure makes F_p multiplicative/character-like in C (it would be in the square-mimicking profinite model).

title: Almost-all exponents → all: Faltings-type finiteness for ES failure configurations
connection: Heath-Brown/Granville deduced FLT for almost all exponents from Faltings' finiteness. ES: find a family of curves X_p (genus ≥ 2, or of general type) whose extra rational/integral points are forced by ES failure at p; uniform finiteness would bound the failures.
why: Moves ES to finiteness of the exceptional set — a big intermediate step (finite exceptions + verification would finish).
first_step: Look for curves in the ES surface family U_p (e.g. intersections with x = λy) whose integral points correspond to certificates; compute genera.

title: Wieferich-type congruences forced on a hypothetical counterexample
connection: Mihăilescu showed a Catalan solution forces p^{q−1} ≡ 1 (mod q²) — strong congruences on the unknowns. ES: a counterexample p must be a square modulo every M for which bounded certificates cover the non-square classes (Mordell: mod 840). Push the list of forced congruences as far as possible and combine with the least-non-residue bound.
why: If 'no certificate with parameters ≤ L' forces (p/ℓ) = 1 for all ℓ ≤ L^c, Burgess (n(p) ≪ p^{0.152}) gives a contradiction for L^c > p^{0.152}.
first_step: For moduli M = 840·m, compute the residues uncovered by certificates with all parameters ≤ L; test whether they are exactly squares mod M and how L must grow with M.

title: Annihilator theory in (ℤ/4C)*: Stickelberger-type relations among divisor classes
connection: Mihăilescu's proof uses annihilators of cyclotomic class groups. The classes of prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)* across many C are linked (the same p); look for annihilator-type relations that prevent all of them from avoiding −1.
why: Odd: ES failure is a statement about a family of subgroups indexed by C; group-ring relations between the families might be forced by the common p.
first_step: Compute for fixed p the vectors (class of q mod 4C) for primes q | 4Cp+1, C ≤ 200, and search for linear relations in the group ring that hold for all p.

title: Primitive divisors of Lucas sequences are ≡ ±1 (mod n): a source of divisors ≡ −1 (mod 4C)
connection: Primitive prime divisors q of a Lucas number u_n satisfy q ≡ (D/q) (mod n); when (D/q) = −1, q ≡ −1 (mod n) — exactly the class ES needs at level n = 4C. Combine with q | 4Cp+1 (i.e. q = 4Cm − 1 with q | p + m).
why: A structural source of divisors in the class −1 mod 4C; BHV guarantees primitive divisors for n > 30.
first_step: For small D and n = 4C, list primitive divisors q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of u_n and test how often p + m ≡ 0 (mod q) can be arranged (it cannot for fixed p unless q | p + m; compute the induced density).

title: Cyclotomic size argument: 'non-certificate part' of Π_C(4Cp+1) must be small
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy: Φ_n(a) is large but its non-primitive part is tiny (only the largest prime of n), so a primitive prime exists. ES analogue: bound the part of Π_{C≤X}(4Cp+1) made of primes that cannot participate in any certificate, and show it is smaller than the whole.
why: A size argument needs no equidistribution; it uses only the explicit CRT census of prime factors (cf. Erdős–Bertrand item).
first_step: Define 'certificate-capable' primes q (those with 4c_q | (q+1)k-type relations) and compute log of the incapable part vs. Σ log(4Cp+1) for test p.

title: Subspace-theorem methods for divisibility relations (Corvaja–Zannier)
connection: Roth → Schmidt's subspace theorem → Corvaja–Zannier results on divisibility a^n − 1 | b^n − 1 and on S-integral points. ES is a divisibility relation (4uC − 1) | (p + u); the subspace theorem controls such relations in exponential/algebraic families.
why: Could prove finiteness of failures in exponential families (e.g. 15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297 — open in the repo) or structure results for certificate-free p.
first_step: Check Corvaja–Zannier's divisibility theorems (e.g. 'On the greatest prime factor of (ab+1)(ac+1)', 'A lower bound for the height of a rational function at S-unit points') for applicability to n = a·b^s + c families with certificate divisibility.

title: 'At most one exception' phase: repulsion between ES-failing primes
connection: Heilbronn–Linfoot/Tatuzawa proved there is at most one exceptional discriminant before the full class-number-one solution. ES intermediate: show two (★)-failing or ES-failing primes p, p′ in a range [X, X²] cannot coexist (repulsion), e.g. because their characters would both be exceptional.
why: Finiteness/at-most-one statements are the classical stepping stone between almost-all and every.
first_step: Check the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ for pairwise relations (p′/p) = 1, shared quadratic-residue profiles, and spacing; compare with random primes having the same individual profiles.

title: Dirichlet–Pell pigeonhole on near-certificates in M₂(ℤ)
connection: Pell is solvable for every non-square D by: infinitely many (x,y) with bounded norm defect, two with the same defect k and residues mod k, divide them to get norm 1. ES Type I/II fail exactly at odd squares — the Pell exception shape. In the SL₂ form, look for near-certificate matrices with bounded defect; two congruent ones give a quotient that is an exact certificate.
why: Pigeonhole + group law is the cleanest every-n mechanism whose only failures are squares; T1 must appear as the reason the quotient fails at squares.
first_step: Define defect for matrices [[a,p],[c,d]] (e.g. det = 1 + δ, or a ≡ −1 only mod c/δ); generate many for a given p and test whether quotients of pairs with equal defect yield exact certificates.

title: Continued-fraction periodicity vs. ES₅ length: Lagrange's proof structure
connection: Pell's solution comes from the periodic CF of √D. ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 (a continued-fraction length condition for rationals with denominator p). Look for a quadratic irrational (depending on p) whose CF period contains an ES₅ witness, so periodicity forces existence.
why: Odd but concrete: links ES₅'s CF-length formulation to the one every-n theorem driven by CF structure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute the CF periods of √p, √(4p+1), (1+√p)/2 and check whether an ES₅ witness can be read off from convergents.

title: Explicit Heegner-type constructions for Mordell-hard classes
connection: Congruent numbers: explicit Heegner points give results for primes in specific classes (5, 7 mod 8). ES: find an explicit CM/Heegner construction producing certificates for p in one Mordell-hard class (e.g. p ≡ 1 mod 840 with an extra splitting condition), as a 'Monsky/Heegner' theorem for ES.
why: Partial class-restricted every-p theorems are new territory for ES and would show which arithmetic the hard classes need.
first_step: Re-read paper/es-typei-heegner-note for which objects are used; test numerically whether Type I certificates for p correlate with CM points of disc −p·k.

title: Smith-type distribution of 'certificate-free levels' in twist families
connection: Smith's method computes distributions of Selmer groups in quadratic-twist families. The set of levels C at which p has no certificate is a 'Selmer-like' local-global object varying with p; its distribution over p could be computed by Smith/Koymans–Pagano-style methods.
why: Exact distributional knowledge of the failing-level profile is stronger than the zero-law heuristics now used.
first_step: Define the profile vector (1[level C fails])_{C ≤ K} and tabulate its empirical distribution over p; compare with a product-of-local-factors model.

title: Non-vanishing criterion (Gross–Zagier style) for the existence of a certificate
connection: Gross–Zagier: a Heegner point is non-torsion iff L′(E,1) ≠ 0 — existence from an analytic non-vanishing. ES: seek a curve/abelian variety A_p with a canonical point whose non-triviality is equivalent to (or implies) an ES certificate, so that a non-vanishing statement proves ES.
why: Converts existence into non-vanishing of a special value, where analytic tools work for every member of a family.
first_step: Look for elliptic fibrations of the ES surface U_p (e.g. fix x/y = λ) and compute whether the integral points relate to multiples of a canonical point.

title: Geometric cancellation via trace functions for divisor-class sums
connection: Deligne's Ramanujan bound comes from geometry (purity). The ES deviation involves sums over characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4C of σ_χ(4Cp+1); for prime moduli these are sums of trace functions (Kummer sheaves) where Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel give square-root cancellation in long sums.
why: If the ES non-genus part X(p) can be written as a sum of trace functions with conductor bounded independently of p, Deligne-type bounds apply pointwise.
first_step: Restrict to prime levels 4C → prime e (windows) and write the e-slice certificate count as a trace-function sum over divisors; compute the conductors.

title: Lower bound by upper bounds on complements (Stepanov/Weil principle)
connection: In the elementary proofs of Weil's bound, the lower bound for N comes from upper bounds applied to complementary objects. ES: find a family {R_j(p)} with R_0 = R(p) whose total Σ_j R_j(p) has a pointwise asymptotic and whose other members have sharp pointwise upper bounds; then R(p) ≥ total − Σ_{j≠0} upper bounds.
why: Upper bounds for divisor counts in fixed classes (Shiu/Brun–Titchmarsh type) are much easier than lower bounds; the total over all classes (τ(4Cp+1) summed over C) has a known asymptotic.
first_step: Quantify at small levels (C ≤ 8, where φ(4C) ≤ 16): total τ-sum asymptotic vs. best upper bounds for each wrong class; how sharp must the upper bounds be for R(p) > 0 to follow?

title: Lenstra/Coppersmith: divisors in residue classes via lattice reduction for large levels
connection: Lenstra (Math. Comp. 42 (1984)): N has ≤ 11 divisors ≡ r (mod s) when s > N^{1/3}, gcd(r,s) = 1, all found in polynomial time; Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj (Math. Comp. 77 (2008)) enumerate constructively for s ≥ N^α, any fixed α > 1/4. For C ≳ p^{1/2}, the modulus 4C exceeds (4Cp+1)^{1/3}, so each level has O(1) candidates computable by lattice reduction.
why: Turns the large-C part of R(p) into a count of short vectors in an explicit family of lattices — a geometry-of-numbers object where Minkowski-type existence arguments live.
first_step: Implement Lenstra's algorithm for (N, r, s) = (4Cp+1, −1, 4C) and test the fraction of certificates with C > p^{1/2}; analyse the lattices as C varies.

title: Hecke-type relations between ES counts at p, pℓ, pℓ² (Soundararajan's no-escape-of-mass)
connection: Soundararajan prevented escape of mass using λ(ℓ)² = λ(ℓ²) + 1, which forbids both λ(ℓ) and λ(ℓ²) small. ES: find exact or approximate relations between certificate counts f(p), f(pℓ), f(pℓ²) (solutions for composite n come from p, from ℓ, and 'mixed') that make f(p) = 0 incompatible with the controlled values at pℓ, pℓ².
why: Multiplicative relations at related integers are a way to get pointwise information from quantities that are easier to bound.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) (or R(n)) for n = p, pℓ, pℓ² for p ≤ 10⁵, ℓ ≤ 50, and fit f(pℓ) ≈ a·f(p) + b·f(ℓ) + c·f(p)f(ℓ) + mixed; study the mixed term.

title: Classify limit measures of normalised certificate data along hypothetical failing sequences
connection: QE (density one) comes from a variance bound; QUE (every) from classifying all possible limits (measure rigidity + entropy). ES: attach to each p a normalised measure (levels/shapes of certificates or profinite residue data); show that the only possible limit along any sequence p_k → ∞ is the 'Haar' one, incompatible with R(p_k) = 0.
why: Shifts from 'bound the variance' (almost all) to 'classify limits' (every) — the exact conceptual step of QUE.
first_step: Define μ_p on the profinite completion (or on (ℤ/M)* for growing M) from the residues of p; check what the square-mimicking points of B1 look like as limit measures.

title: Positive entropy from arithmetic recurrence on certificate shapes
connection: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss: Hecke recurrence forces positive entropy, ruling out concentration on small sets. ES: Hecke-like correspondences on certificate shapes (if they exist, cf. LINNIK-ERG item) would force any limiting distribution of shapes to be spread, hence to charge every region with positive mass.
why: Speculative but it is the precise ingredient that made QUE every-form.
first_step: First establish a correspondence (see Hecke-operator item); then measure numerically the entropy of the shape distribution of (★) solutions as p grows.

title: Complementary failure sets: two ES methods whose exceptions are incompatible
connection: Holowinsky's and Soundararajan's methods each fail only for forms with atypical eigenvalue statistics, in opposite directions; combined they cover every form. ES: the (★) line and the b=1 line never fail simultaneously ≤ 10⁸; find statistics S_A, S_B such that (★) failure forces S_A(p) extreme and b=1 failure forces S_B(p) extreme in an incompatible way.
why: A two-method union is an every-p proof template that does not need either method to be pointwise by itself.
first_step: Compute a battery of statistics (ℓ(p), T(p), L(1,(·/p)), M_BM, level-failure profile) for the 14 (★)-failures, the 3 b=1 failures and controls; look for anticorrelated pairs.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Parametrise ES methods by L(1,(·/p)): one should improve as it grows, another as it shrinks
connection: Holowinsky's bound is in terms of Σ_ℓ (|λ(ℓ)| − 1)/ℓ, Soundararajan's in the opposite tendency. M_BM = M₀ − T(p) is hurt when the weighted sum of (−m/p) is large. Find a second certificate family whose expected count increases with T(p).
why: If the two main terms move in opposite directions with the same character statistic, their sum is bounded below uniformly — Holowinsky–Soundararajan in miniature.
first_step: Compute the expected counts of the b=1 line, windows and ES₅ as functions of the Legendre profile (m/p)_{m ≤ 100}; regress against T(p).
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Amplified second moment over a short family around p
connection: Friedlander–Iwaniec amplification: bound an individual member by a family moment weighted with an amplifier peaked at the target. ES: Σ_{|n−p|≤H} |R(n) − M(n)|²·|A_p(n)|² with A_p(n) = Σ_{ℓ≤L} c_ℓ (n/ℓ)(p/ℓ); if this is ≤ (M(p)|A_p(p)|)²/2, then R(p) > 0.
why: The bookkeeping (family size H vs amplifier length L ~ H) is not immediately hopeless; the hard input is the twisted second moment of R − M over short intervals.
first_step: Numerically evaluate the amplified moment for p ~ 10⁶–10⁷, H ~ 10³–10⁴, Legendre-symbol amplifiers, and compare with the diagonal term.

title: Mollified variance to identify which characters explain R's fluctuations
connection: Mollifiers (Selberg/Levinson/Conrey) dampen large values by a short Dirichlet polynomial. Fit R(n)/M(n) − 1 by a short combination of Legendre symbols (n/ℓ), ℓ ≤ L; the residual variance after mollification measures what remains beyond the genus/BM layer.
why: Tells whether ES fluctuations are dominated by a few small characters (then a Heilbronn-type split is promising) or are spread out (then they are 'X(p)' noise).
first_step: Least-squares fit on n ≤ 10⁷ in Mordell-hard classes; report explained variance as a function of L.

title: Potential ES: count solutions over a quadratic field and use Galois parity
connection: Potential automorphy proves things over extensions and descends via Brauer induction. ES over O_K for real quadratic K: Gal(K/ℚ) acts on K-solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z with totally positive x,y,z; fixed points are ℚ-solutions. If the number of K-solutions in a Galois-stable finite window is odd, a rational solution exists.
why: Parity across a Galois action is a descent mechanism that needs no analysis over ℚ.
first_step: For K = ℚ(√2), ℚ(√5) and small p, enumerate totally positive integral solutions with norms bounded (finite after fixing a fundamental domain for units) and compute the parity of the count of non-rational ones.
refs: Barnet-Lamb-Geraghty-Harris-Taylor, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011) 29-98 (A family of Calabi-Yau varieties and potential automorphy II)

title: Minimal-counterexample descent: failure at p ⇒ failure at a smaller related prime
connection: Khare–Wintenberger: induction on conductor reduces to base cases. ES: find a map Φ such that if ES (or (★)) fails at p then it fails at some smaller Φ(p) (e.g. a prime factor of 4p+1 or of (p+e)/4); with verification to 10¹⁸ this proves ES.
why: Induction on the size of the counterexample is the cleanest every-n mechanism; data on (★)-failures can test candidate maps directly.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, check whether any simple arithmetic function of p (prime factors of 4p+1, 8p+1, (p+3)/4, p−4k², …) systematically produces another (★)-failing prime.

title: Killing ramification: remove small-prime structure from a counterexample
connection: KW lower the level by passing through compatible systems. ES: a counterexample p is a square mod 840; transform the problem (via the e-slice or by passing to n = p·m for auxiliary m) to a 'less ramified' instance where certificates are easier, without losing the failure.
why: Speculative; but ES(pm) → ES(p) fails in general, so the transfer must use primitive certificates of pm (those not coming from m).
first_step: Count primitive (non-inherited) Type II solutions of 4/(pm) for small m and test whether they ever yield information about p's certificates.

title: Product of three sets in SL₂(ℤ): ES words as A·T·A with entry p
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd/Helfgott growth makes products of a few sets fill SL₂(F_q). ES words p = tuv − u − v are length-3 'minus continuants': the (1,1) entry of M(u)M(t)M(v) with M(a) = [[a,−1],[1,0]]. ES ⟺ some product in A·T·A (with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has the right entry.
why: Places ES in the product-set/growth framework where 'every element' theorems exist (at least modulo q).
first_step: Check numerically how the (1,1)-entries of M(u)M(t)M(v), u,v,t ≤ X, distribute modulo small q and whether all residues are hit with the expected frequency (local), then compare with the archimedean count.

title: Birational automorphisms of U_n preserving integral points (Markoff-style moves)
connection: Markoff surfaces have Vieta involutions generating a group whose orbits structure all integral points; BGS/Chen then work. ES 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is linear in each variable (no Vieta involution); X = 1/x makes it a plane. Search Bir(U_n) for maps preserving integrality (beyond permutations).
why: If a nontrivial group acts on integral points of U_n, orbit/strong-approximation methods (and Chen's divisibility) become available.
first_step: Compute a few Cremona-type maps of the ES surface (e.g. from the Type I/II parametrisations) and test integrality preservation on known solutions.

title: Sum-product incompatibility: subgroup-avoidance across windows vs linear structure of N_e = (p+e)/4
connection: Bourgain–Katz–Tao: no set is nearly closed under both + and × in F_p. ES failure at many windows e forces the prime factors of N_e = (p+e)/4 into structured multiplicative sets mod e (e.g. squares when e is prime ≡ 3 mod 4), while N_e varies linearly in e.
why: If the multiplicative constraints at different e were incompatible with the additive progression N_e, ES would follow; sum-product is the canonical incompatibility principle.
first_step: For e prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), record whether all prime factors of N_e are QRs mod e for the hard primes; check how often this 'square-avoidance' happens across e ≤ 10⁴ compared to random.

title: Congruences for certificate counts (Chen's divisibility mechanism)
connection: Chen proved Markoff components have size ≡ 0 (mod p), which with BGS's 'giant component' gives connectivity. ES: find a congruence R(p) ≡ r(p) (mod m) (or for a refined count) with r(p) ≠ 0 determined by p's residue class; then the count cannot vanish.
why: A congruence mod a fixed m is a pointwise statement; R(p) is even, so look at R(p)/2 mod 2, mod 3, or counts weighted by characters.
first_step: Compute R(p)/2 mod m and several refined counts mod m (m = 2,3,4,8) for p ≤ 10⁷ and test whether any is determined by p mod M for small M.
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Graph structure on certificates of a fixed p
connection: BGS/Chen study the connectivity of a graph on solutions. Define moves between ES certificates of the same p (change C keeping u, swap roles of u/B, Type I↔II transforms) and study components; 'one certificate ⇒ many' plus a counting congruence on component sizes might exclude zero.
why: Even if ES is not about connectivity, component structure can produce congruences (as in Chen).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ build the move graph on all ES solutions and record component sizes; look for divisibility patterns.
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Search for quartic/higher reciprocity obstructions in ES sub-routes
connection: The Apollonian local-global conjecture failed because of quadratic and quartic reciprocity obstructions removing families like squares times constants. T1 is a quadratic one for Type I/II at odd squares. Test sub-routes ((★), b=1, ES₅, windows) for failure sets along families n = k·m², k·m⁴ and quartic-residue conditions.
why: Finds hidden structured obstructions before they ambush a proof; for ES itself any such family would be a counterexample candidate.
first_step: For each sub-route compute failure rates on n = k m² and n = k m⁴ (k ≤ 50) versus random n of the same size and residue class, and (2/p)₄-type quartic symbols on prime failures.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)

title: Almost-all does not imply every: a structured-exception audit for ES
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich proved density one for Apollonian curvatures, yet infinitely many exceptions exist. ES's almost-all theorems (Vaughan) are compatible with an infinite thin exceptional family; list the families where every known ES mechanism is weakest (odd squares for Type I/II; Mordell-hard classes; large ℓ(p)) and check ES (any type) explicitly far along them.
why: Disproof-side hygiene: the Apollonian story shows the almost-all→every step can fail exactly through reciprocity.
first_step: Extend adversarial searches along n = m² · (small k) and primes with large ℓ(p) beyond 10¹⁸ using the cheapest e-slices.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)

title: Modular-Zaremba + size control: words with (1,2)-entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and size < 2p
connection: Moshchevitin–Shkredov solve a modular Zaremba problem by growth in SL₂(F_p). ES words: length-3 minus-continuant products; require the relevant entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and bounded by 2p, forcing equality with p. Equidistribution mod p of entries of words of archimedean size ≤ p is the needed input.
why: Separates ES into a modular part (growth, potentially 'every p') and a size part (counting words in a box).
first_step: Numerically test equidistribution mod p of the entries of length-3 words with entries ≤ p (count ≈ p log p) for p ~ 10⁶; measure deviations at 0 mod p.

title: Track full Zaremba as ES's closest structural analogue
connection: Zaremba (bounded partial quotients for every q) is at density one (BK, Huang A=5) but not every q, like ES. Any 'every q' progress for some A (or for structured q like Niederreiter's prime powers) would show what kind of argument crosses that wall.
why: Shared obstruction profile: thin semigroup, polylog-to-power main terms, density-one results.
first_step: Search for post-2020 Zaremba results ('Zaremba conjecture every denominator', Kan, Frolenkov, Shkredov, 2023–2026) and record whether any is 'every q' for some A.

title: Niederreiter's recursive constructions for prime powers → ES exponential families
connection: Niederreiter proved Zaremba for every power of 2, 3, 5 by explicit recursive constructions. The repo proved ES for 3·2^s + 1, 7·4^s + 9, 63·2^s + 1; open: 15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297. Import the recursive (q → 2q, q → 3q) construction idea: produce certificates at n_{s+1} from those at n_s.
why: Recursive constructions along exponential families are the only way Zaremba got 'every member' for infinite families.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1, list known certificates for s ≤ 60 and look for a recursion (u,B,C)_s → (u,B,C)_{s+k}.

title: Counting integral points on the quadric ad − pc = 1 (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak / Eskin–McMullen)
connection: Oppenheim/Margulis and DRS/EM count integral points on affine homogeneous varieties via dynamics.
