The SL₂ form of ES: integer points of the indefinite ternary quadric ad − pc = 1 with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), c ∈ 4ℕ, a, d ≥ 1. Decompose by c into congruence-subgroup cosets and count each via mixing.
why: Homogeneous-dynamics counts are pointwise in the variety (here: in p), unlike sieve averages.
first_step: For fixed c, the conditions define a coset of a congruence subgroup; compute the expected count Σ_c vol(coset ∩ region) and compare with R(p).

title: Values of a rational ternary form near 0 with congruence: the exceptional rational case of EMM
connection: Eskin–Margulis–Mozes: for irrational forms counts are asymptotic, while rational forms of signature (2,1)/(2,2) have exceptional logarithmic behaviour. ES's quadric ad − pc is rational; locate it within the EMM exceptional regime and see whether the log-excess explains the log²p main term.
why: A dictionary between ES's polylog main term and the known exceptional counts of rational quadrics could import their methods.
first_step: Read EMM's treatment of rational forms (Annals 1998) and compute the predicted count for ad − pc ∈ {1} with |a|,|d| ≤ T, c ≤ T.

title: Closed horocycle at height 1/p: equidistribution of (a + i)/p and cusp excursions
connection: Every closed horocycle of length → ∞ equidistributes (Sarnak/Hejhal; sparse versions by Venkatesh, Strömbergsson). Points (a + i)/p, a mod p, lift ES₅-type continued-fraction data of a/p; ES₅ needs a point whose cusp excursion has a specific deep shape.
why: Puts ES₅ into the horocycle-equidistribution world where every-p statements exist — but probably at too deep a cusp scale (B2), which this item would quantify.
first_step: Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into a statement on the cusp depth/shape of some (a + i)/p and compare with the scales reachable by effective equidistribution.

title: Shrinking-target property for every closed horocycle
connection: Logarithm laws (Kleinbock–Margulis) give deep excursions for almost every orbit; ES would need them for the specific closed horocycle of length p and depth ~ p^{θ}. Tseng (Math. Z. 2022) proves shrinking-cusp-target equidistribution for long closed horocycles (effective version included).
why: If a deep-excursion theorem for every closed horocycle exists at depth p^{θ}, the CF-length formulation might follow for a range of shapes.
first_step: Read Tseng, 'Shrinking target equidistribution of horocycles in cusps', Math. Z. 302 (2022), arXiv:2106.00836, and Kelmer, Israel J. Math. 229 (2019), arXiv:1708.08953 (both verified to exist); extract the deepest cusp target reachable for a closed horocycle of length p.

title: Weyl/van der Corput differencing on the exponential-sum form of R(p)
connection: Weyl upgraded to every irrational polynomial by differencing. R(p) = Σ_{u,B} (4uB)⁻¹ Σ_{h mod 4uB} e(h(p+u+B)/(4uB)); apply van der Corput differencing in u (or B) to the nonzero frequencies to extract cancellation for fixed p in smoothed ranges.
why: Standard tool not obviously tried at fixed p; at least gives the true size of the error term in smoothed (★) counts.
first_step: Run the differencing on a smoothed model and compare the predicted error with the numerically observed |R_w(p) − M_w(p)|.

title: Profinite Furstenberg: closed ×k-invariant subsets of Ẑ and the ES-hard set
connection: Furstenberg: every infinite closed ×2,×3-invariant subset of the circle is everything. ES certificate existence is closed under n → kn; the closure in Ẑ (or in the solenoid) of the 'certificate-free' set is invariant under division by units? Formulate the right dynamical system on Ẑ and classify its closed invariant sets.
why: Odd: a topological rigidity statement on Ẑ could say the profinite hard set is exactly the squares, which is the B1 picture.
first_step: Write down the action (ℤ_{>0}, ×) on Ẑ and determine which closed invariant subsets contain the profinite square-mimicking points.
upgrade: Furstenberg x2 x3 (topological every-orbit vs measure)

title: Fake-ES models: same local statistics, almost-all holds, infinitely many failures
connection: Kahane–Katznelson show a.e. results can be sharp for any null set. Build synthetic 'ES-like' problems (random divisor data with ES's congruence statistics, or ES with a perturbed rule) where Vaughan's proof goes through verbatim but failures are infinite; the real proof must use a feature the fakes lack.
why: Identifies which properties of the integers any ES proof must use — the constructive face of the barrier map.
first_step: Construct a random model of 'divisors of 4Cp+1' with independent prime-factor classes, run the almost-all argument, and check what pointwise statement fails.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)
upgrade: Large values / Kolmogorov counterexample (a.e. cannot be upgraded)

title: Compactness/ultraproduct: a nonstandard ES-failing prime
connection: Tao's Sendov proof takes a sequence of counterexamples with degree → ∞ and analyses a limit object. ES: an ultraproduct of hypothetical failing primes p_k → ∞ is a nonstandard prime p* with no internal certificate; internal theorems (Thm 2.2: M_BM(p*) ≥ c log²p*) hold by Łoś. Seek a contradiction in the nonstandard model (e.g. via a Loeb-measure equidistribution statement).
why: Compactness turns 'all large p' into 'one nonstandard p', making limit-object arguments available.
first_step: Write down which standard theorems about p transfer (counts, character sums) and which 'external' statements (limits of normalised counts) could be proved by Loeb-measure arguments.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Large-p regime split by arithmetic configuration
connection: Tao handled different limiting zero configurations by different arguments. Split large p by configuration: (i) ℓ(p) small, (ii) ℓ(p) large but some small window works, (iii) (·/p) mimics a fixed character on all primes ≤ (log p)^A, … and design one certificate family per regime.
why: Each regime has extra structure to exploit; only finitely many regimes are needed if the split is by bounded data plus one 'pretentious' case.
first_step: Define the regime map on primes ≤ 10⁹ and check which certificate family is most robust in each regime.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Fourier reduction of an ES obstruction to a multiplicative (character) obstruction
connection: Tao reduced EDP to completely multiplicative functions by Fourier analysis. ES failure at window e means no divisor ratio ≡ −1 (mod e); reduce this to the existence of a character (or approximate homomorphism) χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1 that is 'large' on the prime factors of N_e.
why: If every obstruction is character-like, the problem becomes one about Legendre/higher-order characters at p — the BM/genus language where tools exist.
first_step: Prove the reduction for prime e: if the ±1-subset products of {g_i} miss −1, is there a character χ with χ(−1) = −1 and Σ_i Re χ(g_i) large? Test on data.

title: Entropy decrement across levels
connection: Tao's entropy decrement shows that for most scales, local statistics at scale H·ℓ are close to those at scale H given residues mod ℓ. ES at fixed p: look for an entropy-decrement statement across levels C (or windows e) that makes certificate events at most levels behave like independent coin flips.
why: Entropy decrement is a pigeonhole-on-scales device that works with a single sequence, matching ES's fixed-p setting better than probabilistic averaging over p.
first_step: Compute the empirical entropy of the joint pattern (D_C(p) > 0)_{C ∈ [K, 2K]} for fixed p across dyadic K and check whether it saturates the independent-model entropy.

title: SAT search for the smallest profinite obstruction to bounded certificate menus
connection: Konev–Lisitsa used SAT for EDP's C=2. Encode 'no certificate with parameters ≤ K' as residue constraints on p modulo M and use SAT/ILP to find all residue classes mod M consistent with failure; verify that they are exactly squares (B1) and find the minimal K for each M.
why: Cheap automated confirmation of the B1 picture and a generator of hard test cases.
first_step: Encode for M = 840·q (q ≤ 50 prime) and K ≤ 200; compare SAT solutions with the square classes.

title: Divisors of squarefree N as a hypercube; certificates as edges of a signed structure
connection: Huang: any induced subgraph of Q_k on > 2^{k−1} vertices has a vertex of degree ≥ √k, via a signed adjacency matrix with A² = kI. Divisors of squarefree N with k prime factors form Q_k; a window/level certificate is a pair of disjoint subsets with product ratio ≡ −1. Look for a signed matrix whose spectral bound forces such a pair once a large subset of divisors lies in one class.
why: Spectral interlacing is a pigeonhole with algebraic leverage; ES needs exactly a pigeonhole on divisor classes.
first_step: Model: vertices = subsets S, label g(S) = Π_{i∈S} q_i mod e; find the maximal size of a set of subsets with no two labels in ratio −1, compare with 2^{k−1}.
refs: arXiv:1907.00847 (Huang, Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture)

title: Multiscale induction on level sizes
connection: Wang–Zahl proved 3D Kakeya by multiscale induction (sticky structure). ES certificates live at scales (C, u, B) with uBC ≈ p/4; formulate a statement S(X): 'every p has a certificate with C ≤ X or a structural reason to have one at scale X²' and attempt an induction on scales.
why: Scale induction is how several every-type geometric statements were proved recently; ES has a natural scale hierarchy.
first_step: From data, record for each p the smallest C with a certificate and the 'near miss' structure at smaller C; look for a recursive pattern across dyadic scales.
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)

title: Slice-rank bounds for certificate-avoiding exponent sets
connection: Croot–Lev–Pach/Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound sets avoiding x + y + z = 0 via slice rank. ES failure constrains the exponent vectors (mod 2, or in the character group) of prime factors of N_e so that no ±1 combination hits the class of −1: a linear-avoidance condition in a 2-group quotient of (ℤ/e)*. Slice-rank-type bounds limit such sets.
why: Gives quantitative 'avoidance is rare' statements in elementary abelian quotients of (ℤ/e)*.
first_step: For e with (ℤ/e)*/squares ≅ F₂^r, formulate the avoidance condition on the F₂-vectors of prime factors and compute the maximal avoiding sets for small r.
refs: arXiv:1605.01506 (Croot-Lev-Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small)

title: ±1-weighted Davenport constant of (ℤ/e)*: long factor sequences force −1
connection: Olson's group-ring proof computes D(G). ES window certificate: Π q_i^{ε_i} ≡ −1 (mod e) with ε ∈ {−1,0,1} over prime factors q_i of N_e (with multiplicity). If the sequence is longer than a ±1-weighted Davenport-type constant and −1 ∈ ⟨q_i⟩, the subset products fill the generated subgroup.
why: Zero-sum theory gives exact thresholds; ES then needs only 'enough prime factors' + 'the right subgroup', separating combinatorics from arithmetic.
first_step: Compute the ±1-weighted covering threshold for (ℤ/e)*, e ≤ 200, and compare with the typical ω(N_e) ≈ log log p; find windows where the threshold is small (e with tiny exponent groups).

title: Kneser's theorem for the divisor-class product set at level C
connection: Cauchy–Davenport/Kneser lower-bound |A₁⋯A_k| in abelian groups, with equality only via stabiliser subgroups. The divisor classes of N = Π q_i^{a_i} mod 4C form the product set Π_i {1, q_i, …, q_i^{a_i}}; level C fails iff −1 is not in it. Kneser forces either a large product set or a subgroup structure.
why: Splits failure into 'too few factors' and 'subgroup trap', each attackable separately.
first_step: For hard primes and C ≤ 100 compute |product set|/φ(4C) and the Kneser stabiliser; classify failures.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz on the trial form
connection: Alon's nullstellensatz proves existence of a nonvanishing point in a grid. R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d(p) | d + 1}: encode 'no d in a grid of structured values works' as a polynomial vanishing on a product set, and look for a monomial whose coefficient is nonzero.
why: A purely algebraic existence argument; most likely to work in a finite-field shadow (mod q) of the problem, giving at least a structural lemma.
first_step: Formulate the mod-q shadow: for prime q, find (u, C) ∈ S₁ × S₂ (small sets) with 4uC − 1 ≡ 0 and p + u ≡ 0 (mod q); test the nullstellensatz coefficient condition.

title: Chevalley–Warning/Ax–Katz divisibility of auxiliary certificate counts
connection: Chevalley–Warning: few-degree systems have solution counts ≡ 0 mod p; with a trivial solution, a nontrivial one exists. ES local solvability is easy, but counts of certificates of p reduced modulo an auxiliary prime q (in a box) might satisfy Ax–Katz divisibility that, combined with a known trivial/degenerate solution, forces a genuine one.
why: Divisibility-forces-existence is the exact mechanism of EGZ/Kemnitz and of Chen's Markoff result.
first_step: Define for auxiliary prime q the F_q-system 'u·B·C·4 − u − B ≡ p, with box constraints encoded by polynomials'; check degrees vs number of variables for Chevalley–Warning applicability.

title: EGZ-style reduction: from 'composite' certificates to prime-level statements
connection: EGZ for n = ab follows from EGZ for a and b by iterated extraction. ES certificates at a level 4C = 4C₁C₂: is a certificate at level C obtainable from structure at levels C₁ and C₂ (e.g. a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C₁ and one ≡ −1 mod 4C₂ combined via CRT)?
why: If levels compose, it suffices to handle prime (power) levels, where character theory is simplest.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ test: when 4C₁p+1 and 4C₂p+1 have certificates, does 4C₁C₂p + 1 have one more often than chance?

title: Reiher's double counting: subsequences of fixed length with prescribed sum
connection: Reiher combined Chevalley–Warning with counting of subsequences of each length. ES analogue: count divisors of N of each 'length' (number of prime factors) in each class mod 4C; parity/divisibility constraints between lengths might force the class −1 to be hit.
why: Fine-grained counts by number of prime factors carry more structure than the total divisor-class set.
first_step: For N = 4Cp+1 with ω(N) ≥ 4, compute the table (k, class) ↦ #{divisors with k prime factors in class}, and look for identities mod 2 or mod 3.

title: Quasirandom 'one more factor' trick — size check for ES in SL₂(F_p)
connection: Nikolov–Pyber: if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m then ABC = G. For ES words A·T·A in SL₂(F_p), |A| ≈ |T| ≈ p while |G|³/m ≈ p⁸: the trick fails by a huge margin; quantify the deficit and check whether replacing SL₂(F_p) by a smaller quotient (Borel, affine group) helps.
why: Records why the canonical almost→every group trick does not apply directly, and where a smaller ambient group might restore it.
first_step: Compute |A|, |T|, |G| and m for G = SL₂(F_p), the Borel subgroup and the affine group F_p ⋊ F_p*; find the smallest ambient group in which ES becomes a product-covering statement.
upgrade: Gowers quasirandom groups / Nikolov-Pyber product covering

title: Almost-all + one more set ⇒ all: ES with a third free 'rescue' parameter
connection: In Gowers's trick, AB covers all but few elements and a third factor rescues the rest. ES: (★) covers all but a thin set of p (the 14 failures ≤ 10¹⁰); b=1 covers all but 3; their union none ≤ 10⁸. Formalise a 'rescue family' whose success set is large in a way that must intersect any thin exceptional set of the first family.
why: Converts the empirical complementarity of routes into a cardinality argument (needs a lower bound on the rescue family's success set within every thin structured set).
first_step: Characterise the (★)-exceptional set structurally (residue conditions, ℓ(p)) and compute the b=1 success rate restricted to primes with that structure.
upgrade: Gowers quasirandom groups / Nikolov-Pyber product covering

title: Move to a nonabelian encoding where character ratios decay
connection: Ore/Waring for finite simple groups works because |χ(g)/χ(1)| is small for large groups (quasirandomness). ES's character expansion lives in abelian groups (ℤ/4uB)* where all ratios are 1 — no decay. Find a nonabelian group encoding (SL₂(ℤ/q), Heisenberg, quaternion units mod q) where the certificate count expands over characters with small ratios.
why: The abelian encoding may be the reason no pointwise cancellation is visible; nonabelian Fourier analysis has built-in square-root savings from representation dimensions.
first_step: Express the SL₂-form certificate condition modulo q as a class-function count in SL₂(ℤ/q) and expand via Frobenius' formula; estimate the non-trivial character contribution.
refs: arXiv:0904.4146? (Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010))
upgrade: Ore conjecture / Waring problem for finite simple groups

title: Nibble + absorber: random greedy first denominator, absorber for the two-term remainder
connection: Designs exist for all large admissible n via an approximate (nibble) decomposition plus a prepared absorber fixing leftovers. ES: choose x so that m = 4x − p is small and smooth (nibble-like), then 'absorb' via the two-term condition (m/(px) = 1/y + 1/z iff px has divisors a, b with a + b ≡ 0 mod m).
why: Separates ES into a flexible step (many x) and a rigid step (two-term splitting); quantifies how often the absorber succeeds.
first_step: For hard primes, enumerate x near p/4 with m ≤ M and measure the success rate of the two-term step as a function of the smoothness and divisor count of x.

title: Keevash template: algebraic identity families + random perturbation for square classes
connection: Keevash's randomized algebraic construction starts from an algebraic template and perturbs it. ES: Mordell identities cover all non-square classes mod 840 (algebraic template); perturb identity parameters randomly to handle the square classes, with an absorber for failures.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities covering squares, but random perturbations of identities are not identities.
first_step: Take Mordell's identities, introduce free integer parameters (k-fold families), and measure how often random parameter choices give certificates for primes in square classes.

title: Closure maps: certificate(p) ∧ certificate(q) ⇒ certificate(r) for some r(p,q)
connection: Wilson's PBD-closure and Graham's 2n+2/2n+9 maps produce 'every large n' from finitely many seeds. ES is closed under n → kn only; search for genuinely bilinear closure operations producing certificates for new primes r from certificates of p and q.
why: Any nontrivial closure operation on certificate-carrying primes would be a completely new structural fact about ES.
first_step: Brute-force search: for pairs of (★) triples (u₁,B₁,C₁), (u₂,B₂,C₂), test small bilinear/polynomial combinations for producing triples of other primes.

title: Extremal vs non-extremal split for ES
connection: EFL/Ringel proofs split into 'extremal' configurations (handled by hand) and 'random-like' ones (absorption). ES: random-like p (character values balanced) vs extremal p (QR at many small primes; square-like mod large M); handle extremal p by forced-congruence arguments (least non-residue) and random-like p by second-moment counting.
why: Gives a concrete division of labour where each part may be tractable; the extremal side is close to the Burgess/least-non-residue world.
first_step: Define an extremality score E(p) (e.g. number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = 1) and examine how certificate counts depend on it.
upgrade: Erdos-Faber-Lovasz / Ringel / Ryser-Brualdi-Stein (all large n via absorption)

title: Unavoidable configurations + discharging over levels
connection: Four colour theorem: every planar graph contains one of 633 reducible configurations (found by discharging). ES: define 'configurations' as local data (p mod small M, factorisation pattern of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K); show by a discharging/averaging argument that every p contains one of a finite list, each of which forces a certificate.
why: B1's Thm M says bounded procedures follow formal runs at square-mimicking points, so the configuration list must include unbounded data; still the method gives a framework for structured case analysis.
first_step: Collect, for p ≤ 10⁸, the minimal 'certificate-forcing' local configurations and see whether a small set covers all p empirically.

title: Minimal counterexample via the e-slice: ES(p) from data of N = (p+e)/4 < p
connection: Four-colour and many combinatorial proofs consider a minimal counterexample. ES(p) ⟸ a property P(N, e) of the smaller integer N = (p+e)/4. Find a property Q(n), inherited along n ↦ (n + e)/4 for some e, such that Q(n) for all n < p implies Q(p) and Q(p) ⇒ ES(p).
why: A successful Q would make ES a consequence of verification (10¹⁸) + induction.
first_step: Data mining: for each p ≤ 10⁷, list e for which N_e carries a certificate and look for a hereditary property of N_e.

title: Spread/expectation threshold of the ES certificate hypergraph
connection: Park–Pham: thresholds are within log of the (fractional) expectation threshold, via 'spread' families. Model ES at p as a random hypergraph where each potential certificate is present with its density; compute its spread and expectation threshold to see whether ES sits 'above threshold' by a log factor or just at it.
why: The repo finds the expected number of 'hit' levels is ≈ (0.44 → 0.97)·log p (critical); a spread analysis would make 'critical vs supercritical' precise.
first_step: Compute the fractional expectation threshold of the (★) certificate family for test p using LP over levels.
refs: arXiv:2203.17207 (Park-Pham, A proof of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture)

title: Entropy inequality for the union of certificate families
connection: Gilmer's entropy argument shows some element is frequent in a union-closed family. ES certificate families are 'union-like' (if a family works for p it works for multiples); an entropy inequality on the joint distribution of certificate indicators across families might force a frequently-successful family.
why: Odd, but entropy methods recently produced constant-factor every-family results from nothing.
first_step: Compute the empirical joint distribution of success indicators of 10 certificate families over primes ≤ 10⁷ and the entropy of their union.
refs: arXiv:2211.09055 (Gilmer, A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture)

title: Derandomised Janson: P(no certificate) ≤ exp(−μ + Δ/2) in a pseudorandom model
connection: Janson's inequality bounds the probability that no event occurs among weakly dependent monotone events. For fixed p, with μ = expected certificates ≍ log²p and Δ the pair-dependency sum, a derandomised Janson (pseudorandomness of p's residues) would give R(p) > 0 when μ − Δ/2 → ∞.
why: Connects the campaign's Poisson zero-law heuristics to a precise inequality; the measured zero law (≈ 1.5–2.8 × swap-Poisson) says what Δ must be.
first_step: Compute μ and Δ for the (★) events (indexed by (u,B,C)) at test p, and compare exp(−μ + Δ/2) with the observed zero probability at the same M.
upgrade: Lovasz Local Lemma / Janson (existence from limited dependence)

title: Entropic Ruzsa distance between divisor-class distributions at different levels
connection: GGMT proved PFR via entropic Ruzsa distance and an entropy-decrement iteration. For fixed p, the distributions of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels C could be compared via entropic distances; structured failure would force small distances to subgroup-uniform distributions.
why: An odd but well-defined way to quantify 'subgroup trapping' of divisor classes across levels.
first_step: Compute entropic distances of the divisor-class distributions to uniform-on-subgroup distributions for hard p.
refs: arXiv:2311.05762 (Gowers-Green-Manners-Tao, On a conjecture of Marton)

title: Ramsey–ES: a monochromatic solution for every finite colouring (stronger statement)
connection: Croot proved every finite colouring has a monochromatic Egyptian representation of 1. Formulate Ramsey–ES: for every finite colouring of ℕ and every large prime p, is there a monochromatic (x,y,z) with 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z? If true, it implies ES and may be accessible to Croot-type density arguments (or be false, which is informative).
why: Strengthenings sometimes have better proofs; falsification would show which colourings are 'ES-hard'.
first_step: Test colourings by 2-adic valuation parity, by residue mod 3, and random 2-colourings for p ≤ 10⁴; look for primes with no monochromatic solution.
refs: arXiv:math/0311421 (Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. Math. 157 (2003))

title: Bloom/Liu–Sawhney machinery for few-term Egyptian representations with dense denominators
connection: Bloom: positive density sets contain S with Σ1/n = 1, via counting with main term + exponential sums on integers with structured anatomy. Ask what the machinery gives for k-term representations of 4/p (k fixed, small) with denominators restricted to structured sets (multiples of p with smooth cofactors).
why: Bloom's framework is the modern Fourier-analytic engine for unit-fraction existence; checking where it breaks for k = 3 localises ES's difficulty.
first_step: Read Bloom's §§2–4 and identify the minimal number of terms the method needs; check if it can handle 4/p = Σ_{i≤k} 1/n_i with k ~ 10 and n_i in a set of density zero.
refs: arXiv:2112.03726 (Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions)
upgrade: Bloom: unit fractions in dense sets

title: Graham's 77-theorem mechanism for ES-like partition problems
connection: Graham: if n is representable then so are 2n+2 and 2n+9, plus a finite check (78–333). The mechanism is affine closure maps. ES is closed under n → kn but no affine map n → an + b preserves solvability in general (it would be a Mordell-type identity). Determine all affine maps that preserve Type II solvability on some residue class.
why: Classifying affine closure maps tells exactly how far identity-based closure can go (Mordell–Schinzel-type limit).
first_step: Search a, b ≤ 100 for which ES-solutions of n map to solutions of an + b on a residue class, via the Type II parametrisation.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)
upgrade: Graham: every n > 77 is a sum of distinct integers with reciprocals summing to 1

title: Look-ahead greedy: provably terminating 3-term splitting rules
connection: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy terminates because the numerator decreases; the odd greedy algorithm is open. For 4/p, analyse non-greedy first-step rules (choose x among ⌈p/4⌉ + k for k ≤ K by a look-ahead criterion) and characterise primes where every rule with K ≤ K₀ fails.
why: A finite-look-ahead rule is a bounded procedure (B1 says it must fail for some p under H), but the failure set's structure is informative and computable.
first_step: For each p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least k such that x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves a two-term-solvable remainder; record the distribution and the extreme p.

title: Restricted-denominator ES: which congruence restrictions on x, y, z keep ES true?
connection: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a sum of distinct odd unit fractions (many terms). For three terms, all-odd is impossible (parity: 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) forces an even denominator). Classify restrictions (x,y,z in prescribed classes mod m) that are consistent with ES for all small p, and test which ones look 'every p'.
why: Restricted versions that hold numerically are stronger statements that may carry more structure for a proof (or reveal new obstructions).
first_step: For m = 3, 4, 5, 8 and all class-restriction patterns, compute the failure set among p ≤ 10⁶.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201

title: ES as an infinite congruence 'covering' of the non-squares; distortion-method analysis
connection: Hough and Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba bound the uncovered density of covering systems via a distorted-measure sieve. ES Type II (★): the classes p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) over all (u,B) must cover every prime; they never cover odd squares (T1). Study the uncovered set of the subsystem with moduli ≤ M within [1, X] as M grows.
why: The distortion method controls the uncovered set precisely for systems with many moduli; ES's system is explicit and its uncovered set is known to contain squares.
first_step: Compute the uncovered set of {−(u+B) mod 4uB : 4uB ≤ M} in [1, X] for M up to 10⁵, X up to 10⁸; compare its size with #squares + #(small sporadic) and track how fast non-squares disappear.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))
upgrade: Erdos minimum modulus problem for covering systems

title: Minimum-modulus-type statement: every certificate system covering a class must use a small modulus
connection: Hough: every distinct covering has a modulus ≤ 10¹⁶. ES analogue: for each Mordell-hard class r mod 840, any finite set of (★) congruences covering all primes in r ∩ [X, 2X] must include moduli of a certain size or divisibility (e.g. divisible by many small primes). Gives structural information on what certificates must look like.
why: Constraints on the moduli of any covering are a form of 'forced structure' usable in a proof by contradiction.
first_step: Empirically compute, for each hard class and dyadic X, the greedy minimum set of moduli covering all primes; record its smallest modulus and prime-divisibility profile.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))
upgrade: Erdos minimum modulus problem for covering systems

title: Left-tail extrapolation: does Σ_p P(R(p) = 0) converge?
connection: Goldbach's other conjecture failed at 5777/5993 where the expected representation count was small. For ES, extrapolate the measured zero law (P(R* = 0 | M)) to estimate Σ_p P(no certificate) over p > 10¹⁸; if it is ≪ 10⁻⁶, the 'heuristic' evidence for ES is overwhelming, and the computation identifies which sub-route is safest to target.
why: Sanity-checks which formulations are heuristically true for all p (needed before trying to prove them).
first_step: Fit log P(R* = 0 | M) on the repo's data and integrate against the distribution of M(p) for p > 10¹⁸; do the same for (★), b=1, union.

title: Modular forms mod ℓ for the ES word series
connection: Ono used half-integral weight forms mod m and Serre's Hecke-nilpotence/Chebotarev results to get congruences for every prime modulus. Reduce the ES word series W(q) = Σ_{t,u,v≥2} q^{tuv−u−v} (or the level series of Thm K) mod 2 or 3 and look for congruences with eta/theta quotients that determine R(p) mod m from p's class.
why: A modular congruence 'R(p) ≡ nonzero (mod m) on a class' is an every-p statement on that class.
first_step: Compute W(q) mod 2, mod 3 to 10⁶ terms and test linear relations with products of θ(q^k), η(q^k) modulo 2/3.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)
upgrade: Partition congruences for every prime modulus

title: Topological existence: Tucker/Ky Fan on a complex built from divisor lattices
connection: Lovász proved Kneser via Borsuk–Ulam; Tucker's lemma is its combinatorial form. Build a simplicial complex from divisor configurations of 4Cp+1 across levels with a free ℤ/2-action (d ↔ N/d swap or u ↔ B swap) such that an equivariant labelling without a 'complementary edge' is impossible, and complementary edges are certificates.
why: Topological methods give existence with no counting at all, immune to the polylog-main-term problem.
first_step: Toy version: for one level C, model divisors as vertices of a cross-polytope (±q_i) and check whether certificate-freeness defines an antipodal-free labelling; compute its index.

title: Strengthen to induct: a stronger ES statement with an inductive parameter
connection: Thomassen proved 5-choosability by proving a much stronger precoloured statement that inducts. ES candidates: 'for every p and every prescribed residue r of x mod 8 (or of C mod 3), a certificate with that property exists' — check numerically which strengthenings hold, then look for an induction parameter (number of prime factors of 4Cp+1, size of e).
why: Often the right strengthening is what makes induction possible; numerics cheaply filter candidates.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁶, which prescribed-property versions of (★)/ES hold for all p; keep the strongest surviving ones.
upgrade: Thomassen: every planar graph is 5-choosable (strengthened induction)

title: Representations with linear side conditions: ES certificates as constrained quaternion norms
connection: Machiavelo–Tsopanidis proved Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture (four squares with a linear condition) for every n. If ES certificates can be phrased as 'p (or 4Cp+1) is a norm from an order with a linear side condition on coordinates', their arithmetic arguments may transfer.
why: Linear side conditions on norm representations are exactly the shape of ES congruence constraints.
first_step: Read Machiavelo–Tsopanidis' method; try to phrase (★) as N(α) = 4Cp+1 with α in an order and a linear congruence on α's coordinates.
refs: arXiv:2003.02592 (Machiavelo-Tsopanidis, Zhi-Wei Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture and variations)

title: Type I via binary forms: divisors of p² + 4c²d in classes mod 4cd
connection: Class field theory decides which primes are represented by which forms. Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd). Divisors of values of X² + 4dY² are constrained by genus/class-group characters of disc −16d; the condition f ≡ −p couples them to p. Compute exactly which classes mod 4cd are possible for divisors, and show −p is excluded exactly when p is a square (T1).
why: Puts Type I in CFT language where every-p statements (Chebotarev, ring class fields) are standard.
first_step: For small d, c enumerate possible classes of divisors of p² + 4c²d mod 4cd via genus characters, and compare with −p's class; verify the T1 exclusion at squares.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)
upgrade: Primes x^2 + n y^2 (class field theory)

title: Bhargava-style composition on (★) triples (2×2×2 cubes)
connection: Bhargava's cubes give composition laws on binary forms. A (★) triple (u, B, C) with 4uBC − u − B = p might be the data of a 2×2×2 integer cube or a pair of binary forms whose composition carries ES structure.
why: A composition law on certificates would be a new structural tool (descent, closure).
first_step: Search for a cube A(u,B,C,p) with small entries whose Cayley hyperdeterminant or derived forms equal expressions like (4uC−1)(4BC−1) = 4Cp+1.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)
upgrade: Primes x^2 + n y^2 (class field theory)

title: Map the proved F_q[T] ES variants to their 'last ingredient'
connection: Function-field analogues (Goldbach over F_q[T], twin primes for large q) became every-degree theorems through RH for curves or étale cohomology. The repo notes ES over F_q[T] has proved variants; identify exactly which ingredient proved them (degree counting? Lang–Weil? an identity?) and its ℤ-analogue.
why: If the F_q[T] proof uses only 'degree' arguments, its ℤ-analogue is a size argument; if it uses Weil, the analogue is a missing RH-type input.
first_step: git grep -il 'F_q\[T\]' and read the relevant memos; extract the decisive step in each proof.
refs: Effinger-Hayes, Additive Number Theory of Polynomials over a Finite Field (1991)
upgrade: Function-field analogues (Goldbach over F_q[T], twin primes for large q)

title: Large-q limit for ES over F_q[T]: a Lang–Weil statement
connection: For fixed degree n and q → ∞, solutions of 4/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with deg bounded are F_q-points of a variety; Lang–Weil/Deligne give counts ~ q^{dim}. Identify the variety and its geometric irreducibility; the ℤ-analogue of 'q large' is a heuristic for which structures make ES easy.
why: Large-q results (Bary-Soroker, Sawin–Shusterman) are how hard ℤ-conjectures got function-field proofs; ES may already be easy there.
first_step: Write the variety of degree-bounded solutions for deg P = n small and compute its irreducible components (Magma/Sage over F_q).
refs: Effinger-Hayes, Additive Number Theory of Polynomials over a Finite Field (1991)
upgrade: Function-field analogues (Goldbach over F_q[T], twin primes for large q)

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł-type short-interval averages of R(n): what is free and what is not
connection: MR show multiplicative functions behave in almost all short intervals of length h → ∞; every-interval statements need h ≥ x^θ. For ES: the average of R(n) over almost all intervals of length (log n)^A is ≈ M; the step to every interval mirrors the step to every n.
why: Clarifies the ladder: every n ⇐ every short interval of length 1; quantify the shortest interval length for which an every-interval result can be proved.
first_step: Combine the short-interval exceptional-set bound (D)30 with the primes-in-short-intervals literature to find the smallest H(x) such that every [x, x+H] contains a prime with a (★) certificate.
refs: arXiv:1501.04585 (Matomaki-Radziwill, Multiplicative functions in short intervals)
upgrade: Matomaki-Radziwill: multiplicative functions in almost all short intervals (stuck mirror)

title: Rédei/Smith-style exact densities of level-failure profiles
connection: Koymans–Pagano proved Stevenhagen's density via Smith's method + reflection principles. The joint law of 'level C fails' events over p (governed by multiplicative structure of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)*) might be computable exactly by similar reflection/Rédei-symbol techniques, giving the true density of p failing (★) at all levels ≤ K.
why: Exact densities would sharpen the zero-law heuristics and could expose genuine structure among failures.
first_step: Compute empirical densities of failing-at-all-C ≤ K for K = 1..20 and compare with the independence model and with a Rédei-type model.

title: Tower of moduli with auxiliary primes (Shafarevich-style embedding problems)
connection: Shafarevich realised solvable groups by solving embedding problems step by step, choosing auxiliary primes to control local behaviour. ES: build a certificate as a sequence of lifts through moduli 4 → 8 → 24 → 840 → … with auxiliary prime factors of 4Cp+1 chosen at each step, keeping a global integer solution possible at each stage.
why: Gives a stepwise view of where integrality is lost; the final step (a genuine integer) is the crux.
first_step: Trace actual (★) certificates for hard primes: at which modulus in the tower does the certificate's structure become determined?
refs: Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Ch. IX
upgrade: Shafarevich: every solvable group is a Galois group over Q

title: Gradient ladder: infinitely many → positive proportion → 100% → every, for ES sub-statements
connection: Hardy→Selberg→Levinson→Conrey climbed the ladder for zeros on the line. For ES sub-routes (e.g. 'certificate with C ≤ (log p)^A', 'Type II with u = 1'), place each on the ladder (infinitely many / positive proportion / 100% / every) to find the highest rung reachable for a restricted family.
why: Restricted families at '100%' rung are cheap wins; the transition points show which restriction kills 'every'.
first_step: Tabulate known/expected rungs for 10 restricted sub-routes using repo results and quick numerics.
upgrade: Zeros on the critical line: infinitely many -> positive proportion (stuck gradient)

title: AKS-style 'too large and too small' group argument for a counterexample
connection: AKS: if n is not a prime power, a group of polynomials would be both ≥ a binomial lower bound and ≤ n^{√t}. ES: if p has no certificate, the set of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels generates a structure (e.g. a subgroup of Π_C (ℤ/4C)* avoiding all −1's) that might be shown both large (many independent prime factors across C) and small (avoidance).
why: The most striking conditional→unconditional derandomisation used exactly this double counting.
first_step: Define G_K(p) = subgroup of Π_{C≤K} (ℤ/4C)* generated by the vectors (q mod 4C)_C over primes q dividing some 4Cp+1; compute its index and whether it avoids the −1 pattern for hard p.
upgrade: PRIMES is in P (randomized / conditional -> deterministic unconditional)

title: Miller → AKS: deterministic certificate search for every p, with a provable bound
connection: Miller's test needed ERH to bound the search; AKS removed the hypothesis by a different certificate. ES certificate searches are fast in practice; a provable polynomial-time (in log p) algorithm that always returns a certificate would prove ES. Even a conditional one (under GRH) would be a new result.
why: Algorithmic formulations sometimes admit unconditional proofs via a cleverer certificate.
first_step: State precisely what a GRH-conditional 'ES certificate in time (log p)^A' would need (BM_CORRECTED says GRH gives only M_gen ≥ log log p) and what kind of different certificate could avoid that.
upgrade: PRIMES is in P (randomized / conditional -> deterministic unconditional)

title: Partial-colouring pigeonhole: collisions of near-certificates yield certificates
connection: Spencer/Beck: exponentially many colourings fall into few buckets, two collide, their difference is a good partial colouring. ES: generate many near-certificates for p (objects mapping to a small 'defect' space), pigeonhole two into the same bucket, and combine them (difference/quotient) into an exact certificate — the Pell/Dirichlet mechanism with an entropy count.
why: The entropy count tells exactly how many near-certificates are needed versus the bucket count; if near-certificates are power-many while buckets are polylog-many, collisions are guaranteed.
first_step: Identify a combination law (SL₂ quotients, divisor ratios) and a defect space; count near-certificates vs buckets for test p.
refs: Spencer, Trans. AMS 289 (1985) 679-706 (Six standard deviations suffice)
upgrade: Spencer's six standard deviations (random -> every set system)

title: Euler's false conjecture: an 'obstruction class' that turned out solvable
connection: Euler believed n ≡ 2 (mod 4) had no orthogonal Latin squares; only 2 and 6 fail. Mordell-hard square classes look like an obstruction class for identities, yet ES holds there numerically. BSP's recursive constructions crossed the class barrier — look for recursive (product) constructions for ES certificates that move from easy classes into square classes.
why: Product/recursive constructions are exactly what identities (polynomial in p) cannot do; ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn) is a product construction but goes the wrong way.
first_step: Search for constructions producing certificates for p from certificates for auxiliary integers in easy classes (e.g. via the e-slice N = (p+e)/4 structure).
upgrade: Euler's 36 officers: orthogonal Latin squares for every n != 2, 6

title: Residue-class case split with per-class constructions (Ringel–Youngs) — and its limit
connection: Ringel–Youngs proved the Heawood bound by 12 residue cases, each with its own construction family. ES: Mordell's identities do this for non-square classes mod 840; the square classes need infinitely many sub-cases. Measure how the number of needed per-class families grows with the modulus (cf. B1).
why: Quantifies the 'case explosion' and hence how far case-analysis approaches can go.
first_step: For M = 840·k, count the minimal number of polynomial certificate families needed to cover all non-square classes mod M; plot vs M.

title: Covering-system obstructions: could a finite set of primes block all certificate families at once?
connection: Erdős showed infinitely many odd n are not p + 2^k because a covering system makes every candidate divisible by a small prime — invisible to density heuristics and not Brauer–Manin. ES has no BM obstruction (BL), but check whether ES certificate families admit a covering-type obstruction on some infinite set (all certificates forced to be non-integral by a finite set of primes).
why: Disproof-side hygiene: covering obstructions are the classical way heuristically-true statements fail infinitely often.
first_step: Argue structurally: ES certificate existence is not a 'primality of many shifts' condition, so covering obstructions should not apply; make this precise by checking that certificate conditions are open in the profinite topology for non-squares.
refs: Erdos, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113-123 (On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems)
upgrade: Erdos: odd numbers not of the form p + 2^k (covering-system obstruction; cautionary)

title: p-adic interpolation along exponential families (Skolem–Mahler–Lech)
connection: SML proves zero sets of linear recurrences are periodic + finite via p-adic analytic interpolation. ES along n_s = a·b^s + c: certificate conditions involve divisors of 4C·n_s + 1 = 4Ca·b^s + (4Cc + 1), an exponential sequence; p-adic interpolation of 'divisibility by a fixed d' gives periodic structure in s, possibly proving ES for open families like 15·2^s + 1 by periodic covering + finitely many checks.
why: The repo already proved several exponential families via windows; SML-type periodicity could organise the remaining ones.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1 compute, for each small (C, d) with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the set of s with d | 4C·n_s + 1 (periodic in s); check whether a finite union of these covers all s.

title: Dual certificates: an exact 'magic function' proving positivity of a weighted ES count
connection: Viazovska's proof found an exact auxiliary function (from modular forms) satisfying sign conditions — a dual certificate. ES: seek weights w on certificate shapes and an exact identity Σ w·(certificates of p) = (explicit positive function of p) + (manifestly nonnegative terms), with the identity coming from modular forms (Thm K level series).
why: Positivity via an exact identity with sign conditions is a way to bypass error terms entirely.
first_step: Using the Thm K series, search linear combinations of level series (with q-expansion coefficients) whose p-th coefficient is a nonnegative combination of R_t(p) plus a known positive term.
refs: arXiv:1603.04246 (Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8)

title: LP/Positivstellensatz duality: proof-complexity view of ES failure
connection: Cohn–Elkies LP bounds have dual certificates; for integer feasibility, Positivstellensatz/Nullstellensatz/cutting-plane proofs certify infeasibility. If ES failed at p, a refutation exists in a strong enough system; show that refutations of 'no certificate with parameters ≤ X' in some algebraic proof system have degree growing with X, while the certificate-search space is fixed.
why: A proof-complexity lower bound for ES-refutations would be a new kind of evidence (and occasionally of proof).
first_step: Encode 'no (★) certificate with u, B, C ≤ X' for a fixed true p as an infeasible polynomial system and compute Nullstellensatz degree for small X.
refs: arXiv:1603.04246 (Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8)

title: Dimension-zero exceptional set as an intermediate target
connection: Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss showed Littlewood's exceptional set has Hausdorff dimension 0 via measure rigidity. ES analogue: E(N) ≪ N^ε (zero 'dimension') — strictly between the current N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) and finiteness.
why: A measure-rigidity or entropy approach might reach 'dimension 0' even if CRT sieves stop at exponent 3/4 (EXCEPTIONAL_KARY3).
first_step: Formulate the profinite/adelic dynamical system whose invariant measures would control ES exceptions and check whether an entropy argument bounds the counting dimension of the exceptional set.

title: Rademacher-type exact series for the ES level/word series
connection: Rademacher turned the Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotic into an exact convergent series for every n, with an explicitly bounded tail; Bringmann–Manschot extended exact expansions to some meromorphic Jacobi forms. METAPLECTIC Thm K writes the level series as Kronecker theta quotients θ(X²)/θ(X)² (meromorphic Jacobi-form-like); an exact Rademacher-type expansion of their coefficients would give R_t(p) as main term + explicit tail.
why: An exact formula with first term ≍ main term and an explicit tail is a pointwise-in-n statement by construction.
first_step: Check the modular/Jacobi properties of θ(X²)/θ(X)² as a function of (τ, z) and whether Bringmann–Manschot's framework (or Appell–Lerch sum expansions) applies; compute the first few terms numerically.
upgrade: Rademacher exact formula (asymptotic -> exact for every n)

title: Positivity from an exact divisor-sum formula: where the tail can be bounded
connection: For the partition function, positivity is trivial but Lehmer bounded the Rademacher tail explicitly. ES level counts are exact divisor-class sums (R_t(n) = D_t^−(tn+1) − β_t(n)); summing over t with weights, the 'tail' is the order-≥3 character part X(n). Ask for the explicit size of X(n) relative to M_BM in the exact formula at small levels.
why: Even without analysis, the exact formula tells which levels dominate and how much the tail can at most remove.
first_step: Compute M_BM(p) and X(p) separately for p ≤ 10⁷ and plot X(p)/M_BM(p); identify primes where it approaches −1.
upgrade: Rademacher exact formula (asymptotic -> exact for every n)

title: Monotone-quantity flow on certificate space
connection: Perelman finished Poincaré with a flow and monotone entropy that forces termination at a canonical object. ES: define a deterministic 'flow' on candidate triples (x, y, z) for 4/p (e.g. a descent on the defect 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) using local moves) with a monovariant that can only stop at a certificate, and prove no other stopping states exist (or classify them).
why: Odd but concrete: a local-move dynamical system on integer triples is easy to experiment with; classification of its sinks is a finite-ish problem per p.
first_step: Design local moves (change one coordinate by ±1, or by divisor-jumps) decreasing |defect| and compute sinks for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Σ over the first denominator of a two-term representation function (ternary-Goldbach shape)
connection: Ternary Goldbach averages a binary problem over one prime: Σ_p r₂(n − p). ES: R_ES(p) = Σ_x r₂^{EF}((4x − p)/(px)), where r₂^{EF}(m/N) = #{1/y + 1/z = m/N} is a divisor-pair count (a + b ≡ 0 mod m over divisor pairs of N). The average over x is the extra variable that made Goldbach-type problems pointwise.
why: Makes the 'three-variable' structure explicit with a sum over a long free variable x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4), whose length is power-size even if the main term is not.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of r₂^{EF} over x and the correlation between consecutive x; check whether the x-sum behaves like a sum of independent rare events.

title: Real-variable circle method for 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p
connection: Count near-solutions via ∫ S(α)³ e(−4α/p) K(α) dα with S(α) = Σ_{x≤X} e(α/x) (van der Corput sums of smooth phases); exact solutions need tolerance ~ 1/(pxyz), far below what such integrals resolve.
why: Not nonsense: it gives the density of near-solutions and the scale at which arithmetic must take over; it locates the 'resolution gap' quantitatively.
first_step: Estimate the number of triples with |1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 4/p| < δ as a function of δ via the integral and compare with exact counts for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Is M_BM a Siegel–Weil mass? A genus/class decomposition of certificates
connection: Tartakowsky/Siegel: the main term is a mass formula Σ_{classes in genus} r_L(n)/|Aut L| / Σ 1/|Aut L|. Check whether the BM-corrected main term M_BM(p) is a mass formula over some 'genus of certificate types'; if so the deviation splits into class/spinor contributions with their own theory.
why: A mass-formula interpretation would identify the analogue of the cusp part and of spinor exceptions (T1) in a conceptual way.
first_step: Express M_BM as Π of local densities (singular series) for the (★) variety and compare with the BL Brauer-corrected Siegel–Weil heuristics; look for the 'classes' whose average it is.
upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: Liouville/Mordell class-number formulas for xy + yz + zx = n meet ES
connection: Mordell (Amer. J. Math. 45 (1923) 1–4; verified) gives, for prime n, the number of positive solutions of yz + zx + xy = n as 3G(n) − 3 with G a class-number quantity — exactly the prime case ES needs. ES reads σ₂(x,y,z)/σ₃(x,y,z) = 4/p, i.e. xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/p: solutions with prescribed σ₂ = m and σ₃ = pm/4 are a sub-count of a class-number-sized count.
why: Connects ES directly to a classical every-n identity with class-number size (power-size) counts; the extra σ₃ condition is the cost.
first_step: Take Mordell's prime-n formula; then for ES solutions of small p tabulate m = xy+yz+zx and the class-number formula's prediction at n = m.

title: τ₃ in progressions beyond 1/2 (Type III / Kloosterman–Deligne) for the shifted-d₃ reading
connection: Zhang/Polymath used Type III estimates: the ternary divisor function in APs to moduli beyond √x via Deligne's bounds (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown, Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel). ES words count (u,B,C) with 4uBC = p + u + B — a shifted d₃-type count; METAPLECTIC notes a shifted-d₃/GL(3)-Eisenstein reading.
why: If ES can be put as 'τ₃-like function of a shifted argument in a progression', Type III technology offers power savings in exactly the needed shape.
first_step: Write the (u, B, C) count as Σ_{n} τ₃-like(n) over n in a progression determined by p; identify the modulus size relative to the length.
upgrade: GPY -> Zhang/Maynard (conditional EH -> unconditional bounded gaps)

title: Weak subconvexity: ES needs only an ε-saving over the trivial bound R ≥ 0
connection: Soundararajan's weak subconvexity extracts a (log)^{−δ} saving from multiplicativity and mean values alone. ES: R = M_gen + X with X ≥ −M_gen trivially (R ≥ 0); ES is exactly 'X > −M_gen', any saving over the trivial bound. Seek a multiplicativity-driven argument producing X ≥ −(1 − δ)M_gen.
why: Frames ES as the weakest possible improvement over a trivial bound, the regime where 'soft' multiplicative arguments sometimes succeed.
first_step: Identify the multiplicative structure of the coefficients in X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4uB evaluated at p) and test whether a Halász-type mean-value argument applies.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Zeta-type packaging of Type I/II counts at p^k (T1 kills even k)
connection: Hasse–Davenport/Weil: point counts over all extensions assemble into a rational zeta function, so a few counts determine all. T1 gives f_{I,II}(p^{2k}) = 0 for odd p. Study f_{I,II}(p^{2k+1}) and the series Σ_k f(p^k) t^k: any rationality or recursion linking f(p³), f(p⁵), … to f(p) would make f(p) > 0 follow from large odd powers.
why: Odd powers of p may have solutions that do not come from p; a recursion would be a Hecke-type relation in the 'p-power direction'.
first_step: Compute f_I, f_II at p, p³, p⁵ for small primes p ≤ 200 and look for linear recurrences in k.

title: Critical exponent of the ES word set on the Bourgain–Kontorovich dimension scale
connection: BK's density-one Zaremba needs the Hausdorff dimension of the bounded-quotient Cantor set above 5/6 (positive proportion above 1/2, etc.). The ES word set (minus-continuants of length 3 with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has #words ≤ X ≈ X log X; compute its effective 'critical exponent' and where it sits relative to BK thresholds.
why: Places ES in the thin-orbit hierarchy: it is 'fat' (exponent 1 with log), explaining density one, and shows the every-p question is about the log factor.
first_step: Count ES words ≤ X for X up to 10⁹ and fit X^δ (log X)^a; compare with the semigroup Hausdorff-dimension heuristics.

title: Rotation structure: fixing two word parameters makes ES a progression
connection: BGS's middle game uses 'rotations' (fix one Markoff coordinate → conic with a cyclic action). ES words p = tuv − u − v: fixing (t, u) gives v(tu − 1) = p + u, an arithmetic condition mod tu − 1; fixing (u, v) gives t·uv = p + u + v. Use these one-parameter 'rotations' to move between certificate-bearing and non-bearing configurations.
why: The local-to-global passage in BGS relies on such fibrations; ES has them in elementary form.
first_step: For hard p, compute for each (t,u) with tu ≤ T the residue of p + u mod tu − 1 and visualise the hit structure; look for orbit-like propagation.
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Goldfeld–Gross–Zagier-type effectivity: an auxiliary L-function with a high-order zero
connection: Goldfeld showed that an L-function with a zero of order ≥ 3 at s = 1/2 makes Siegel effective (Gross–Zagier supplied it). For an ineffective ES theorem (via Siegel), an analogous auxiliary object with a forced high-order vanishing would make p₀ explicit.
why: Only relevant once an ineffective all-large-p ES theorem exists, but it shows the route from ineffective to effective is not blocked in principle.
first_step: List places where Siegel's theorem could enter an ES argument (main-term lower bounds via L(1,χ)) and check whether Goldfeld's effective bound (h(−d) ≫ log d) is enough there.
upgrade: Heilbronn: class number h(-d) -> infinity (Gauss conjecture)

title: Modular units / Weber functions as certificate generators
connection: Heegner and Stark solved class number one through values of modular functions at CM points giving explicit Diophantine equations. Look for modular functions whose values at CM points related to p (disc −4p, −16p) are algebraic integers that factor into ES certificate data.
why: CM values give 'always-existing' algebraic objects attached to p; if their norms produce divisors in the right classes, existence follows.
first_step: Compute norms of Weber-function values f(√−p) or of singular moduli j((1+√−p)/2) differences for small p and check their prime factors against −1 (mod 4C) classes for the relevant C.

title: 8/n exceptions as a built-in falsification test
connection: Kolmogorov/Kahane–Katznelson show almost-everywhere statements can fail on prescribed null sets. ES has a real-world analogue: 8/n fails at 131 and 241 while being 'almost all'. Any ES argument that is uniform in the numerator m without a threshold would prove 8/131 — use this as a mandatory test for every candidate mechanism.
why: Cheap and decisive filter for proof attempts (already in FRONTIER (J)41); worth applying to each upgrade template in this list.
first_step: For each template here (complementary methods, pigeonhole + group law, Hecke relations, …) check whether its ES version would also apply verbatim to 8/131.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)
upgrade: Large values / Kolmogorov counterexample (a.e. cannot be upgraded)

title: Group-ring/Fourier formula for the window certificate count
connection: Olson's method works in group rings. For window e and N = Π q_i^{a_i} (coprime to e), the number of coprime divisor pairs (a, b) with ab | N and a ≡ −b (mod e) equals (1/φ(e)) Σ_{χ mod e} χ(−1) Π_i (1 + Σ_{1≤j≤a_i} (χ(q_i)^j + χ̄(q_i)^j)). ES at window e ⟺ this is > 0.
why: An exact character-sum formula for each window; non-vanishing is a statement about one finite character sum, open to zero-sum/Fourier techniques.
first_step: Implement the formula, verify against brute force, then study which characters dominate when the count is 0 for hard (p, e) pairs.

title: Certificate-search complexity as a heuristic proxy
connection: Three cubes is 'computation only' because representations are astronomically large. ES certificates are tiny and fast to find; measure the asymptotic cost of the cheapest search (e.g. via Lenstra divisors-in-classes or e-slice scans) as p grows to quantify how 'easy' every p is.
why: If the search cost provably stays polylog for all p in a model, a proof by 'algorithm + analysis' (AKS-style) becomes a natural target.
first_step: Benchmark the cheapest certificate finder on the adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵ and fit cost vs log p.

title: Dvir-type bound for certificate-free residue sets modulo q
connection: Dvir's polynomial argument shows Kakeya sets are large. Dual question for ES: how large can a set A of residues r mod q (q prime) be such that no r ∈ A admits a (★)-type certificate with parameters in a box (u, B, C ≤ Q)? A low-degree polynomial vanishing on A and its 'directions' could bound |A|.
why: Upper bounds on certificate-free residue sets mod q translate into 'most residues are covered' statements with explicit polynomial-method constants.
first_step: Compute certificate-free residue sets mod q for q ≤ 10⁴ and box sizes Q; compare their sizes with q·(1 − c) and check for algebraic structure (squares?).
refs: arXiv:0803.2336 (Dvir, On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields)

title: Special-function positivity (Askey–Gasper) for weighted ES counts
connection: de Branges reduced every n to the Askey–Gasper positivity of Jacobi-polynomial sums. Seek weights w_C on levels such that Σ_C w_C · D_C(p) is expressible as a positive combination of 'basis' quantities via a classical positivity identity (e.g. Fejér kernels, Jacobi sums), valid for all p.
why: Every-n positivity theorems often reduce to one special-function inequality; ES weighted counts have explicit Fourier expansions over characters.
first_step: Write the character expansion of Σ_C w_C D_C(p) and search for weights making the coefficient vector positive-definite (Bochner/Fejér-type), at least in a model where p's character values are free.

title: Case-by-case → uniform: the small-n Bieberbach proofs were all different
connection: Before de Branges, each n (2–6) needed a different method; the uniform proof came from changing the statement (Milin's stronger conjecture). ES analogue: the repo's exponential families each needed bespoke windows; look for a stronger uniform statement (Milin-like) that implies all of them.
why: Suggests searching for the right stronger statement rather than more cases.
first_step: List the proved families (3·2^s+1, 7·4^s+9, 63·2^s+1, 4^s+k) and extract the common certificate mechanism; formulate a single conjecture implying all and test it on the open families.

title: Collatz wall vs ES wall: what Tao's 'almost all' could not do
connection: Tao proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via 3-adic mixing of the Syracuse random variable; every orbit is out of reach for the same quantifier reason as ES. Compare the precise failure point of both arguments (single-orbit vs averaged mixing).
why: A side-by-side 'what fails' analysis of two famous almost-all walls can suggest which extra structure ES has that Collatz lacks (ES has algebraic structure: divisors, characters, modular forms).
first_step: Write a one-page comparison: Tao's Syracuse estimate vs Vaughan/ES exceptional-set estimates; note where ES has exact algebraic identities (Thm K) that Collatz lacks.
refs: arXiv:1909.03562 (Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values)
upgrade: Collatz: almost all orbits attain almost bounded values (stuck mirror)

title: Logarithmic density as an intermediate notion for ES-type sub-routes
connection: Tao's Collatz and Chowla results hold in logarithmic density, which is easier than natural density. For ES sub-routes whose failure sets might be infinite (e.g. (★) alone), compute logarithmic-density statements and the corresponding 'log-averaged' tools (Tao's entropy decrement).
why: Log-averaging made several almost-all results possible where natural density was stuck; useful for sub-route exceptional sets.
first_step: Estimate Σ_{p ≤ X, (★) fails} 1/p numerically and check whether log-averaged tools give a finite bound.
refs: arXiv:1909.03562 (Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values)
upgrade: Collatz: almost all orbits attain almost bounded values (stuck mirror)

title: Ultraproduct transfer between F_q[T]-ES and ℤ-ES statements
connection: Ax–Kochen: first-order statements true for F_p((t)) for almost all p transfer to Q_p for almost all p. ES over F_q[T] has proved variants; ES itself is not first-order in the needed way (it quantifies over integers of unbounded size), but bounded-complexity sub-statements (certificates of bounded 'shape') are. Identify which transfer.
why: Clarifies precisely which ES-type statements a model-theoretic transfer could ever reach (and that the full statement likely cannot).
first_step: Formulate ES sub-statements with bounded quantifier complexity (e.g. 'a certificate with C dividing a fixed polynomial in p') and check whether they are decidable/transferable.
upgrade: Ax-Kochen: Artin's C2 conjecture for all large p (via ultraproducts)

title: All-but-finitely-many with genuine small exceptions (Terjanian) — ES-type numerator analogues
connection: Ax–Kochen's statement is true for p > p₀(d) and false for some small p (Terjanian). The ES numerator family behaves similarly: 4/n has no known exception, but 8/n fails at 131, 241. A structural explanation of where p₀(m) lies for m/n would show what makes m = 4 special.
why: Understanding why 4 behaves like 'p₀ = 1' while 8 has small exceptions is a sharp test of any mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate the exceptions of m/n for m ≤ 30 (PW data) and search for a statistic predicting their largest exception (cf. Schinzel's exp(m^{1/3+o(1)})).
upgrade: Ax-Kochen: Artin's C2 conjecture for all large p (via ultraproducts)

title: Covering-system disproof search on exponential families (Sierpiński-type)
connection: Sierpiński/Erdős obstructions arise when every member of an exponential family is forced to have a small prime factor. For ES families n_s = k·2^s + 1, check whether a covering system could force every certificate condition to fail for all s (it would give infinitely many ES counterexamples).
why: Disproof-side: open families (15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297) are exactly where such an obstruction would show up first.
first_step: For n_s = 15·2^s + 1, compute for small (C, d) the periodic sets of s with a certificate; check whether their union is all s (proof) or misses a progression (potential covering obstruction).
refs: Erdos, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113-123 (On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems)
upgrade: Erdos: odd numbers not of the form p + 2^k (covering-system obstruction; cautionary)

title: Splitting-condition families: ES for all p with (p/ℓ) = −1 for a fixed small ℓ
connection: Linnik's ergodic method proved Duke-type equidistribution under a fixed splitting condition. Intermediate ES goal: prove ES (or (★)) for all p in the set {p : (p/ℓ) = −1} for one fixed ℓ (e.g. ℓ = 3 excluded by Mordell classes; ℓ = 11, 13, …), where the BM main term at levels involving ℓ is guaranteed.
why: A fixed non-residue gives a guaranteed positive BM contribution (SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9); a theorem for one fixed ℓ would be the first infinite every-p family of Mordell-hard primes.
first_step: For ℓ = 11, 13, 17 compute the (★) and ES₅ counts restricted to levels using ℓ, over primes with (p/ℓ) = −1; check whether these restricted counts ever vanish.
refs: Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss-Michel-Venkatesh, Ann. Math. 173 (2011) (Distribution of periodic torus orbits and Duke's theorem for cubic fields) / Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems (Duke's theorem and Linnik's ergodic method)
upgrade: Linnik's ergodic method (equidistribution on spheres) -> ELMV

title: Ineffective all-large p for the subfamily of p with a bounded non-residue profile
connection: Duke–Schulze-Pillot's theorem is ineffective but for every large n. Target: 'for every fixed L, all sufficiently large p with ℓ(p) ≤ L satisfy ES' (ineffectively). Since ℓ(p) ≤ L for 100% of primes as L → ∞, this would be a strong almost-all-with-structure result.
why: Combines the guaranteed BM positivity at small ℓ with a Siegel-type ineffective control of the error at those levels.
first_step: Formulate the restricted count using only levels built from primes ≤ L and estimate its main term vs error for fixed L as p → ∞.

title: Escape of mass for ES: certificates drifting to extreme shapes
connection: Soundararajan's step was 'no escape of mass': limiting measures are probability measures. ES analogue: as p → ∞, could the certificates' normalized shape distribution (log C / log p, log u / log p) concentrate at the boundary (C ≈ 1 or C ≈ p), so that 'typical' regions are empty? Show mass stays in the bulk.
why: If certificates escape to extreme shapes for hard p, proofs focusing on bulk shapes miss them; if not, bulk counting suffices.
first_step: For hard primes vs controls, compute the empirical distribution of (log C/log p, log u/log p) of all certificates.

title: Pell-shaped conjecture: Type I ∪ II for all odd non-squares beyond a finite list
connection: Pell is solvable exactly for non-squares. ES Type I/II fail at all odd squares (T1) and, per the repo, U(n) fails at odd squares plus {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}. Formulate the precise 'Pell-shaped' conjecture (Type I ∪ II solvable for every odd non-square n outside an explicit finite list) and treat it as the natural target with the right exception set.
why: A conjecture whose exception set is exactly squares + finite list has the shape of classical every-n theorems (Pell, three squares).
first_step: Extend the Type I ∪ II census over odd non-squares (not just primes) to 10⁹ and confirm the exception list.

title: Entropy count of near-certificates vs defect buckets
connection: Spencer's partial colouring needs (#objects) > (#buckets)·(something). For ES, near-certificates of p with defect δ in a set of size Q number ~ p^{a}; buckets (defect, residues) number ~ Q^{b}. If a > b·log Q / log p, collisions are forced; compute a and b for concrete combination laws.
why: A pure counting check that tells whether any pigeonhole + combination mechanism can possibly work for ES.
first_step: For the SL₂-form near-certificates (det = 1 + δ with |δ| ≤ Δ), count objects with entries ≤ p and the number of congruence buckets needed for the quotient to be integral.
refs: Spencer, Trans. AMS 289 (1985) 679-706 (Six standard deviations suffice)
upgrade: Spencer's six standard deviations (random -> every set system)

title: Affine-group encoding: (★) as a product-covering statement in Aff(ℤ/q)
connection: In small groups (affine group of F_q, order q(q−1)) the Gowers/Nikolov–Pyber thresholds are less demanding. The (★) condition (4uC − 1) | (p + u) can be read as an affine relation x ↦ 4uC·x − u evaluated mod divisors; look for a formulation as 'target ∈ A·B·C' in an affine group with sets of size ≈ q^{2/3}.
why: If an encoding into a small quasirandom-enough group exists, the 'one more factor' trick could cover every target mod q; integrality still needs a size argument.
first_step: Search encodings: map (u, C) ↦ affine maps mod q and check whether the product set of three natural sets covers Aff(F_q) for q ≤ 101.
upgrade: Gowers quasirandom groups / Nikolov-Pyber product covering

title: Parity of Ω(4Cp+1) and certificate existence
connection: Chen's theorem lives at the parity barrier (P₂ but not primes). Certificates at level C need a divisor in a class; if 4Cp+1 is prime, the only divisors are 1 and itself (class 1), so prime values of 4Cp+1 are useless. Measure the dependence of certificate probability on Ω(4Cp+1).
why: Tells whether ES needs 'many prime factors' (sieve-friendly almost-primes in reverse) and quantifies the loss from prime values.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁹ and C ≤ 10⁵ tabulate P(certificate at C | Ω(4Cp+1) = k) for k = 1..8.

title: Basis of order 3 vs order 4: Egyptian 'order' of 4/p is ≤ 4 trivially
connection: Schnirelmann bounds the order of a basis. For unit fractions, 4/p is always a sum of 4 unit fractions (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)), and 3/m splits into ≤ 3 terms); ES asks for order 3. Study the 'order-3 deficiency': which 4-term representations of 4/p are 'one merge away' from a 3-term one (two terms with 1/a + 1/b a unit fraction)?
why: Turns ES into a merging problem on abundant 4-term representations, a different combinatorial entry point.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ enumerate 4-term representations with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; compare with the number of 3-term solutions.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706
upgrade: Schnirelmann constant (Goldbach-type every n with bounded number of primes)

title: Hooley's GRH-conditional pointwise proofs: what GRH buys ES pointwise
connection: Hooley proved n = p + x² + y² for all large n under GRH before Linnik's unconditional proof. The repo says GRH gives only M_gen(p) ≥ (1 − o(1)) log log p for ES. Pin down exactly which GRH-type statement (GRH for which family, with which uniformity) would give a pointwise ES theorem, as Hooley's did.
why: Knowing the exact conditional input needed is the first step of any conditional → unconditional upgrade (Hooley → Linnik pattern).
first_step: Re-derive SINGLE_P_COUNT (J)98 and identify where GRH's log-log loss arises (number of characters vs. length); test whether 'GRH + pair correlation' or 'GRH for higher-order characters' changes it.
refs: Linnik, The dispersion method in binary additive problems (AMS 1963)

title: Quaternion (Hurwitz) proof of four squares: Euclidean order as the 'every p' engine
connection: Lagrange's theorem has a proof via the Hurwitz order being (left) Euclidean: p = ππ̄ factors, giving p as a norm. ES quaternion reformulations (repo) would need an order with a Euclidean-like property relative to a congruence structure tied to 4C.
why: If the relevant order (or its Eichler sub-order of level 4C) has class number one for small C, ES at those levels follows from factorisation.
first_step: Compute class numbers of Eichler orders of level 4C in the Hurwitz quaternion algebra (Sage) for C ≤ 20 and compare with which levels never fail.

title: Genus-theory exclusion at squares mirrors the 4^a(8b+7) exclusion
connection: Three squares fail exactly on 4^a(8b+7) — a local obstruction at 2. T1 is a global (reciprocity) exclusion at odd squares for Type I/II. Look for a ternary/quaternary encoding where the T1 exclusion becomes a local obstruction (at 2 or at an auxiliary prime) after a change of variables, which would make it 'genus visible'.
why: If T1 could be made local in some encoding, the remaining problem would be a pure genus-to-class question.
first_step: Test encodings: n ↦ 4Cn + 1 for small C; at odd squares n = m², check whether 4Cm² + 1's divisor-class failure is explained by local conditions at 2 or at primes dividing C.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: GRH + computation template for ES sub-routes with explicit exceptions
connection: Ono–Soundararajan: GRH-conditional explicit threshold + computation to 2·10¹⁰ gives an exact exception list. For a sub-route whose failures are explicitly known (b=1 line: 193, 2521, 66529 ≤ 10¹¹), attempt a GRH-conditional proof that there are no further failures.
why: A conditional complete classification for a sub-route would be a first 'every p' theorem (conditional) in the ES landscape.
first_step: Identify the sub-route with the simplest certificate condition (b=1: p + 4d has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4d) and attempt a GRH-conditional lower bound for its count with explicit constants.
upgrade: Ramanujan's ternary form x^2+y^2+10z^2 (stuck at conditional)

title: Corrected local-global: formulate ES sub-routes with their reciprocity exceptions removed
connection: After the Apollonian disproof, the corrected conjecture excludes the reciprocity families. For ES sub-routes, formulate 'corrected' versions (e.g. Type I/II for all non-squares; (★) for all p outside an explicit reciprocity-defined set) and test which corrected statements have finite exception sets.
why: Ensures the targets are the right ones before attempting proofs.
first_step: Use the repo's census data to fit, for each sub-route, its failure set to explicit reciprocity conditions; report residual sporadic failures.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)

title: Large-degree analogue: ES for m/p as m grows with p
connection: Tao's Sendov proof works for sufficiently high degree, using the degree as a large parameter. ES has a natural large parameter family: m/p for growing m (ES_m). Uniform-in-m results exist for the exceptional set ((D)31: E_m(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4} m^{−1/4})); study the regime m ≈ log p where Schinzel-type exceptions appear, as a 'large-parameter' analogue.
why: The large-m regime has genuine exceptions; the transition region may show which mechanism protects m = 4.
first_step: Compute the least m(p) for which m/p fails (3-term) for primes p ≤ 10⁵, and the distribution of m(p)/log p.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Zero-sum over levels: among many levels, some combination of near-certificates is exact
connection: EGZ guarantees a zero-sum subsequence of prescribed length. ES near-certificates at different levels C carry 'defect classes' in groups (ℤ/4C)*; if defects lived in a common group, a zero-sum subsequence of defects could combine into an exact certificate (requires a combination law across levels).
why: Odd: needs a multiplicative combination law; but zero-sum theory exactly converts 'many near-misses' into 'one hit'.
first_step: Find a common quotient group for defects at levels C ≡ 0 (mod M) (e.g. (ℤ/M)*) and test whether products of near-certificates at different levels produce certificates at the lcm level.

title: Croot's 'one target, all colourings' as a pointwise model for ES
connection: Croot's theorem is pointwise in the target (exactly 1) and uniform over colourings — the quantifier structure ES needs (one target 4/p, every p). Study Croot's proof for which step converts averaged Fourier information into a single-target statement.
why: Croot's argument is one of the few in Egyptian fractions where a specific target is hit for every configuration; its key lemma may transfer to 'every p' with a family of targets.
first_step: Read Croot (Ann. Math. 2003) and isolate the single-target step; test whether its numerics (number of terms, smoothness) can be squeezed to 3 terms for targets 4/p.
refs: arXiv:math/0311421 (Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. Math. 157 (2003))

title: Explicit inequalities + finite check as the complete proof shape
connection: Bertrand's postulate is fully proved by an explicit inequality for n ≥ n₀ plus a hand check. For ES, collect every inequality-type sufficient condition (e.g. M_BM(p) > |X(p)| bound, Lagrange-pigeonhole ratio > 1 for some e, single-prime certificate count ≥ 1) and see if any admits an explicit lower-bound/upper-bound argument for all p ≥ p₀ with p₀ ≤ 10¹⁸.
why: Forces each mechanism to be phrased as an inequality between explicit quantities — useful even if none closes.
