first_step: Write the 5 most promising sufficient conditions as explicit inequalities and evaluate both sides numerically at p ~ 10¹⁸ for the adversarial primes.

title: Modularity of an ES generating object and a 'level-lowering' contradiction
connection: Ribet's level lowering forced a hypothetical form to level 2 where none exists. ES generating functions (Thm K level series) are modular of level t; a failure of ES at p might force some auxiliary modular form (e.g. a twisted combination vanishing at p) to have a special property that lowers its level or weight to a space that is empty.
why: Speculative, but 'empty space of modular forms' contradictions are the archetypal every-n mechanism.
first_step: Search for linear combinations of level-t series whose p-th coefficient is R(p) times a nonzero constant, and determine the space they live in; ask whether vanishing at all ES-failing p would force membership in a smaller space.

title: Family of twists by characters mod p: R as a coefficient of a p-twisted object
connection: Subconvexity in the q-aspect uses the family of all characters mod q. ES at p involves characters mod p evaluated at small integers ((−m/p) in T(p)); consider the family {R_χ(p) : χ mod p} of character-twisted certificate counts and its moments, where orthogonality mod p is available.
why: The q-aspect family is the natural family for a fixed p (it does not need varying p), so moment methods apply without leaving p.
first_step: Define R_χ(p) = Σ_{certificates} χ(u)… for χ mod p; compute Σ_χ |R_χ(p)|² exactly by orthogonality and see whether it controls the trivial-character term.

title: Frobenius count in SL₂(ℤ/q) for the SL₂ form of ES
connection: Ore-type proofs count solutions of word equations via Σ_χ χ(g)/χ(1). The SL₂ form asks for γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c); reduced mod q this is a count of elements in a double-coset-type subset of SL₂(ℤ/q); its character expansion has nontrivial terms bounded by 1/χ(1) ~ 1/q.
why: Shows how much cancellation is available 'for free' in a nonabelian encoding (local information only, but with strong decay).
first_step: Compute for primes q the number of solutions mod q via characters of SL₂(F_q) and compare with the abelian (genus) expansion's error.
refs: arXiv:0904.4146? (Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010))
upgrade: Ore conjecture / Waring problem for finite simple groups

title: Distribution of certificates across dyadic level ranges
connection: Primes in every short interval vs almost all: the analogue at fixed p is whether certificates appear in every dyadic level range [K, 2K] (K ≤ p^{1/2}) or cluster. With R(p) ≍ log²p spread over ≍ log p dyadic ranges, ≍ log p certificates per range are expected.
why: If every dyadic range typically carries certificates, a proof could target one range of convenient size (e.g. C ≈ p^{1/3}) where tools are best; if they cluster, that range is fixed by the data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10¹⁰ in the hard list, histogram certificates by ⌊log₂ C⌋ and record the empty ranges.
upgrade: Primes in short intervals for every x

title: Saving in x versus saving in H: the exact form an every-n exceptional bound must take
connection: Every-interval results for primes need savings depending on the location x, not only on the interval length H. For ES, (D)30 gives E(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4}); a bound E(I) ≪ H·exp(−c(log x)^θ) uniform down to H = 1 would be < 1 for H ≤ exp(c(log x)^θ), hence ES. So the target is an x-dependent saving in short intervals.
why: Makes precise how 'almost all in short intervals' must improve to reach 'every': any argument giving savings in log x at fixed small H is already pointwise.
first_step: Re-examine the (D)30 proof and identify where the saving is tied to H (the number of n averaged) rather than to x; ask whether any piece gives x-dependent savings.
upgrade: Primes in short intervals for every x

title: Extreme-value statistics of the least certificate parameter
connection: Linnik-type theorems bound the least prime in a class. Measure the least certificate parameter (least C for (★), least e for windows) as p grows and fit an extreme-value law; a provable bound of the observed shape would be the 'Linnik constant' of ES.
why: Calibrates which quantitative statements are plausible (e.g. C(p) ≤ (log p)^A for all p?) before trying to prove any.
first_step: From the repo's census (and adversarial primes at 10¹⁸–10²⁵) tabulate max over p ≤ X of least C and least e versus log X.

title: Integral Brauer–Manin for the (u,B,C) threefold as a family of affine conics over the C-line
connection: For fixed C, (★) is the hyperbola (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1) = 4Cp + 1, an affine conic. Integral Hasse/BM results for families of affine quadrics (Colliot-Thélène–Xu, strong approximation with BM) treat such fibrations; analyse the total space over the C-line.
why: BL computed Br for the ES surface; the (u,B,C) threefold is a different model where fibrewise integral BM is classical.
first_step: Compute the Brauer group of the generic fibre (a split conic? then trivial) and the integral obstruction for the total space; compare with BL's ℤ/2.
refs: Davenport, Phil. Trans. A 251 (1959)/ Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963)
upgrade: Hasse principle for forms in many variables

title: Vinogradov's smooth-number trick for divisor classes
connection: Vinogradov bounded n(p): if every ℓ ≤ y is a QR, all y-smooth numbers are QRs, contradicting character-sum bounds since smooth numbers are plentiful. ES: if level C fails, no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (mod 4C); if additionally we know the classes of small primes, smooth parts of 4Cp+1 are constrained. Count C for which 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor in a forced class.
why: Transfers a proven every-p argument shape (n(p) bounds) to divisor classes, using smooth numbers in APs (Granville, Harper).
first_step: Model: fix the classes mod 4C of primes ≤ y; count C ≤ X such that 4Cp+1 has a y-smooth divisor d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) using smooth-number distribution; compare with data.

title: Kummer-style 'regular' primes for ES: an invariant κ(p) that makes ES provable
connection: Kummer proved FLT for regular primes (p ∤ class number) long before Wiles. Look for an arithmetic invariant κ(p) (class number of ℚ(√−p), 2-rank/4-rank, parity of the fundamental unit norm of ℚ(√p), ℓ(p)) such that ES (or a sub-route) is provable for all p with κ(p) in some set, giving an infinite every-p family.
why: Partial every-p theorems on natural infinite sets of Mordell-hard primes do not yet exist; Kummer's theorem is the historical model.
first_step: Correlate (★)/ES₅ counts with κ(p) candidates for p ≤ 10⁸ and look for an invariant whose small/large values guarantee many certificates.

title: Limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (a Sato–Tate/Cohen–Lenstra-type law)
connection: Sato–Tate identified the exact limiting law of normalised a_p. For ES, determine the limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (and of f(p)/log³p) as p → ∞ through Mordell-hard primes; its behaviour near 0 is what decides ES heuristically.
why: A precise conjectural law with a computable left tail sharpens the heuristic case for ES and indicates which normalisation is 'right'.
first_step: Histogram R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes in windows at 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰; test convergence and fit the left tail.
refs: Barnet-Lamb-Geraghty-Harris-Taylor, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011) 29-98 (A family of Calabi-Yau varieties and potential automorphy II)

title: Ramanujan-type congruences for ES counts on progressions
connection: Ramanujan/Ono congruences say p(An + B) ≡ 0 (mod m). Search for progressions An + B on which f_II(n) or R(n) is always ≡ 0 (mod m) (m = 2, 3, 4, 8) beyond the trivial evenness; such congruences would reveal modular structure that might also produce nonzero congruences at primes.
why: Systematic congruence mining is cheap and has historically uncovered hidden modular structure.
first_step: Compute f_II(n), R(n) for n ≤ 10⁷ and test all A ≤ 840, B mod A for congruences mod 2, 3, 4, 8.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)
upgrade: Partition congruences for every prime modulus

title: ES as an orbifold Euler-characteristic realisation problem (triangle groups, Hurwitz spaces)
connection: Chen's Markoff theorem is a statement about Hurwitz spaces. Note: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1 is the orbifold Euler characteristic of the sphere with cone points of orders x, y, z. So ES(p) ⟺ some triangle orbifold S²(x,y,z) has χ^orb = (4 − p)/p, i.e. hyperbolic area 2π(p − 4)/p.
why: Gives ES a geometric/topological reading where covering-space and Hurwitz-space divisibility arguments (as in Chen) might apply.
first_step: Work out what Riemann–Hurwitz says for covers of S²(x,y,z) with χ = (4 − p)/p (index must be divisible by p); look for a moduli space whose nonemptiness is equivalent to ES(p).
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Prime-capture problems: every prime is caught by an infinite family of Chebotarev conditions
connection: Chebotarev forbids any finite family of splitting conditions from catching every prime; ES Type II (abelian conditions p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB) and Type I (dihedral conditions via ring class fields) are infinite families with conductors up to ≍ p. List known 'every prime is captured by a family with conductor ≤ f(p)' theorems (e.g. least non-residue: some ℓ ≤ p^{0.152} has (p/ℓ) = −1) and place ES among them.
why: Identifies the closest proven 'prime-capture' statements and how their conductor bounds compare with what ES needs.
first_step: Write the conductor/size of the capturing family for ES sub-routes and for known capture theorems (Burgess, Linnik, Vinogradov) in one table.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)
upgrade: Primes x^2 + n y^2 (class field theory)

title: Class-number parity (genus theory, Rédei) as the source of oddness for a Zagier-type argument
connection: Heath-Brown's/Zagier's proofs use a set whose size parity is forced. Natural sets attached to p have sizes tied to class numbers h(−4p), h(−8p), whose parities/2-parts are governed by genus theory and Rédei symbols. Find an ES-related finite set whose cardinality equals (up to known even terms) such a class number with known parity.
why: Supplies the 'odd cardinality' input a parity proof needs from established theory.
first_step: Compute |S_p| for candidate sets (e.g. reduced forms of disc −16p with an extra congruence) and compare parity with h(−4p), h(−8p) and Rédei-symbol predictions.

title: Polynomial certificate families in the Gaussian variables (a,b), p = a² + b²
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in n covering the square classes; identities in the variables (a, b) with p = a² + b² are a different class. T1 requires that at odd-square points (Pythagorean (a,b)) such an identity yield only non-Type-I/II (imprimitive) solutions, which is not obviously impossible.
why: A genuinely new parametrisation space for identity searches, exactly where the classical obstruction may not bite.
first_step: Search low-degree X, Y, Z ∈ ℚ[a,b] with 4XYZ = (a²+b²)(XY+YZ+ZX) identically and X,Y,Z positive integral on a congruence region; check behaviour at Pythagorean points.

title: Genus-theoretic parametrisations: Mordell-hard primes as values of principal-genus forms
connection: Gauss's genus theory: p is a square mod 840-type moduli iff p lies in principal genera of the relevant discriminants, so p = Q(x, y) for a form Q in a principal genus (disc −4·210 etc.). Seek certificate families polynomial in (x, y) for p = Q(x, y), exploiting that Mordell-hard classes are exactly where these representations exist.
why: Turns 'square classes' from an obstacle into a parametrisation: hard primes come with extra representations.
first_step: For Mordell-hard primes ≤ 10⁷, compute representations by forms of discriminants dividing −4·840 and correlate (x, y) with known certificates (u, B, C).
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Large prime factors in the AP {4Cp + 1 : C ≤ K} (Sylvester–Schur/Shorey–Tijdeman)
connection: Sylvester–Schur: products of consecutive integers have a large prime factor; Shorey–Tijdeman extend to AP terms. For ES, a single prime q | 4Cp+1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is a certificate. Large prime factors are guaranteed in the product over C ≤ K; the class condition q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is the extra requirement.
why: Gives a guaranteed supply of large prime divisors; the problem reduces to a class-distribution question for these forced large primes.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁹, list the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10⁴ and test the rate at which it is ≡ −1 (mod 4C) against 2/φ(4C)-type models.
refs: Erdos, J. London Math. Soc. 9 (1934) 282-288 (A theorem of Sylvester and Schur)
upgrade: Sylvester-Schur (prime factors of products of consecutive integers / AP terms)

title: Legendre-formula bookkeeping for Π_C(4Cp+1): which primes can make up the product?
connection: Sylvester–Schur works by bounding the contribution of small primes via Legendre's formula. For Π_{C≤K}(4Cp+1) the contribution of each prime q is explicit by CRT (q divides the terms with C ≡ c_q mod q). Compute the share of the product coming from primes q that could serve as single-prime certificates, versus the rest.
why: Makes the 'size argument' quantitative: if certificate-capable primes must contribute a definite share of log Π, one of them must divide some term in the right class.
first_step: Compute Σ_{q} (number of C ≤ K with q | 4Cp+1)·log q split by whether 4c_q | q+1-type conditions can hold.
refs: Erdos, J. London Math. Soc. 9 (1934) 282-288 (A theorem of Sylvester and Schur)
upgrade: Sylvester-Schur (prime factors of products of consecutive integers / AP terms)

title: Erdős–Selfridge distinct-small-parts mechanism for consecutive levels
connection: Erdős–Selfridge: writing consecutive factors as a_i·(power) forces the a_i to be distinct and small, contradiction by counting. ES failure forces each 4Cp+1 (C = 1, …, K) into a thin multiplicative set S_C; write 4Cp+1 = a_C·b_C with b_C the S_C-compatible part and look for a forced-distinctness/smallness contradiction among the a_C.
why: An elementary combinatorial mechanism for consecutive terms that might bite on the explicit sets S_C at small C.
first_step: For C ≤ 8 characterise S_C explicitly (e.g. S_1: all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) and test numerically how small K can be such that no prime has 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K... (there are such primes for each K; record their density decay).
upgrade: Erdos-Selfridge: a product of consecutive integers is never a perfect power

title: Instance transformation that preserves certificate existence but amplifies counts
connection: Reingold transformed every graph into an expander while preserving connectivity. ES: find a transformation p ↦ (structured object with power-many 'attempts') such that ES(p) ⟺ the object has a 'connected/nonzero' property that is robustly detectable (e.g. a spectral quantity), amplifying the polylog main term.
why: If the count can be amplified while preserving the zero/nonzero status, the polylog-main-term barrier (B2) changes character.
first_step: Look at natural equivalences ES(p) ⟺ ∃e (window) and ES(p) ⟺ ∃C (level); build a graph on (e, divisors of N_e) whose connectivity property is equivalent to ES(p), and compute its spectral gap for small p.
refs: Reingold, J. ACM 55 (2008) Art. 17 (Undirected connectivity in log-space)
upgrade: Undirected connectivity in logspace (randomized -> deterministic for every graph)

title: Randomized certificate search with provable success → derandomize
connection: Before Reingold, connectivity was in randomized logspace. ES certificates are found by trying random e or C; a proof that a random attempt succeeds with probability ≥ 1/poly(log p) for every p would already be ES; the derandomization view asks for an explicit small 'hitting set' of attempts for every p.
why: Hitting-set language matches B1's analysis of bounded procedures and suggests pseudorandom-generator constructions (attempt sets that fool the certificate test).
first_step: Define the certificate test as a function of the attempt (e, or C); compute the minimal hitting set for all primes ≤ 10⁸ and its growth.
refs: Reingold, J. ACM 55 (2008) Art. 17 (Undirected connectivity in log-space)
upgrade: Undirected connectivity in logspace (randomized -> deterministic for every graph)

title: Wielandt-style orbit counting: a group action whose non-certificate orbits have size ≡ 0 (mod m)
connection: Wielandt proves Sylow existence because |X| = C(p^a m, p^a) ≢ 0 (mod p), so some orbit has size prime to p. ES: find a finite set X_p (e.g. 4-term or 'imprimitive' representations, or divisor configurations) with a group G (ℤ/3 permuting coordinates, S₃, or a dihedral group of moves) acting so that every orbit not containing a certificate has size divisible by m while |X_p| ≢ 0 (mod m).
why: Generalises the Zagier involution (m = 2) to larger groups where the needed congruence of |X_p| may be easier to establish.
first_step: Enumerate candidate (X_p, G) pairs for small p and check orbit-size divisibility; look for one where |X_p| mod m is given by a formula in p.
upgrade: Counting modulo p via group actions (Wedderburn/Witt, Wielandt's Sylow proof)

title: Class-equation divisibility: Φ_n(q)-type obstruction to 'no certificate'
connection: Witt's proof of Wedderburn: the class equation has all terms but one divisible by Φ_n(q), forcing a contradiction. For ES, write an exact counting identity for a quantity attached to p (e.g. Σ_C τ(4Cp+1) over a full period, or a divisor-class census over (ℤ/4C)*) as a sum over 'orbits' where all non-certificate terms are divisible by some cyclotomic-type number.
why: A divisibility contradiction needs no asymptotic analysis.
first_step: Look for counting identities over complete residue systems (C mod q) where certificate-free contributions have a forced common factor.
upgrade: Counting modulo p via group actions (Wedderburn/Witt, Wielandt's Sylow proof)

title: Arithmetic constructions cover some classes, interlacing covers all: the LPS → MSS lesson
connection: LPS/Morgenstern built Ramanujan graphs arithmetically only for degrees d − 1 = prime power; MSS proved existence for every d by a non-arithmetic existence method (interlacing families). ES: Mordell identities (arithmetic) cover all non-square classes mod 840; the square classes may need a non-identity existence method of a comparable kind.
why: Historical precedent that 'arithmetic constructions stop at a class barrier, existence methods cross it'.
first_step: Identify the analogue of 'expected characteristic polynomial' for ES: a polynomial built from the family of attempts (levels C or windows e) whose real-rootedness/root location certifies existence for some member.
refs: arXiv:1304.4132 (Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava, Interlacing families I: all degrees)
upgrade: Interlacing families: Ramanujan graphs of every degree; Kadison-Singer

title: Interlacing families over windows: real-rooted averages certify a good window
connection: MSS: if a family of real-rooted polynomials has a common interlacer, some member's largest root is ≤ that of the average. Define for each window e a polynomial f_e(t) (e.g. Π over prime factors q of N_e of (t − Re χ(q)) for a character χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1) whose root location detects certificates; average over e.
why: Converts 'some e works' into a statement about an averaged polynomial, which can be computed or estimated.
first_step: Construct toy f_e for small e, test interlacing numerically for hard p, and check whether the average polynomial's root implies a certificate for some e.
refs: arXiv:1304.4132 (Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava, Interlacing families I: all degrees)
upgrade: Interlacing families: Ramanujan graphs of every degree; Kadison-Singer

title: Exceptional set of the two-term step is tiny: 'almost all two-term + rescue' structure
connection: Goldbach–Linnik used that the binary Goldbach exceptional set is small enough for a sparse rescue set. In ES, the two-term step m/N = 1/y + 1/z (after choosing x) fails on a thin set of (m, N); show that for every p, among the ≍ p choices of x the pairs (m_x, N_x) cannot all lie in that thin set, using its explicit structure.
why: The thin exceptional set of the two-term problem is explicit (divisor-class avoidance), so 'cannot all avoid' is a concrete combinatorial statement.
first_step: Characterise {(m, N) : m/N not a sum of two unit fractions} for small m and compute the fraction of x ∈ (p/4, p/2) for which (4x − p, px) lands in it, for hard p.

title: Eventual periodicity of 'ES-easy' residue structures (Wilson-style)
connection: Wilson showed the set of orders admitting designs is eventually periodic, so finitely many residue classes need checking. For ES sub-routes, test whether 'the set of levels C at which the BM main term is positive for all p in a class r mod M' is eventually periodic in C, giving a finite description of guaranteed-positive levels.
why: Eventually periodic structures can be checked by finite computation and then fed into an every-p argument.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each hard class r the set of C ≤ 10⁴ with M_C^lev > 0 for all p ≡ r (mod M·4C) and test periodicity in C.

title: Precoloured version: ES with a prescribed denominator divisible by a given small prime
connection: Thomassen's induction works for a stronger precoloured statement. Candidate strengthening: for every prime p and every small prime r, there is an ES solution with r | x (or r ∤ any denominator). If such a refined statement holds numerically, its extra structure might allow an induction over r or over the e-slice.
why: Strengthenings with an inductive parameter are how many every-n combinatorial theorems were proved.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, check which (r, condition) refinements hold for all p; record the first failure for each.
upgrade: Thomassen: every planar graph is 5-choosable (strengthened induction)

title: Uncovered density of the (★) system restricted to moduli with bounded prime factors
connection: Hough's argument tracks how the uncovered set shrinks as primes are added to the moduli. Restrict ES congruences p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) to moduli 4uB built from primes ≤ y; compute the uncovered density δ(y) among integers in the hard classes and its decay in y.
why: A precise decay law for δ(y) (power of log y? exp?) quantifies how many prime 'layers' certificates need — a structural fingerprint of ES.
first_step: Compute δ(y) for y ≤ 50 by inclusion over moduli dividing a bounded smooth number, restricted to n ≤ 10⁸ in hard classes.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))
upgrade: Erdos minimum modulus problem for covering systems

title: Variance-to-mean ratio of R(p) as a quasi-independence diagnostic
connection: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard's key was showing overlaps are small on average (quasi-independence). For ES, the variance of R(p) over primes near X relative to its mean measures overlap; Poisson-like behaviour (ratio ≈ 1 after removing the genus fluctuation) indicates quasi-independent events.
why: If the residual variance after the BM/genus layer is ≈ mean, the second-moment method is near-optimal and the remaining obstacle is purely the 'single realisation' issue.
first_step: Compute Var(R(p) − M_BM(p))/E[R(p)] in windows at 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰.

title: Primitive part of 4Cp+1 relative to smaller levels as a 'new divisor' source
connection: Zsigmondy isolates primes dividing a^n − 1 but no earlier term. For fixed p, call a prime factor q of 4Cp+1 'new' if q ∤ 4C′p+1 for C′ < C (equivalently c_q = C). New primes have c_q = C < q, and a new prime q is a single-prime certificate iff 4C | q + 1. Study the number of new primes at each level.
why: New-prime counts give an explicit, level-ordered supply of candidates with a clean certificate test.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ compute the new primes at each level and the frequency of 4C | q + 1.

title: From Tijdeman (effective finiteness) to Mihăilescu (exact): bound first, then algebra
connection: Catalan moved from 'finitely many, bounded effectively' to 'exactly one' via algebra that did not need the bound. For ES-type finiteness targets (e.g. finitely many (★)-failures), an algebraic characterisation of failures (all 14 known (★)-failures share a property P) might give the exact list without analysis.
why: The 14 known (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ are a finite data set where an exact algebraic description is testable.
first_step: List the 14 primes with their factorisations of 4Cp+1 for small C, residues mod 840·k, and ℓ(p); look for a shared algebraic property and test it as a predictor above 10¹⁰.

title: Euler-system-style bounds on the 'obstruction group' of certificate-free levels
connection: Kolyvagin bounded Selmer groups with an Euler system of Heegner points. Define for p the 'obstruction group' O_p = set of levels/windows that fail with their local data; a norm-compatible system of near-certificates across levels (if it existed) would bound O_p and force it to be smaller than the set of all levels.
why: Highly speculative, but Euler systems are the one tool that converts a supply of compatible objects into a bound on an obstruction.
first_step: First check whether near-certificates at levels C | C′ satisfy any norm/trace compatibility (e.g. divisor classes mod 4C′ reducing to classes mod 4C).

title: Furstenberg-set analogue: certificate 'lines' in the (C, d) plane
connection: Kakeya/Furstenberg estimates bound unions of lines/tubes from below. For fixed p, each prime q gives the 'line' {C ≡ c_q (mod q)} of levels where q | 4Cp+1; certificates are incidences of these lines with the conditions 4C | (product of chosen q's) + 1. An incidence-geometry lower bound might force a certificate.
why: Incidence bounds are robust every-configuration statements; ES at fixed p is an incidence problem between residue lines and divisibility conditions.
first_step: Plot, for small p, the incidence structure (q, c_q) and the certificate incidences; ask for the right incidence theorem (Szemerédi–Trotter over ℤ/q? Bourgain–Katz–Tao in F_q?).
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)

title: Slice-rank of the ES 'certificate tensor' modulo q
connection: The cap-set proof bounds sets avoiding a pattern via the slice rank of the pattern's indicator tensor. Consider the tensor T(u, B, C) = 1[4uBC − u − B ≡ p (mod q)] over F_q³; its slice rank bounds how large a product set of parameter values can avoid certificates mod q.
why: Gives polynomial-method bounds on 'certificate-avoiding parameter sets' mod q, a local statement with sharp constants.
first_step: Compute the slice rank (or a polynomial-method upper bound) of T for small q and compare with the largest avoiding product sets found by search.
refs: arXiv:1605.01506 (Croot-Lev-Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small)

title: Union-closed structure of the family of ES-solvable sets of numerators
connection: Gilmer's method applies to union-closed families. For each n, the set A_n = {m : m/n is a 3-term Egyptian fraction} — is the family {A_n} (or its complements) closed under unions/intersections in a way that forces a frequent element (a numerator m that works for most n)? For m = 4 the conjecture is 'all n'.
why: Odd, but the numerator–denominator incidence structure (with 8/n failing at 131, 241) is a natural set system to analyse with these tools.
first_step: Compute A_n ∩ [1, 30] for n ≤ 10⁵ and test closure properties and element frequencies.
refs: arXiv:2211.09055 (Gilmer, A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture)

title: Is ES critical or supercritical? Fractional expectation threshold of the level hypergraph
connection: Park–Pham relate thresholds to expectation thresholds. The repo measures ≈ (0.44 → 0.97)·log p expected hit levels (critical regime). Compute, in a random model matching ES's level statistics, the threshold for 'some level hits' and see whether ES sits above it by a growing margin.
why: If ES is only 'critically' above threshold in natural models, any proof must exploit non-random structure; if supercritical, second-moment-type methods are favoured.
first_step: Simulate the matched random model and compute P(no hit) as a function of the scaling parameter; compare with data for hard primes.
refs: arXiv:2203.17207 (Park-Pham, A proof of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture)

title: Classify all 'transfer maps' between ES instances via the e-slice
connection: Graham's closure maps transfer representability from n to 2n+2, 2n+9. For ES, the e-slice transfers between p and N = (p+e)/4. Classify maps T: (N, e) ↦ (N′, e′) such that a certificate for (N, e) yields one for (N′, e′); a rich enough transfer system could connect every instance to verified ones.
why: Transfer systems are the engine of closure-type every-n proofs.
first_step: Search small linear maps (N, e) ↦ (aN + b, ce + d) preserving −1 ∈ Rat_e(N) on all data with N ≤ 10⁶.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)
upgrade: Graham: every n > 77 is a sum of distinct integers with reciprocals summing to 1

title: Harmonic-sum thresholds for the denominator set of ES solutions
connection: Liu–Sawhney: a set A ⊂ [1, N] with Σ_{n∈A} 1/n ≥ (log N)^{4/5+o(1)} contains S with Σ_{S} 1/n = 1. ES solutions for p use denominators in {multiples of p} ∪ {numbers ≈ p/4 … p²}; compute the 'harmonic mass' of the possible denominator sets and compare with such thresholds (for 3 terms, thresholds are presumably different, but the bookkeeping shows the gap).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from the regime where density-based unit-fraction theorems apply.
first_step: Compute Σ 1/n over the set of denominators appearing in any ES solution for p (data) and over natural supersets.
refs: arXiv:2112.03726 (Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions)
upgrade: Bloom: unit fractions in dense sets

title: Antipodal structure: the swap involution u ↔ B as a free ℤ/2-action on near-certificates
connection: Borsuk–Ulam/Tucker need a free ℤ/2-action. The (★) data (u, B) ↦ (B, u) is a ℤ/2-action, free off the diagonal u = B; certificates come in swap pairs (R(p) even). Study the ℤ/2-index of the space of near-certificates (a cell complex over levels) — a non-trivial index would force a fixed configuration, i.e. a certificate.
why: Uses a symmetry ES already has (R(p) even) in a topological rather than parity way.
first_step: Build a small complex for p ≤ 10³ (cells = near-certificates, faces = relaxations) and compute its ℤ/2-index.

title: Multiplicative-function structure of the level indicator at fixed p
connection: MR's method uses multiplicativity in n. At fixed p, the function C ↦ D_C(p) is not multiplicative in C, but N ↦ 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod t] is 'multiplicative-ish' in N for fixed t. Study the Dirichlet-series/Halász structure of n ↦ D_t^−(tn + 1) for fixed t (its mean value over n is controlled by Halász-type theorems).
why: Halász/MR techniques give 'every interval of length h' results for multiplicative functions; level-t certificate indicators along n might be accessible.
first_step: Express 1[D_t^−(tn+1) > 0] via the multiplicative set S_t and compute its mean in short intervals of n numerically; compare with Landau–Ramanujan-type predictions.
refs: arXiv:1501.04585 (Matomaki-Radziwill, Multiplicative functions in short intervals)
upgrade: Matomaki-Radziwill: multiplicative functions in almost all short intervals (stuck mirror)

title: Rédei-type reciprocity explains T1 — look for its 'higher' analogues in ES sub-routes
connection: Negative Pell's obstructions beyond local ones come from Rédei symbols (higher reciprocity). T1 is a quadratic-reciprocity cancellation. Search for Rédei-symbol-type (quartic/biquadratic) conditions that predict extra failures of sub-routes ((★), b=1, ES₅) among primes, beyond what the BM/genus layer explains.
why: If found, such conditions refine the main term (like Stevenhagen's refinement) and sharpen targets; if absent, the genus layer is complete.
first_step: Compute Rédei symbols [a, b, p] for small a, b and correlate with (★) failures / low counts.

title: Auxiliary-prime choice with prescribed local behaviour for windows
connection: Shafarevich's embedding-problem induction succeeds by choosing auxiliary primes with prescribed local behaviour at each step. For ES windows, choose the window prime q with prescribed splitting behaviour in fields built from p (e.g. q splits in ℚ(√p, i) or has given Frobenius in a Kummer extension) so that Rat_q(K) is forced to contain −1.
why: Chebotarev guarantees auxiliary primes with any prescribed Frobenius; if the window certificate were a Frobenius condition, existence would follow.
first_step: Test whether success of window q for p is predicted by the Frobenius of q in ℚ(ζ_8, √p) or in Kummer fields ℚ(ζ_4, p^{1/4}).
refs: Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Ch. IX
upgrade: Shafarevich: every solvable group is a Galois group over Q

title: Positive proportion of levels with a certificate is false — find the right normalisation
connection: Selberg's positive-proportion step needed the right normalisation (zeros up to height T). For ES at fixed p, only ≍ log²p of ≍ p levels carry certificates; identify the natural finite set of 'attempts' of which a positive proportion succeed (e.g. levels C ≤ (log p)^A, windows e ≤ (log p)^B with weights), so that a positive-proportion statement would be meaningful and imply ES.
why: A positive-proportion statement over a small set of attempts is a pointwise statement; finding the set where proportions are stable is the first step.
first_step: For hard primes, compute success proportions over attempt sets of various shapes and sizes; find shapes where the proportion stays bounded below as p grows.
upgrade: Zeros on the critical line: infinitely many -> positive proportion (stuck gradient)

title: Measure-rigidity on the adelic space of 'residue profiles' of p
connection: EKL used higher-rank diagonal actions and entropy. The residue profile of p (its classes modulo all 4C) lives in Ẑ; the joint action of multiplication by many integers on Ẑ is 'higher rank'. Ask whether invariant measures for such actions with positive entropy are classified, and whether ES-failing profiles would support an invariant measure.
why: A structural (measure-rigidity) description of the profinite failure set could bound its 'dimension' (Littlewood-style intermediate result).
first_step: Formulate the action of (ℕ, ×) on Ẑ restricted to the closure of ES-failing profiles, and check against Furstenberg/Rudolph-type rigidity statements for ×a, ×b actions on solenoids.

title: Fourier interpolation/uniqueness: ES data at primes determine a function vanishing somewhere?
connection: Radchenko–Viazovska Fourier interpolation shows a function is determined by values at √n. Odd idea: the function n ↦ R(n) (or its smoothed version) is determined by data on a sparse set via modular identities (Thm K); if R vanished at p, interpolation formulas would force a contradiction with positivity elsewhere.
why: Interpolation/uniqueness theorems from modular forms are a way to transfer information between sparse and dense sets of n.
first_step: Check whether Thm K level series admit Rademacher/Fourier-interpolation-type formulas expressing R(p) via values at other n with explicit kernels.
refs: arXiv:1603.04246 (Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8)

title: Hardest residue cases needed new constructions: identify ES's 'case 3 mod 12'
connection: In Ringel–Youngs some residue classes (e.g. cases 1, 9 mod 12) took years and ad hoc ideas. Among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 (1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529), measure which is hardest (lowest counts, most sub-route failures) and focus constructions there.
why: Concentrating effort on the hardest class mirrors the historical endgame.
first_step: From census data, compute per-class mean/minimum of R(p)/log²p and sub-route failure counts.

title: Power-size main terms are not enough: p + m² is open with a √n main term
connection: Hardy–Littlewood's conjecture that every large non-square n is p + m² has main term ≍ √n/log n, yet is open pointwise (binary). So 'lift ES to a count with a power-size main term' (TART items) is necessary but not sufficient: the lifted problem must also have enough free variables (ternary-or-more) for minor-arc control.
why: Self-correction for the power-main-term items: specifies the extra requirement (dimension) any lift must meet.
first_step: For each proposed lift V_p of ES, count the number of free variables after fixing p and compare with the Kloosterman/circle-method thresholds (≥ 4 for quadratic-type, more for cubic).
refs: Hardy-Littlewood, Partitio Numerorum III, Acta Math. 44 (1923) (Conjecture H)
upgrade: Hardy-Littlewood: every large non-square n = p + m^2 (stuck mirror with a square obstruction)

title: Two square degeneracies: algebraic factorisation (p + m²) vs reciprocity (ES Type I/II)
connection: p + m² degenerates at squares because n − m² = (a − m)(a + m) allows at most one representation (m = a − 1); T1 makes Type I/II fail at odd squares through a reciprocity cancellation. Compare: exceptional-set technology for p + m² is power-saving (H. Li 2003: E(X) ≪ X^0.982; verified), more advanced than ES's; can ES's T1 be rewritten as an algebraic factorisation in some model (e.g. 4Cm² + 1 or (p + e)/4 at squares)?
why: If T1 becomes algebraic in some coordinates, Hardy–Littlewood-type machinery for 'non-square n' transfers more directly.
first_step: At n = m², examine 4Cm² + 1 and (m² + e)/4 for algebraic factorisations that explain the absence of certificates (e.g. Sophie Germain-type identities).
refs: Hardy-Littlewood, Partitio Numerorum III, Acta Math. 44 (1923) (Conjecture H)
upgrade: Hardy-Littlewood: every large non-square n = p + m^2 (stuck mirror with a square obstruction)

title: Exact characterisation of sub-route success sets (Brjuno-type)
connection: Yoccoz showed the Brjuno condition is exactly the linearisable set, turning 'almost every' into 'iff'. For ES sub-routes, seek the exact arithmetic characterisation of the success set (e.g. Type I ∪ II succeeds iff n is not an odd square and n ∉ finite list; (★) succeeds iff …), including a mechanism producing the failures.
why: An exact 'iff' is the strongest form of an every-type theorem and forces understanding of the failure mechanism.
first_step: For (★) and b=1, fit the failure sets ≤ 10¹⁰/10¹¹ to candidate closed-form conditions and look for a constructive mechanism that produces the failures (as Yoccoz constructed non-linearisable examples).
upgrade: Siegel/Brjuno/Yoccoz: from almost-every to an exact characterisation

title: Brjuno-type sum as a certificate-difficulty index
connection: The Brjuno sum Σ log q_{n+1}/q_n measures cumulative small-divisor difficulty. Define an analogous additive difficulty index for p (e.g. Σ over small levels C of −log of the probability that level C fails given p's residues) and test whether ES certificate counts are governed by it.
why: A single scalar controlling difficulty would focus both proofs and adversarial searches.
first_step: Compute the index for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p), least certificate C and sub-route failures.
upgrade: Siegel/Brjuno/Yoccoz: from almost-every to an exact characterisation

title: Lehmer's τ(p) ≠ 0 as a structural twin of ES
connection: τ(p) ≠ 0 is open for every p although density-one non-vanishing is known and congruences (mod 691, 2^k, 3^k, 5, 7, 23) exclude vanishing on all but a thin set of residue classes. ES: Mordell identities exclude all but six classes mod 840; the remaining classes need size/structure input. Compare the two endgames.
why: Two famous 'non-vanishing at every prime' problems with identical architecture (congruence exclusion + thin residual set) — methods for one may inspire the other.
first_step: Write the comparison: what is known about the residual set for τ (e.g. τ(p) = 0 forces p in specific classes mod large M) vs ES's square classes; check whether ES has analogues of the mod-ℓ Galois-image arguments.
upgrade: Lehmer's conjecture tau(n) != 0 (stuck mirror; congruences give non-vanishing on classes)

title: Congruence mod ℓ from a mod-ℓ Galois image: ES counts with large-image structure
connection: Swinnerton-Dyer's classification of exceptional primes for τ gives congruences τ(p) ≡ explicit function of p (mod ℓ). If ES counts (or a weighted combination of level series, Thm K) were coefficients of a form with a mod-ℓ Galois representation, congruences R(p) ≡ g(p) (mod ℓ) would follow, and ES would hold wherever g(p) ≢ 0.
why: Turns ES non-vanishing into a congruence problem with explicit exceptions — the τ approach.
first_step: Check whether the theta-quotient/Eisenstein parts of Thm K have coefficients satisfying Eisenstein-type congruences mod small ℓ (they are divisor sums twisted by characters, so congruences like σ_χ(N) ≡ … mod ℓ may exist).
upgrade: Lehmer's conjecture tau(n) != 0 (stuck mirror; congruences give non-vanishing on classes)

title: Jacobi-symbol parity forces a prime factor in a nonresidue class — how far toward the exact class?
connection: Elkies: (−D/H_D(j)) parity forces a prime factor inert in ℚ(√−D). ES windows: (N_e/e) = (p/e) for N_e = (p+e)/4, so if (p/e) = −1 then N_e has a prime factor q with (q/e) = −1 (FORCED_WINDOW's condition). ES needs more: a divisor ratio exactly ≡ −1. Identify what extra 'forcing' (higher-order characters, sign/size of N_e) could pin the class.
why: Clarifies the gap between the proven quadratic forcing and the needed exact-class statement; Elkies needed only a quadratic class.
first_step: For window primes e ≡ 3 (mod 4) with (p/e) = −1, measure the distribution of the forced nonresidue factors' classes and how often a complementary divisor completes −1.
upgrade: Elkies: every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many supersingular primes

title: Sign/size arguments on special values: choose auxiliary objects whose values have forced factors
connection: Elkies chose D so that H_D(j(E)) has a controlled sign and size. ES: choose auxiliary integers built from p (values of polynomials P(p) or norms from auxiliary fields) whose sign/size/Jacobi symbol forces a prime factor in a class tied to a level C, with the factor also dividing 4Cp + 1.
why: A systematic search space for 'forcing' constructions that guarantee prime factors in classes.
first_step: Search quadratic polynomials P with P(p) | (4Cp+1)·(something) for families of C and compute Jacobi-symbol constraints on their prime factors.
upgrade: Elkies: every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many supersingular primes

title: Conjecture I3 as ES's cleanest 'universality' cousin of Cauchy/Waring
connection: Cauchy's polygonal theorem and Waring are universality statements. Conjecture I3 (FRONTIER §7: every n > 2 433 600 is tuv − u − v with t, u, v ≥ 3) is a sign-free, prime-free universality statement for a cubic polynomial; universality proofs for polynomials (Cauchy's lemma, Linnik's 7 cubes via ternary forms) are natural models.
why: I3 drops ES's 4ℤ constraint on t; a proof technique for I3 is the right first test of any universality mechanism.
first_step: Read EXSET_I3.md / I3_DEEP_ASTRA.md; then try a Cauchy-lemma-style reduction: for fixed t, tuv − u − v = n ⟺ (tu − 1)(tv − 1) = tn + 1 — ask which t make 'tn + 1 has a factorisation into two factors ≡ −1 (mod t), both ≥ 3t − 1' provable for all large n.
refs: Nathanson, Proc. AMS 99 (1987) 22-24 (A short proof of Cauchy's polygonal number theorem)

title: Universality classification for the family a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d
connection: Bhargava classified universal quadratic forms by finite criteria. For the cubic family F(t,u,v) = a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d with lower bounds on t, u, v, classify which members represent every large integer (I3 is the member a = b = c = 1, d = 0, bounds ≥ 3) and find the nearest universal member to ES's constrained form.
why: Mapping the universality frontier in a family containing ES shows which constraint (4 | t, sign of d, bounds) is decisive.
first_step: Compute exception sets up to 10⁸ for small (a, b, c, d) and bounds; record which appear finite.

title: Uniformity obstruction for linear-forms-in-primes certificate schemes at fixed p
connection: For fixed p, every ES certificate has bounded size (denominators ≤ O(p²)), so any 'auxiliary primes' scheme needs prime tuples of linear forms in a box of size ≍ p whose coefficients depend on p. Green–Tao–Ziegler asymptotics are not uniform in coefficients comparable to the box, so they do not apply directly (correcting the BHS item).
why: Records precisely why the conditional→unconditional (Harpaz–Skorobogatov–Wittenberg) move does not transfer to ES as stated, and what uniformity would be needed.
first_step: State the needed uniform version: count of t ≤ T with L_i(t) all prime for forms with coefficients ≤ T^{1+ε}; compare with known uniform results (e.g. for a single form: Brun–Titchmarsh / Siegel–Walfisz ranges).
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)

title: Polynomial-in-m identities for n = m² + k (Schinzel's obstruction is in n, not in m)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbid identities polynomial in n covering square classes. For families n = m² + k (k ≠ 0) parametrised by m, identities X(m), Y(m), Z(m) with 4/(m² + k) = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z on congruence classes of m are not excluded by that theorem. Determine for which k such identities exist.
why: Would give every-m theorems for quadratic families — a new kind of infinite family for ES beyond exponential ones.
first_step: Search polynomial X, Y, Z of degree ≤ 4 in m for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 (with congruence conditions on m), via undetermined coefficients.
refs: arXiv:2005.02998 (Skorobogatov-Sofos, Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points)
upgrade: Schinzel Hypothesis H for 100% of polynomials (stuck mirror)

title: Trivial vs needed pointwise bound for the non-genus part X(p)
connection: Ramanujan/Deligne improved the trivial (Hecke) bound to the sharp one. For ES, compute the trivial pointwise bound for |X(p)| (from the character expansion) and the bound needed (|X| < M_gen); quantify the gap in powers of log p.
why: Measures how much 'Ramanujan-type' saving ES needs in the non-genus part.
first_step: Bound |X(p)| ≤ Σ_q Σ_{χ mod q, ord ≥ 3} |stuff|/φ(q) trivially and evaluate numerically against M_gen for test p.

title: Exact CRT independence in the level variable at fixed p
connection: LLL/Janson need limited dependence. At fixed p, the events {q | 4Cp + 1} for distinct primes q are exactly independent and uniform over complete periods of C (CRT); the only C-dependence that breaks independence is the class condition modulo 4C itself. Separate the two: write certificate events as (CRT-random divisibility pattern) × (C-dependent class test).
why: Identifies a genuine source of exact independence at fixed p, which probabilistic arguments could exploit without averaging over p.
first_step: Formalise for C in a range [K, 2K] with periods Q = Π_{q ≤ y} q: the divisibility pattern is equidistributed over C mod Q; compute the conditional certificate probability given the pattern and the size of C.
upgrade: Lovasz Local Lemma / Janson (existence from limited dependence)

title: The b=1 line as a 'Goldbach's other conjecture' model with sporadic failures
connection: The b=1 line fails at 193, 2521, 66529 and nowhere else ≤ 10¹¹ — like 5777 and 5993 for Goldbach's other conjecture. Fit the expected b=1 count at these primes and test whether failures are 'explained' by small expected counts; calibrate the same model on (★) (14 failures ≤ 10¹⁰).
why: Validates the heuristic models on sub-routes with real failures before trusting them for ES.
first_step: Compute the b=1 model main term at all p ≤ 10⁷ and the empirical P(fail | main term); check that the three failures sit at the extreme low end.

title: Descent to universal torsors: more variables for the circle method
connection: Heath-Brown and others proved Manin-type results via universal torsors, which have more variables and simpler equations. ES's Type I/II parametrisations (Elsholtz–Tao) look like torsor coordinates; identify the universal torsor of the ES surface (BL computed its Brauer/Picard data) and count integral points on its twists with fixed p.
why: More variables after descent is the standard route to circle-method feasibility; the torsor equations may be quadratic in many variables.
first_step: From BL's description of Pic of the compactification of U_n, write torsor equations and compare with the ET parametrisation n = 4abcd − … ; count variables per equation.
refs: Davenport, Phil. Trans. A 251 (1959)/ Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963)
upgrade: Hasse principle for forms in many variables

title: Elsholtz's windmill framework for sums of two squares and related problems
connection: Zagier's proof was generalised combinatorially (Elsholtz, 'A combinatorial approach to sums of two squares and related problems', Additive Number Theory: Festschrift for M. B. Nathanson, Springer 2010, 115–140; verified). Elsholtz is also an ES author (ET 2013); check whether the windmill framework was ever applied to ES-like equations.
why: A direct bridge from the canonical parity proof to ES by an author who knows both problems.
first_step: Read the paper; list the equations handled (x² + ky², etc.) and try its windmill construction on the (★) set or on {(u,B,C) : 4uBC − u − B = p}.

title: Non-vanishing on the line Re s = 1 analogue: a level Dirichlet series that cannot vanish
connection: PNT/Dirichlet need L(1 + it, χ) ≠ 0 via the 3-4-1 positivity trick (Mertens). For fixed p consider F_p(s) = Σ_C D_C(p) C^{−s} (finite sum): ES ⟺ F_p ≢ 0. A '3-4-1'-type positivity combination of F_p, its twists, and F at related p might force non-vanishing.
why: Odd, but 3-4-1 is the archetype of extracting non-vanishing from positivity of a trigonometric polynomial.
first_step: Look for nonnegative trigonometric polynomials in a 'twist' variable (characters mod 4C) such that the combination of twisted level counts is ≥ c·(untwisted total) − (controlled).

title: Chebyshev-type explicit bounds for the certificate-capable prime mass
connection: Chebyshev proved x/log x-type bounds for π(x) by explicit factorial inequalities. Define the 'certificate-capable prime mass' Θ_p(K) = Σ_{q certificate-capable at some C ≤ K} log q and try to prove Chebyshev-type explicit lower bounds for it at fixed p using only CRT structure of Π_C(4Cp + 1).
why: Explicit elementary lower bounds are exactly what turns into 'every p ≥ p₀'.
first_step: Compute Θ_p(K) numerically for hard p and K up to 10⁵; compare with the elementary upper/lower bounds derivable from Π_C (4Cp+1).

title: Two-candidate version: (★) and b=1 as Heath-Brown's 'one of three' with two
connection: Heath-Brown's argument needs three candidates because two can both fail. ES data show (★) and b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸; test whether a third family (e.g. ES₅, small windows) is needed to make a proof-style argument robust, by finding primes where any two of three fail.
why: Determines the minimal number of families an 'at least one works' argument must juggle.
first_step: Compute joint failure sets of (★), b=1, ES₅ and the first-k windows up to 10⁹; report pairs/triples that fail together.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)
upgrade: Artin primitive root conjecture: all but two exceptions

title: Hecke operators on ES counts as functions of n: R(nℓ) vs R(n) for split/inert ℓ
connection: QUE uses Hecke operators T_ℓ acting on eigenfunctions. Define T_ℓ on functions of n by (T_ℓ f)(n) = f(nℓ) + (character)·f(n/ℓ) and test whether R (or f_II) is approximately an eigenfunction of some T_ℓ on Mordell-hard n, with eigenvalue depending on (n/ℓ).
why: An approximate Hecke structure would give the multiplicative relations needed for Soundararajan-type arguments.
first_step: Regress f_II(nℓ) on f_II(n) for n prime and ℓ ≤ 50, separately for (n/ℓ) = ±1.

title: Moments in the level aspect at fixed p: Σ_C |D_C(p) − E_C|² via spectral methods
connection: Subconvexity proofs bound moments of families by spectral decomposition. At fixed p, the family of levels C gives the moment Σ_{C ≤ X} |D_C(p) − E_C|²; express it via sums of Kloosterman sums (Kuznetsov) and bound it pointwise in p.
why: A good level-aspect second moment at fixed p would show the deviations are small for most levels — then a positive proportion of levels with expected positive counts carry certificates.
first_step: Compute the moment numerically for p ~ 10⁸ and compare with Σ E_C (if Var ≈ mean, the moment is Poisson-like).

title: Uniform spectral gap for the 'ES move graph' on residues mod q
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd give uniform expansion of Cayley graphs mod q. Define a graph on (ℤ/q)³ (or on SL₂(ℤ/q)) by ES-preserving moves (change of one word parameter) and test for a uniform spectral gap in q; uniform mixing would give quantitative equidistribution of words mod q with archimedean size control.
why: Uniform-in-q expansion is the input for affine-sieve/Bourgain–Kontorovich-type counting, which is how thin-orbit local-global results are proved.
first_step: Compute the spectral gap of the move graph for primes q ≤ 200 and look for uniformity.

title: Multiplicative energy of divisor classes vs additive shifts N_e = (p + e)/4
connection: Sum-product: sets with small multiplicative energy have large sumsets. The divisor-class multisets of N_e across consecutive windows e (an additive progression in N) — compute their multiplicative energies; ES failure across many windows would force large multiplicative structure (subgroup trapping) along an additive progression.
why: Quantitative version of the sum-product incompatibility item, measurable on data.
first_step: For hard primes, compute E^×(classes of divisors of N_e mod e) for e ≤ 10³ and compare with random integers.

title: Unipotent flows and ES words: the horocycle parametrisation of minus-continuants
connection: Margulis used unipotent orbits. The matrices M(t) = [[t, −1],[1, 0]] are products of a unipotent [[1, t],[0, 1]] and a fixed rotation, so ES words M(u)M(t)M(v) are points on products of horocycle segments. Read ES as a statement about a three-step 'unipotent walk' hitting a target integer matrix.
why: Puts ES words into the language of unipotent dynamics, where every-orbit statements exist.
first_step: Write M(u)M(t)M(v) = n(u) w n(t) w n(v) w and characterise which targets [[p, ·],[·,·]] are reachable with t ∈ 4ℤ; compare with horospherical equidistribution scales.

title: Effective equidistribution scale vs the required cusp depth (quantify the B2 gap)
connection: Every-orbit equidistribution theorems come with effective rates (Strömbergsson, Venkatesh). ES₅/word formulations require hitting regions of measure ≈ (log p)²/p-ish; compute the smallest measure of target region that current effective rates for closed horocycles of length p can resolve.
why: Turns 'B2' into a number in the dynamics language: the exponent gap between the required and available resolution.
first_step: From Strömbergsson's effective rate (Duke Math. J. 123 (2004): subsegments longer than ℓ^{1/2+ε} of a closed horocycle of length ℓ equidistribute; verified), compute the minimal region measure resolvable at length p and compare with the ES₅ target measure.

title: Equidistribution of (−(4p)⁻¹ mod d)/d as d varies: the trial-form sequence
connection: Weyl-type equidistribution of sequences {f(d)} mod 1. In the trial form, R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d | d + 1} with c_d = −(4p)⁻¹ mod d; the normalised residues c_d/d equidistribute in [0,1] as d varies (Kloosterman-type, Hooley/Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec for modular inverses). ES needs the finer event 4c_d | d + 1, i.e. c_d/d near 0 with a divisibility condition.
why: Equidistribution of modular inverses is a proven every-p theorem (for each fixed p as d varies); the certificate event is a thin, arithmetic refinement of it.
first_step: Measure the discrepancy of {c_d/d : d ≤ D} for fixed p, and the hit rate of 4c_d | d + 1 among d with c_d/d < 1/(4·k).

title: Non-lacunary semigroups of levels: multiplicative closure of 'working levels'
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity uses non-lacunarity of {2^a 3^b}. If level C works for p, does level C·k work for p for many k? (If d | 4Cp + 1 with d ≡ −1 mod 4C, then nothing obvious at level Ck.) Study whether the set of working levels for p is close to a multiplicative semigroup.
why: If working levels had semigroup structure, rigidity theorems for multiplicative semigroups could constrain failure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷ compute the set of working levels and test closure under multiplication by small k.
upgrade: Furstenberg x2 x3 (topological every-orbit vs measure)

title: Huang-type degree bound on the 'divisor-class hypercube' for windows with ω(N_e) = k
connection: Huang: any 2^{k−1}+1 vertices of Q_k induce max degree ≥ √k. For N_e squarefree with k prime factors, label each subset S by its class g(S) mod e; ES at window e ⟺ two disjoint subsets with g(S)/g(T) ≡ −1. Bound the largest family of subsets with no such pair; if it is ≤ 2^{k−1}, a signed-hypercube argument forces a certificate whenever 'many' subsets share a structure.
why: A precise extremal question about labelled hypercubes that directly encodes window certificates.
first_step: Compute by brute force, for e ≤ 50 and k ≤ 12 with random labels, the maximum certificate-free subset family size.
refs: arXiv:1907.00847 (Huang, Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture)

title: Fixed-length subproducts: ES with a prescribed number of prime factors in the divisor
connection: Kemnitz/Reiher control zero-sums of prescribed length. Refine ES: is there always a certificate whose divisor d has exactly k prime factors for some small k (e.g. k ≤ 2)? If 'k ≤ 2' holds empirically, ES reduces to a statement about prime pairs (q₁ q₂ ≡ −1 mod 4C) — a zero-sum of length 2.
why: A bounded-length version is much more structured (pairs of primes in classes) and amenable to sieve/character methods.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸, record for each p the minimal Ω(d) over certificates; find primes requiring Ω(d) ≥ 3.

title: Chevalley–Warning for the window system modulo e with a forced trivial solution
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives a nontrivial zero when the number of zeros is ≡ 0 (mod char) and a trivial zero exists. For window e (prime), consider the system over F_e in variables (exponent choices) encoding Π q_i^{ε_i} ≡ −1 · (trivial adjustment); design it so ε = 0 is a solution and the degree condition holds, forcing a nonzero ε.
why: The classical algebraic route from 'many variables relative to degree' to existence; here variables = prime factors of N_e.
first_step: Write the system for e = 3, 7, 11 with k prime factors and compute degree vs variables; find k at which Chevalley–Warning applies.

title: Absorbers from Mordell identities: reserve identity-covered structure to fix square classes
connection: Absorption reserves a structure that can repair any leftover. Mordell identities cover non-square classes; for a hard p, consider auxiliary integers N related to p (e.g. N_e = (p + e)/4, which may lie in easy classes) whose identity-certificates can be 'absorbed' into a certificate for p via the e-slice.
why: Transfers the power of identities (which fail only on square classes) to hard p through an auxiliary object.
first_step: For hard p, compute which N_e lie in identity-covered classes and whether their identity certificates translate into window certificates for p.
upgrade: Erdos-Faber-Lovasz / Ringel / Ryser-Brualdi-Stein (all large n via absorption)

title: Approximate-group structure of failing divisor-class sets
connection: PFR says sets with small doubling are close to subgroups (cosets). If at many levels the divisor-class sets of 4Cp + 1 have small doubling (as they would if trapped in subgroups avoiding −1), PFR-type structure theorems identify the subgroups; ES failure ⇒ many approximate subgroups ⇒ contradiction with CRT independence.
why: Structure theorems turn 'avoidance' into explicit algebraic objects that can be compared across levels.
first_step: Compute doubling constants |A·A|/|A| of divisor-class sets for hard p at levels C ≤ 200.
refs: arXiv:2311.05762 (Gowers-Green-Manners-Tao, On a conjecture of Marton)

title: Distinct-denominator and ordering refinements as stronger every-n statements
connection: Breusch/Stewart required distinct denominators of a given parity. ES refinements: x < y < z distinct (automatic except special cases), x ≤ p/2, z ≤ p²/2, gcd conditions. Determine the strongest refinement that still holds for all p ≤ 10⁹; it defines the 'tightest' every-p target.
why: The tightest true statement carries the most structure for a proof and the most information for disproof searches.
first_step: Tabulate, for p ≤ 10⁹, the minimal max-denominator over solutions normalised by p², and other extremal statistics.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201

title: Odd greedy algorithm as a cautionary every-n problem
connection: The odd greedy expansion (always choose the smallest odd denominator) is conjectured to terminate for every rational with odd denominator, but this is open even though Breusch/Stewart show odd representations exist. ES has the same split: existence vs a specific algorithm. Keep proofs about existence, not about a fixed procedure (consistent with B1's bounded-procedure barrier).
why: Prevents investing in 'prove algorithm X always succeeds' routes that are harder than existence.
first_step: List ES approaches in the repo that are algorithmic (fixed search order) and mark which could be restated as pure existence.

title: Sun-style refinements as data: four-square-like refinements of ES
connection: Sun formulated many 'refined Lagrange' conjectures by computer search; several were proved. Generate ES refinements automatically (x + y or z constrained to be a square, a prime, ≡ r mod m, etc.), test them to 10⁷, and keep those that never fail — new conjectures whose extra structure may make them provable or reveal hidden symmetries.
why: Automated conjecture generation found provable statements for sums of squares; ES has never been mined this way systematically (check repo).
first_step: Write a search over ~200 refinement predicates P(x, y, z, p) and test on all p ≤ 10⁶; report survivors.
refs: arXiv:2003.02592 (Machiavelo-Tsopanidis, Zhi-Wei Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture and variations)

title: Distribution of R(p) modulo small primes ℓ (Ono-style equidistribution vs bias)
connection: Ono/Ahlgren studied p(n) modulo m: every residue class occurs. For ES, study R(p)/2 mod ℓ: equidistribution would be 'no structure', while a bias toward nonzero residues on some class would be a usable congruence. In particular check whether R(p)/2 ≡ 0 (mod ℓ) occurs with frequency ≈ 1/ℓ.
why: Cheap probe for hidden modular structure in the counts.
first_step: Compute the distribution of R(p)/2 mod 2, 3, 5, 7 over primes in each Mordell-hard class up to 10⁷.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)
upgrade: Partition congruences for every prime modulus

title: Sperner/Tucker on the level × divisor grid
connection: Sperner's lemma forces a fully-labelled cell in any boundary-respecting labelling. Lay out levels C (one axis) and divisor sizes log d / log N (other axis); label grid cells by the class of the divisor relative to −1 (mod 4C); boundary conditions come from trivial divisors (1 and N always in class 1). A fully-labelled cell would be a certificate.
why: Odd, but Sperner-type lemmas give existence from boundary data alone.
first_step: Construct the labelled grid for small p and check whether natural boundary conditions hold and what a fully-labelled cell means.

title: Recursive product constructions: certificates for p from certificates for pieces of 4Cp + 1
connection: Bose–Shrikhande–Parker built orthogonal Latin squares of composite orders from smaller ones. For ES, 4Cp + 1 = N₁N₂ (coprime): if N₁ has a divisor ≡ a (mod 4C) and N₂ one ≡ b with ab ≡ −1, the product is a certificate. Study 'recursive' constructions splitting N and combining class information from each piece.
why: Product constructions are the combinatorial counterpart of the Kneser/product-set items, with an explicit recursive structure.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate coprime splittings of 4Cp + 1 and compute the class sets of divisors of each piece; count combinations giving −1.
upgrade: Euler's 36 officers: orthogonal Latin squares for every n != 2, 6

title: Periodicity of certificate patterns along n = a·b^s + c (p-adic interpolation), automated
connection: SML's p-adic interpolation implies periodic structure of divisibility along exponential sequences. Automate: for each open exponential family in the repo and each small certificate shape (C, d-class), compute the set of s where it applies (periodic mod ord_d(b)); solve the resulting covering problem over s with an ILP.
why: Mechanises the repo's family proofs and either proves open families or identifies a residual progression of s as a disproof candidate.
first_step: Implement for 15·2^s + 1 and 4^s + 297 with d ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 10³.

title: Surgery on near-certificates: local modifications that remove a single obstruction
connection: Perelman's surgery removes singularities and continues the flow. For a near-certificate at level C (a divisor d of 4Cp + 1 in a class ≠ −1), define 'surgeries' changing one prime factor (moving to another level C′ sharing that factor via CRT) and study whether repeated surgery reaches a certificate.
why: Gives a local-move graph on near-certificates across levels, linked by shared prime factors.
first_step: Build the graph (nodes: (C, d); edges: share a prime factor q, C ≡ C′ (mod q)) for small p and search paths to certificates.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Current-graph-style explicit constructions for one residue class mod a large modulus
connection: Ringel–Youngs used 'current graphs' — compact algebraic data generating a whole family. For one Mordell-hard class r mod M (M large, e.g. 840·1001), search for compact algebraic data (a finite list of certificate templates with parameters depending on p's residues mod M′) covering all primes in that class up to 10⁹.
why: Even if B1 forbids bounded templates for all p, the minimal template count per class reveals growth rates and hidden structure.
first_step: Run a greedy set-cover of primes in the class by parametric templates (Type II with C | M′) and plot template count vs X.

title: Landau–Siegel 'at most one exceptional modulus' analogue for ES levels
connection: Landau: at most one real character mod q ≤ Q has L(1,χ) tiny. ES analogue: among the characters χ_{−4uB} driving M_BM, show at most one (or boundedly many) can be 'exceptional' at p (strongly biased), so M_BM stays large except via one identifiable character whose effect can be handled separately.
why: The 'at most one exception' structure is what makes Siegel-type arguments work; ES's main term is a sum over many real characters.
first_step: Model T(p) as a sum over real characters and quantify how much a single character can reduce M_BM; compare with the observed minima of M_BM/L².
upgrade: Siegel's theorem (average class numbers -> individual lower bound)

title: Polynomial congruence certificate: an identity in ℤ[X]/(X^r − 1, p) detecting ES
connection: AKS used a polynomial congruence that holds iff n is prime. Ask whether ES(p) has a characterisation by a polynomial identity modulo (X^r − 1, p) or modulo auxiliary moduli (e.g. a product over levels of polynomials whose evaluation detects certificates), testable deterministically.
why: Odd: algebraic characterisations sometimes admit clean counting proofs (as in AKS's group-size argument).
first_step: Construct the generating polynomial P_p(X) = Π_{C ≤ K} (1 − X^{[level C fails]}) style objects and look for algebraic relations they satisfy for all p.
upgrade: PRIMES is in P (randomized / conditional -> deterministic unconditional)

title: Thin-semigroup local-global with the ES constraint t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p): local obstructions?
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich require knowing the local (congruence) obstructions of the semigroup before counting. Compute the reductions mod q of the ES-word set with the constraint on t (4ℤ for one branch, 8ℤ − p for the other, which depends on p!) and determine exactly which residues of p are locally admissible; check that only squares-related obstructions appear (T1-type).
why: The p-dependent constraint (8ℤ − p) is unusual for thin-orbit theory; its local analysis is a concrete, finite task.
first_step: For q ≤ 200 compute the set of p mod q (and mod 8q) hit by words with each constraint branch.

title: Strong approximation mod p for the ES surface fibre U_p (BGS-style) — sanity check
connection: BGS proved Markoff surfaces satisfy strong approximation mod p for most p. For ES, check the analogous local statement: does U_n(ℤ) → U_n(ℤ/q) have dense image for various q (it is BM-obstructed for strong approximation by BL)? Quantify the BL obstruction concretely on data.
why: Makes BL's 'BM obstruction to strong approximation always exists' concrete and shows which residue patterns ES solutions avoid.
first_step: For small n with many solutions, compute the reductions of solutions mod q and compare with U_n(ℤ/q).
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Erdős–Vaaler-type restricted versions: ES with levels restricted to squarefree or prime C
connection: Before Duffin–Schaeffer was proved in general, restricted cases (ψ supported on special sets) were proved first. Restrict ES (★) to prime levels C (or squarefree C): the overlap structure simplifies (gcd(C, C′) = 1). Study the prime-level-only (★) failure set and its overlap model.
why: Restricted versions with clean overlap structure are the natural first targets of a Duffin–Schaeffer-type method.
first_step: Compute (★) restricted to prime C for p ≤ 10⁹ and list failures; fit an independence model.

title: Divisor sum over shifted primes reversed: Σ_{q prime} 1[q | p + m] for structured m
connection: The Titchmarsh divisor problem counts divisors of shifted primes. The trial form needs prime (or general) divisors of p + u in the class −1 mod (stuff tied to u); reverse the roles: for fixed p, count primes q ≡ 3 (4) with q | p + u and q = 4uC − 1 for some C — a 'Titchmarsh problem with a tied modulus' at a single p.
why: Relates single-prime certificates to the distribution of prime divisors of p + u, a classical object.
first_step: Count, for fixed p, pairs (u, q) with q | p + u, q ≡ −1 (mod 4u), q prime; compare with heuristic Σ_u τ*/φ(4u).

title: Siegel–Weil for indefinite ternary forms with congruence: ES's SL₂ quadric
connection: For indefinite forms in ≥ 3 variables representing a number, Siegel–Weil and strong approximation (spin groups) give local-global with spinor exceptions. The SL₂ form ad − pc = 1 is an indefinite ternary quadric; the ES congruence a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c) is not a lattice coset condition (modulus = coordinate), so classical theory does not apply directly. Find a reformulation where the congruence becomes a fixed-modulus coset condition.
why: If achieved, strong approximation for spin groups (no spinor obstruction ⇒ every locally represented integer is represented) would be the closing theorem.
first_step: Try substitutions a = ck − 1, d = cl − 1 and fix c's residue class; examine whether the resulting variety in (k, l, c) is homogeneous for a group with strong approximation.
upgrade: Tartakowsky / Kloosterman: quadratic forms in >= 4-5 variables

title: No minor arcs: positivity lets ES discard all but the smallest levels
connection: Goldbach-type proofs must bound minor arcs because terms cancel. ES counts are sums of nonnegative level counts, R(p) = Σ_C D_C(p) ≥ Σ_{C ≤ K} D_C(p); so ES ⟸ a certificate among levels C ≤ K = (log p)^A, where the expected count is still ≍ (log p)·(log K) → ∞. The whole problem is a lower bound for a short, explicit 'major-level' sum.
why: Reframes which part of the analytic machinery is needed: only lower bounds on a few explicit structured counts, no cancellation estimates for the bulk.
first_step: For p in the hard lists, find the least K(p) such that some level ≤ K(p) carries a certificate, and fit K(p) against (log p)^A.

title: Baseline: a single level already gives density one
connection: Level C = 1 works for p iff 4p + 1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) (it then automatically has two, so both cofactors are ≥ 3); the primes p for which 4p + 1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) have density zero (≍ X/(log X)^{3/2}). So 'almost all p' is cheap; all information sits in how fast the exceptional set of K levels decays.
why: A sanity baseline for every almost-all statement in this list: improvements must be measured in exceptional-set decay, not in 'density one'.
first_step: Compute the counting function of primes failing all levels C ≤ K for K = 1..10 up to 10⁹ and fit X/(log X)^{α_K}; compare α_K with Σ_{C≤K} δ_C from Landau–Ramanujan-type densities.

title: Sieve of growing dimension: when do the thin sets S_C (C ≤ K) exhaust all primes?
connection: Failing levels 1..K means 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K, an intersection of thin multiplicative sets of total 'dimension' Σ_{C≤K} δ_C. Upper-bound sieves for such intersections are standard for fixed K; ES needs K growing with p until the expected number of survivors near X is < 1 — a sieve problem of growing dimension.
why: Puts the ES exceptional-set question in the language of high-dimensional sieves (Diamond–Halberstam–Richert), where the dependence on dimension is explicit.
first_step: Compute Σ_{C≤K} δ_C as a function of K and the K(X) at which X·(log X)^{−Σδ} < 1; compare with the observed least K(p).

title: Pretentious distance D((·/p), 1; y) as the controlling statistic for ES difficulty
connection: Tao's EDP and Granville–Soundararajan's pretentious theory organise multiplicative functions by their distance to characters. The BM main term (via T(p)) and the least non-residue are governed by how much the Legendre symbol (·/p) 'pretends' to be 1 on small primes. Test whether all ES sub-route difficulty is a function of D((·/p), 1; y) for suitable y.
why: If one pretentious distance controls difficulty, the problem reduces to the 'pretentious case' (p a QR mod many small primes), where structure is strongest.
first_step: Compute D² = Σ_{ℓ ≤ y} (1 − (ℓ/p))/ℓ for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p)/M₀(p), least certificate C, and sub-route failures.

title: Affine-sieve strengthening: certificates with prime or almost-prime parameters
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak's affine sieve produces almost-primes in orbits once expansion is known. Ask whether every p has a (★) certificate with u, B (or 4uC − 1, 4BC − 1) prime or with ≤ r prime factors; if true numerically, sieve methods on the word set apply and the strengthened statement has more structure.
why: Strengthenings with prime parameters connect ES to the affine-sieve toolkit and to Chen-type almost-prime results.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least r such that a certificate with Ω(4uC − 1) ≤ r and Ω(4BC − 1) ≤ r exists; find primes needing large r.

title: Supersingular points and maximal orders: ≈ p/12 objects attached to every p
connection: Every prime p has ≈ p/12 supersingular j-invariants, in bijection (Deuring) with maximal-order types of the quaternion algebra ramified at p and ∞. These always exist, like Elkies's CM values; map them (or their small-norm elements, Eichler orientations) to ES certificate data.
why: Supplies power-many canonical objects for every p; if any natural map lands in certificates with positive probability, existence follows from their number.
first_step: Read the repo's supersingular/Eichler memos; for small p compute the maximal orders' reduced norms forms and test whether ES certificates appear as small vectors.
upgrade: Elkies: every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many supersingular primes

title: ES over imaginary quadratic rings (ℤ[i], ℤ[ω]): does unit freedom make it easy?
connection: Potential-automorphy-style arguments work over extensions first. For ES over O_K (K imaginary quadratic), 4/π = 1/ξ + 1/η + 1/ζ with ξ, η, ζ ∈ O_K and no positivity (no real place): the extra units and the lack of positivity might allow identity-based proofs for every prime π. Determine what makes ℤ-ES hard (positivity at the real place? the square classes?) by seeing which ring versions are easy.
why: Isolating the role of the archimedean positivity constraint tells whether the difficulty is archimedean or arithmetic.
first_step: Search the literature ('Erdős–Straus number field', 'Gaussian integers Egyptian fractions'); experimentally find identities for 4/π over ℤ[i] covering all Gaussian primes up to norm 10⁶.
refs: Barnet-Lamb-Geraghty-Harris-Taylor, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011) 29-98 (A family of Calabi-Yau varieties and potential automorphy II)

title: Large deviations of Euclid's algorithm at a fixed denominator (Hensley, Baladi–Vallée)
connection: The CF length of a/p, a mod p, is asymptotically Gaussian with mean ≍ log p (Heilbronn, Hensley, Baladi–Vallée via transfer operators, with power-saving errors for fixed denominators). ES₅ (λ(p) ≤ 3) asks for an extreme left-tail event (length 3, prescribed shape). Large-deviation estimates for fixed p from the dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm would give lower bounds in exactly this quantifier order.
why: The dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm is 'every p' by construction (it averages over a, not p); the question is how far into the tail its estimates reach.
first_step: Read Baladi–Vallée ('Euclidean algorithms are Gaussian', J. Number Theory 2005; check) for fixed-denominator large-deviation statements and the error terms; compare the reachable tail with length-3 events (count ≍ log²p out of p).

title: Why do Markoff-type surfaces have infinitely many integral Hasse failures, and does ES escape the mechanism?
connection: Ghosh–Sarnak: the integral Hasse principle for x² + y² + z² − xyz = k holds for almost all k but fails for infinitely many, via reduction theory of the Vieta-group action (all orbit representatives in a fundamental set excluded by congruences). ES shares the (log)²-scale counts and BM picture (FRONTIER §2.4 caution) but has no group action. Pin down whether 'no group action' removes the failure mechanism or merely hides it.
why: The closest precedent for an almost-all statement that is false for infinitely many cases; understanding why ES differs is mandatory hygiene.
first_step: Read Ghosh–Sarnak §§4–6 and extract the failure construction; try to replicate it for ES with a 'reduction theory' given by the smallest denominator x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4) or by minimal certificate parameters.
refs: arXiv:1706.06712 (Ghosh-Sarnak, Integral points on Markoff type cubic surfaces, Invent. Math. 229 (2022))
